Chapter One — The Key

Before You Read

Five words you will need from the first page:

die Warnung — warning

bereit — ready

der Koffer — suitcase

der Flughafen — airport

wütend — angry

Try to catch them in context before checking the full list at the end.

The Flugzeug landed twelve minutes early.

That should have been my first Warnung. Nothing in my life had ever been early. Not my Geburt — I came out screaming two weeks late, according to my Großmutter — not my flights, not my Gefühle. But Berlin wanted me to arrive before I was bereit.

I grabbed my Koffer. One bag. I had learned to travel like I had learned to love: leicht enough to leave fast. No photos, no gifts, no souvenirs that would break in my Rucksack. Just clothes, a phone charger, and a Reisepass with more stamps than I deserved.

The Flughafen was quiet for a Tuesday afternoon. A few families hugged at the Ankunftsbereich. A woman cried into her phone. A man in a too-thin coat leaned against a pillar, scrolling through his phone like he had all the Zeit in the world.

He was the one who called my name.

"Yves!"

I turned.

The man from the pillar. He wasn't tall. He wasn't smiling. His coat was grau, his hair was dunkel, and his eyes were the colour of the February sky outside — grey, but warm in a way that made me wütend. Why was he warm? I didn't know him.

"You're Matei," I said.

"You're late," he said.

I looked at the clock. "The plane was early. That's the opposite of late."

He didn't lachen. "My train was late."

"So we're both enttäuscht."

He almost smiled. Fast. The corner of his mouth twitched like he had caught himself. Then he picked up my Koffer without asking — didn't even look at me for permission — and walked toward the Ausgang.

I followed.

That's how it started. Me following a man who didn't ask permission.

Outside, Berlin was grau and kalt and exactly as unforgiving as I needed it to be.

The Wind cut through my jacket like it had something to prove. I had been in cold weather before — Lagos could get chilly in December, if you squinted — but this was different. This was cold that wanted you to know you were a Gast here.

"Do you like it?" Matei asked. He was already three steps ahead of me, my Koffer rolling behind him like a loyal dog.

"I don't know yet."

"You will."

He said it like a Tatsache. Not a hope. A Tatsache. Like he had decided my opinion for me and was just waiting for me to catch up. I wanted to be annoyed. I was annoyed. But also — and I hated this — I wanted to believe him.

We took the Bus. He paid for my ticket without asking. I opened my mouth to protest, but he just looked at me and said, "You don't have Euro yet." He was right. I closed my mouth.

We sat in the back, away from the other passengers. The Bus was almost leer. An old woman with a shopping cart. A teenager with headphones so large they looked like ear muffs. And us.

He smelled like Kaffee and cold smoke — the good kind, not cigarette smoke but something woodier, like a Kamin that had just been put out. It reminded me of someone I had never met. A person I had erfunden in my head when I was younger. Someone who would hold me without explanation.

"Why are you here?" Matei asked. Not looking at me. Looking out the window at the grey buildings sliding past.

I could have gelogen. I was good at lying. I had spent years telling my Großmutter I was fein, telling my coworkers I was glücklich, telling myself I wasn't running away. I had a whole catalogue of polite Lügen prepared. For work. To see the city. A fresh start. All true enough to pass.

But I was müde. And his eyes — when he finally turned to look at me — were warm.

"I wanted to leave."

"Leave from where?"

"Home."

He didn't say I'm sorry or that's sad or any of the things people say when they don't know what else to say. He just put his hand on mine. His hand was warm too.

We stayed like that for the rest of the Fahrt. Neither of us spoke. Neither of us pulled away. Outside, the city changed from airport glass to apartment blocks to old buildings with stories written in their cracked Putz. I watched it all through the window, but I didn't see any of it. I was too aware of his fingers against mine.

When we got off the Bus, he let go. He didn't sich entschuldigen. He just pointed at a building across the street — five storeys, faded yellow paint, a door that had been painted over so many times it looked like a geology experiment. Bicycles chained to a railing. A bakery on the ground floor, closed for the night.

"That's my Wohnung," he said. "You sleep on the Sofa."

I looked at the building. Then at him.

"Only for one night."

"Only for one night," he agreed.

We both knew that was a Lüge. I don't know how I knew. Maybe it was the way he said it — too fast, like he was trying to convince himself. Maybe it was the way I didn't argue. But something in the air between us had already decided that one night wasn't going to be enough.

The stairs were eng and knarrten like they remembered every person who had ever climbed them.

His Wohnung was on the fourth floor. No Aufzug. By the time we got to his door, I was out of breath and he wasn't even sweating. Angeber.

He unlocked the door. Pushed it open. Stepped aside to let me in first.

The Wohnung was klein. That's the kindest thing I can say about it. One room that was supposed to be the living room, bedroom, and dining room all at once. A tiny kitchen in the corner, separated by a Theke with two stools. A door that I assumed led to a Badezimmer. One window that faced the street. One Lampe on a table that wobbled if you breathed on it. Two mismatched chairs — one wooden, one plastic. And a Sofa that had seen better decades. The fabric was worn thin in places, and one of the cushions had a dark Fleck that I decided not to investigate.

"It's not much," Matei said. He set my Koffer by the door and stood in the middle of the room with his hands in his pockets. For the first time, he looked nervös. Not scared — Matei didn't seem like the kind of person who got scared — but uncertain. Like he was waiting for me to judge him.

"It's enough."

He nodded. Some of the Anspannung left his shoulders.

I walked around the room, pretending to look at things. A Bücherregal crammed with paperbacks in German, Romanian, English. A Kalender on the wall with a photo of the Alps. A small stereo on the floor next to a stack of CDs — old ones, the kind I hadn't seen since I was a kid. I spotted a Frank Ocean album and felt something loosen in my chest.

"You like Frank Ocean?"

He looked at the CD like he had forgotten it was there. "He's okay."

"You have the album. That's more than 'okay.'"

"My Ex left it." Flat. No emotion. But his jaw tightened for just a second.

I decided not to ask about the Ex. Not yet. Maybe not ever.

He went into the kitchen — if you could call it that. I heard water running. Cabinet doors opening and closing. The sound of a mug being set on the counter. Then he came back. He was holding a Schlüssel.

It was small. Silver. Ordinary. The kind of key that opens a door you don't think about twice.

"Here," he said, and handed it to me.

I took it.

The metal was warm — from his pocket, from his hand, from whatever strange Schwerkraft he carried. I turned it over in my palm. It was still just a key. But it felt schwerer than it should have.

"For the door?"

He looked at me. Really looked. Like he was trying to decide if I was worth the Risiko. His grey eyes held mine for a long moment. The Lampe flickered. The street outside was quiet.

"For you," he said.

I didn't know what that meant. A key for me? For me to keep? For me to come back? He didn't explain. He just turned around and walked back to the kitchen, leaving me standing there with a warm key in my hand and a thousand Fragen I was too tired to ask.

I sat on the Sofa. The cushion sank lower than I expected. The fabric was scratchy against my neck. But it was soft in the middle, where someone had clearly spent a lot of nights. I wondered if that someone was Matei. Or the Ex. Or someone before the Ex.

He came back with two mugs of tea. Black tea, no sugar, no milk. He handed me one without asking how I took it. I took a sip. It was perfekt. I hated that it was perfekt.

"How do you know how I drink tea?"

"You told me. Two years ago. In a Nachricht."

I scrolled through my memory. Two years ago. We had been talking online — I had almost forgotten. Late nights, time zones, confessions that felt safe because they weren't real. I must have mentioned it. A throwaway line. And he remembered.

"That was two years ago."

"I remember things." He sat on the wooden chair across from me, his mug cradled in both hands. Dampf rose between us.

"That's creepy."

"That's accurate."

I laughed. I hadn't expected to laugh. But something about him — his deadpan delivery, the way he didn't try to be charming — caught me off guard.

"You laugh," he said. "Good."

"Why is that good?"

He shrugged. "You seemed sad at the Flughafen."

I didn't know what to say to that. Because he was right. I was sad. I had been sad for years. I had gotten good at hiding it — smiling when people expected it, saying the right things, being the version of myself that was easy to be around. But he saw through it in the first ten minutes.

"I'm not sad."

"Okay." He didn't push. He just drank his tea.

We sat in silence for a while. The Lampe buzzed softly. The Heizung clicked. Somewhere downstairs, someone was playing music — something slow, maybe Frank Ocean again, or someone who sounded like him. The city outside was dark now. I could see a sliver of the sky through the window. No stars. Berlin didn't seem like a city that showed its stars.

"You can take the bed," Matei said eventually.

"You said I sleep on the Sofa."

"I changed my mind."

"Why?"

He set his mug down. Looked at me. "You're müde. The Sofa is old. Take the bed."

I should have argued. I was a guest — barely even that, a stranger he had invited into his home because of messages sent two years ago. But my body was heavy, and the bed was right there, and his voice was low in a way that didn't invite negotiation.

"Okay. Danke."

He nodded. Stood up. Walked to the closet and pulled out a clean Laken and a Decke. He made the bed — not neatly, but carefully, like he was doing something he had done a thousand times for someone else. When he was done, he stepped back.

"Gute Nacht Nacht, Yves."

"Gute Nacht Nacht, Matei."

He went to the Sofa. I went to the bed. The sheets smelled like laundry detergent and something else — something I couldn't name. I lay there in the dark, listening to him settle onto the old cushions. The Sofa creaked. He sighed. Then silence.

I held the Schlüssel he had given me.

The metal had cooled now. But I could still feel the Wärme of his hand in it.

That's how I ended up with a key to a city I had never seen, a man I didn't understand, and a story I hadn't agreed to be in.

Typical.

Grammar Spotlight

From this chapter: "I could still feel the Wärme of his hand in it."

In German, when in means "inside/within," it takes the dative case.

Examples from the chapter:

English German (dative)

in his pocket in seiner Tasche

in the dark im Dunkeln (in dem)

with me mit mir

from his hand von seiner Hand

in a message in einer Nachricht

Why this matters: You don't need to memorize declension tables. You will see im (in dem), vom (von dem), zum (zu dem) hundreds of times in this book. Your brain will learn the pattern naturally — through the story.

Key pattern from this chapter: "in seiner Wohnung" (in his apartment) — the possessive sein takes -er for feminine dative. You don't need to know that now. You just need to see it.

Writing Prompt

Write three sentences from Matei's perspective as he waits at the airport. Use at least two German words from this chapter. Don't aim for perfect German — aim for honest Matei.

Or: Yves has been in Berlin for one week. He texts his grandmother. What does he say — and what does he not say?

Shadowing Script

Read this exchange aloud, then again louder. Try to match the rhythm — Matei's lines are short and flat; Yves's land harder.

Matei: You're late.

Yves: The plane was early. That's the opposite of late.

Matei: My train was late.

Yves: So we're both enttaeuscht.

Notice: enttaeuscht falls at the end of Yves's line and carries the stress. Say it like it costs something.

Chapter Two — The First Morning

Before You Read

Six words for this chapter:

schlafen — to sleep

die Zukunft — future

der Chirurg — surgeon

entspannt — relaxed

bewusst — deliberate / conscious

ueberdenken — to overthink

Notice: ueberdenken is a separable verb. Watch for the prefix at the end of sentences.

I didn't schlafen.

Not because the bed was uncomfortable — it was actually better than any bed I had slept in for the last six Monate. Not because of the Jetlag — my body had given up on time zones somewhere over the Atlantic. I didn't schlafen because I could hear Matei atmen on the Sofa.

It was a quiet sound. Stetig. The kind of breathing that said I have no problem falling asleep anywhere, anytime, because I am a normal person who doesn't überdenken everything. I hated him for it. I also wanted to lie on the floor next to the Sofa and listen to it all night, which was a much bigger Problem.

Around 3 Uhr morgens, I gave up pretending. I stared at the Decke. The building made noises — pipes groaning, floorboards settling, someone upstairs walking to their Badezimmer in the Dunkeln. Berlin sounds. Not the sounds of Lagos, where the night was never really quiet — always a generator, always a car alarm, always someone's television bleeding through the wall. Here, the silence was so loud it felt like Druck.

I thought about the Schlüssel. It was on the table next to the Lampe. I could see its shape in the dim light. For you, he had said. What did that even mean? People didn't just give you keys. Keys were for something. A door, a locker, a city. A Zukunft.

I closed my eyes and tried to remember his face at the Flughafen. The way he had said my name. The way he had picked up my Koffer without asking.

I must have fallen asleep eventually, because the next thing I knew, light was hitting my face through the window, and I could smell Kaffee.

Matei was in the kitchen.

His back was to me. He wore the same graues shirt from yesterday — or maybe a different grey shirt, I couldn't tell — and he was pouring water into a French Press with the concentration of a Chirurg.

I watched him for a minute before I said anything. His shoulders were entspannt. His hair was messier than it had been at the Flughafen, like he had run his hands through it a few times. He moved slowly, bewusst, like he had done this a thousand mornings and would do it a thousand more.

"You're staring," he said without turning around.

"I'm observing. There's a Unterschied."

He turned. His grey eyes found mine.

"What's the difference?"

"Staring is creepy. Observing is wissenschaftlich."

He almost smiled again. Almost.

"And which one is this?"

"Scientific. Definitely scientific. I'm collecting Daten."

"What data?"

I sat up. The Laken fell to my waist. I was still wearing the clothes I had traveled in — jeans, a black sweater, socks that had lost their partner somewhere over the Sahara. I probably looked like a Katastrophe. He didn't seem to notice.

"Data on how Berliners make coffee. For my Forschung."

"Your research."

"I'm a student of Kultur."

He snorted. Actually snorted. It was the first undignified sound I had heard him make.

"You're a student of avoiding questions."

"Same thing."

He poured the coffee into two mugs — plain white ceramic, no logos, no sentimental messages. He handed me one. Black. No sugar. No milk. Perfekt again.

"You remembered."

"I told you. I remember things."

I took a sip. It was strong. Bitter. Exactly how I liked it. The heat spread through my chest and woke up parts of my brain that had been winterruhend.

"So. What's the Plan?"

"Plan?"

"For today. For the week. For me not sleeping on your Sofa forever."

He sat on the wooden chair across from me. The plastic one was still empty. He held his mug in both hands, staring into it like it contained Antworten to questions he hadn't asked yet.

"You need a Job."

"I need a lot of things."

"A job first. Geld. Then you can find your own place."

I nodded. That was logisch. Practical. The kind of thing a normal person would say. But something about the way he said it — your own place — made my stomach clench. Like he was already planen for me to leave.

"I didn't come here to be a Last."

"You're not."

"I'm sleeping on your Sofa."

"You're sleeping on my Sofa because I offered. That's not a burden. That's a Wahl."

I wanted to argue. I wanted to say you don't even know me and why are you being nice and what do you want from me. But I didn't. Because I was afraid of the Antworten.

Instead, I said, "What kind of job?"

He shrugged. "There's a Café around the corner. The owner is old. She needs help in the mornings."

"I don't speak Deutsch."

"You don't need to. You just need to carry plates and say bitte and danke. You can learn the rest."

I stared at him.

"You already asked her."

He didn't confirm or deny. He just drank his coffee.

"Matei."

"What?"

"You already asked her, didn't you?"

He set his mug down. Met my eyes.

"She needs someone starting tomorrow. I told her I knew a person."

"You told her before I even arrived."

"I was optimistisch."

I laughed. I couldn't help it. The Absurdität of it — this man I had only talked to online, who I had met in person less than twelve hours ago, who had already arranged a job for me in a city I had never seen — was too much.

"You're verrückt."

"Probably."

"What if I had said no?"

"You didn't."

"What if I'm terrible at carrying plates?"

"Then you learn to be less terrible."

"What if I drop everything and she hates me?"

He stood up. Walked to the kitchen. Rinsed his mug in the sink. When he came back, he was holding a piece of Papier — a handwritten note with an Adresse and a time.

"Tomorrow. Nine AM. Don't be late."

I took the Papier. His handwriting was small and neat, the kind of handwriting that belonged to someone who thought before they wrote.

"You really don't know me," I said leise.

He looked at me for a long moment. Then he said something I would replay in my head for weeks.

"I know you drink your coffee black. I know you laugh when you're uncomfortable. I know you left home because staying hurt more than leaving. And I know you're still here, on my Sofa, even though you could have gone anywhere."

He paused.

"That's enough to start."

I didn't have an Antwort. So I just held the Papier and watched him put on his coat.

"Where are you going?"

"Work. I'll be back at sechs."

"You work on Saturdays?"

"I work most days."

He grabbed his keys from a hook by the door. Not the key he had given me — a different one, smaller, for his own Schloss. He paused with his hand on the door.

"The Café is called Morgenlicht. Morning Light. Tell the owner Matei sent you."

"What if she asks who I am?"

He opened the door. The cold air from the hallway rushed in.

"Tell her you're the friend I mentioned."

Then he was gone. The door clicked shut. I sat there in the grey morning light, holding a job offer from a man who called me a friend after knowing me for twelve hours.

I drank my coffee. It was cold now. I drank it anyway.

The Wohnung felt different without him. Bigger. Leerer. The silence wasn't peaceful anymore — it was just silence. I could hear the Heizung clicking, the fridge humming, the street below coming to life. A woman called to her dog. A bicycle bell rang. Someone laughed.

I looked at the Schlüssel on the table. For you.

I picked it up. Walked to the door. Schloss it from the inside. Schloss Auf Wiedersehen. Locked it again. The mechanism was old — it stuck a little, required a gentle tug to turn all the way. I memorized the feel of it.

Then I went back to the Sofa, lay down, and stared at the ceiling until the morning became Nachmittag.

At noon, I finally got up.

I took a Dusche. The water pressure was terrible — a weak stream that took forever to rinse the shampoo out of my hair — but the water was hot, and the Badezimmer smelled like Matei's Seife. Something clean and neutral. Not floral, not musk. Just clean.

I put on fresh clothes. The same jeans. A different sweater — dark green this time, because I had packed like a person who only owned dark colours. I looked at myself in the Spiegel over the sink. Dark circles under my eyes. Hair still wet. Haut that hadn't seen the sun in months.

You're the friend I mentioned.

I didn't feel like a friend. I felt like a stranger who had wandered into someone else's life and didn't know how to leave.

I left the Wohnung anyway.

The stairs were narrower in the Tageslicht. The walls were covered in old posters — concerts from the 1990s, a faded ad for a bakery that no longer existed, a handwritten sign asking tenants to please close the door quietly. I walked down slowly, counting the steps. Siebenunddreißig from the fourth floor to the ground. I didn't know why I counted. It just felt like information I might need later.

The street was different at noon. Brighter. Lauter. People walked past with shopping bags and bicycles and children holding their hands. A man sold Brezeln from a cart on the corner. The bakery on the ground floor was open now — I could see pastries in the window, a woman behind the counter with grey hair and kind eyes.

I almost went in. But I didn't have Euro yet. And I didn't know the word for pastry.

Morgenlicht. Morning Light.

I found the Adresse on the Papier. It was three blocks away, down a street with trees and benches and a small playground where a toddler was screaming with Freude. The Café was small — smaller than Matei's Wohnung, somehow — with a green awning and chalkboard signs advertising coffee and Kuchen.

I stood across the street and looked at it.

Tomorrow at nine. I would be here. Carrying plates. Saying bitte and danke and probably dropping things.

I should have been nervös. I was nervös. But underneath the nervousness, there was something else. Something that felt like the moment before a song drops — that breathless, electric second when you know something is about to change.

I pulled out my phone. No messages. No missed calls. No one had tried to reach me since I left. My Großmutter, probably, but she didn't know how to text. My coworkers, maybe, but I hadn't given them my new number. The people I had left behind — they were behind me now. Physisch. Emotionally. Whatever.

I opened my messages. The last conversation was with Matei, from two years ago. Before I had decided to come. Before I had bought the ticket. Before any of this was real.

Matei (two years ago): If you ever come to Berlin, I have a Sofa.

Me: That's a dangerous offer.

Matei: I'm not dangerous.

Me: Everyone says that.

Matei: I mean it.

I had thought he was flirting. Or being polite. Or both. I hadn't thought he actually meant come tomorrow, I'll have a key and a job waiting.

I looked up at the Café again. Morgenlicht.

Morning Light.

Maybe that was what this was. Not a fresh start — I didn't believe in those. But Licht, at least. A little bit of it. Enough to see where I was going.

I walked back to the Wohnung. Counted the steps again. Siebenunddreißig. Unlocked the door — the Schlüssel worked, of course it worked — and let myself in.

The Wohnung was still empty. Still quiet. But I had been outside. I had seen the street. I had found the Café. I had taken one step toward the life Matei had apparently already geplant for me.

I sat on the Sofa. Pulled out my Notizbuch — the one I wrote in when I didn't want to forget anything. And I wrote:

Day 1. Berlin. Grey and cold.

Matei gave me a key. And a job. And didn't ask why I came.

I think he already knows.

Then I closed the Notizbuch and waited for sechs Uhr.

Grammar Spotlight

From this chapter: "I picked it up. Walked to the door. Schloss it from the inside. Schloss Auf Wiedersehen."

In German, many verbs have a prefix that separates and goes to the end of the clause.

Examples from the chapter:

Infinitive Meaning Present tense example

abschließen to lock Ich schließe die Tür ab

aufschließen to unlock Er schließt die Tür Auf Wiedersehen

anrufen to call (by phone) Sie ruft mich an

Key pattern: The prefix (ab-, Auf Wiedersehen-, an-) goes to the end of the sentence. The main verb is conjugated and stays in position 2.

From later in the story you will see: "Ich rufe dich später an" (I'll call you later).

Why this matters: You don't need to memorize the rule. You just need to notice that every time Matei locks or unlocks a door, abschließen and aufschließen appear with the prefix at the end. After seeing it 20+ times, your brain will expect it.

Writing Prompt

Describe Matei's apartment from Matei's perspective. He doesn't think of it as small — he thinks of it as enough. Three sentences maximum.

Or: Write the note Matei would have left on the table the first morning if he'd wanted to say something real instead of just 'Don't burn the milk.'

Shadowing Script

Read this aloud twice — once at normal speed, once slower.

Yves: You're staring.

Matei: I'm observing. There's a Unterschied.

Yves: What's the difference?

Matei: Staring is creepy. Observing is wissenschaftlich.

Focus on wissenschaftlich — five syllables: wis-sen-schaft-lich. Put the stress on WISS.

Chapter Three — Six O'Clock

Before You Read

Six words for this chapter:

der Nachbar — neighbour

der Kuehlschrank — refrigerator

verlegen — embarrassed

der Supermarkt — supermarket

die Schicht — shift (work)

kompetent — competent

This chapter has the first extended cooking scene. Pay attention to how Matei watches.

I spent the Nachmittag trying not to watch the door.

It is harder than it sounds. The Wohnung was klein. The door was right there, three meters from the Sofa, with its old brass handle and the crack in the wood where someone had probably kicked it once. Every time a Nachbar walked up the stairs, I looked up. Every time someone laughed in the Flur, I held my breath. By half past five, I had given up pretending and was just openly staring at the handle, waiting for it to turn.

This was erbärmlich. I knew it was erbärmlich. I had known Matei for less than twenty-four hours. He was a Fremder. A nice stranger who gave me keys and job leads and coffee made exactly the way I liked it, but still. A Fremder. I didn't need to be counting the Minuten until he came back.

And yet.

At 5:47, the stairs creaked. Footsteps. Slow, bedacht, the kind of footsteps that belonged to someone who wasn't in a hurry because they knew exactly where they were going. I recognized them. Which was verrückt, because I had only heard him walk once, last night, when he had gone from the kitchen to the Sofa. But I recognized them anyway.

The Schlüssel turned in the Schloss. The door opened. Matei stepped inside, bringing a gust of cold air and the smell of the street — diesel, Regen, something baking from the bakery downstairs.

He looked at me. I looked at him.

"You're still here," he said.

"You sound surprised."

"I'm not surprised." He hung his coat on a hook by the door. "I'm just... bemerkend."

He walked to the kitchen. I heard him open the Kühlschrank. Then the freezer. Then the Kühlschrank again.

"I didn't buy food," he said.

"I noticed."

"I was going to buy food."

"But you didn't."

He turned around. His expression was almost verlegen — a faint flush at the tops of his cheeks.

"I forgot."

Matei, it turned out, was the kind of person who forgot to buy groceries because he was too busy working and arranging jobs for strangers and being quietly kompetent at everything except feeding himself. I filed that information away in the useful part of my brain.

"There's a Supermarkt around the corner," I said. "I saw it when I went out."

"You went out?"

"To find the Café. The one you got me the job at."

"Ah." He nodded slowly. "And?"

"And it exists. It has a green awning. It smells like bread from three blocks away."

"That's the one."

We stood there for a moment. The Kühlschrank hummed. Somewhere upstairs, someone was playing the same Frank Ocean album I had seen on his Regal.

"I can cook," I said. "If you buy the food."

He raised an eyebrow. "You can cook?"

"I can cook. Don't look so surprised."

"You just arrived in a country where you don't speak the language, you're sleeping on a stranger's Sofa, and you're telling me you can cook."

"I'm full of surprises."

He almost smiled again. That was three times now. I was keeping count.

He grabbed his coat. "Komm."

The Supermarkt was called Netto and it was exactly as depressing as every budget supermarket I had ever been in. Leuchtstoffröhren, Linoleum floors, shopping carts with wonky wheels. But it was warm, and it had food, and Matei walked through the aisles like a man on a mission.

I followed him with a Korb. He threw things in without looking at prices. Pasta. Tomaten. A tube of tomato paste. Zwiebeln. Knoblauch. A block of Parmesan that cost more than my entire outfit.

"You're not going to let me pay for any of this, are you?" I said.

"You don't have Euro."

"I can get Euro."

"Tomorrow. After your first Schicht. Tonight, I buy."

I wanted to argue. I always wanted to argue. Arguing was my Standardeinstellung — it kept people at a distance, which was where I liked them. But Matei wasn't looking at me like he expected a fight. He was just... buying groceries. Like it was the most normal thing in the world to feed a stranger.

"What are we making?" he asked.

"Pasta."

"Simple."

"I'm a simple person."

He glanced at me. His grey eyes caught the Leuchtstofflicht.

"No, you're not."

I didn't know what to say to that. So I grabbed a bag of Salz and threw it in the Korb and didn't say anything.

Back at the Wohnung, I took over the kitchen.

It wasn't much of a kitchen — two Brenner, a sink, a mini-fridge that made a sound like a dying animal. But the knife was sharp, and the pot was the right size, and I had made this Soße a hundred times in a dozen different kitchens. It was the only Rezept I knew by heart. My Großmutter's, sort of. She had never written it down. I had watched her make it for years, standing on a Hocker so I could see the counter, and by the time I was fifteen, I could make it with my eyes closed.

Matei sat on the plastic chair and watched me chop Zwiebeln. He didn't talk. He didn't hover. He just sat there with his hands in his lap, observing.

"You're staring," I said, not looking up.

"I'm observing. There's a Unterschied."

I laughed. "That's my line."

"I know." His voice was quiet. "I liked it."

The onions made my eyes water. Or maybe it was something else. I wiped my face with the back of my hand and kept chopping.

The Soße came together the way it always did — onions first, until they were soft and golden, then Knoblauch, then the Tomaten, then a long, slow simmer while the pasta water boiled. The kitchen got hot and steamy. The windows fogged up. The whole Wohnung started to smell like my childhood, which was a weird thing to experience in Berlin, in a stranger's kitchen, with a man watching me from a plastic chair.

"You've done this before," Matei said.

"Once or twice."

"More than once or twice."

I stirred the Soße. "My Großmutter taught me. She said a man who can cook will never starve and will never be alone."

"She sounds weise."

"She sounds like she wanted me to get married."

He made a sound — not quite a laugh, but close.

"Did it work?"

"I'm here, aren't I? Alone. Cooking for a stranger."

The word alone hung in the air. I hadn't meant to say it. But it was true. I was alone. I had been alone for years, even when I was surrounded by people. Maybe especially then.

Matei stood up. He walked to the kitchen — the three steps it took — and stood next to me at the counter. Close enough that I could feel the heat from his arm. Close enough that I could smell his coat on his skin — cold air and coffee.

"You're not alone right now."

I didn't look at him. I stared at the Soße. It was bubbling, which meant I should turn down the heat, but my hand wouldn't move.

"You don't know me," I said again. It was becoming my Refrain.

"I know enough."

"That's not the same as knowing someone."

He was quiet for a moment. Then he said, "No. It's not. But it's a start."

I turned the heat down. My hand was steady. I was proud of that.

We ate at the table. The two mismatched chairs — me on the wooden one, him on the plastic one. The Lampe cast a yellow circle of light over our Teller. The pasta was good — not great, but good. The Soße had simmered long enough. The cheese was expensive enough to taste like actual cheese instead of sawdust.

Matei ate slowly. Methodisch. He twirled the pasta around his fork like he had been taught to do it properly, which was more than I could say for myself. I stabbed mine and hoped for the best.

"This is good," he said.

"You sound surprised."

"I'm not surprised. I'm... anerkennend."

"Same thing."

"No." He set his fork down. "Surprised means I didn't expect it. Acknowledging means I knew you could do it, and now I'm saying thank you."

I stared at him.

"You knew I could cook?"

"You told me. Two years ago. In a Nachricht."

I searched my memory. Late nights, phone screens, words that felt safe because they were going to someone who couldn't see my face. I had told him a lot of things. Some of them I had forgotten. Some of them I was trying to forget.

"I don't remember telling you that."

"You did." He picked up his fork again. "You said your Großmutter's pasta was the only thing that made you feel like you had a home."

The fork in my hand stopped halfway to my mouth.

"I said that?"

"You said a lot of things."

I put the fork down. My appetite was gone. Not because the food was bad — it wasn't — but because I was realizing, slowly and painfully, that Matei had been paying attention. To everything. To throwaway lines from two years ago. To the way I drank my coffee. To the fact that I was sad at the Flughafen even though I was smiling.

"Why do you remember all of that?"

He chewed. Swallowed. Took a sip of water. Then he looked at me with those grey eyes, and for the first time, he didn't look calm. He looked uncertain. Like he was deciding whether to tell the truth.

"Because no one had ever told me anything like that before. And I wanted to know why."

"Why what?"

"Why you sounded so einsam."

The word hit me like a door slamming. Lonely. Not sad. Not tired. Lonely. He had seen it in my messages, in my voice, in the way I had laughed when he picked up my Koffer. He had seen it, and he had remembered, and he had given me a key anyway.

"I'm not lonely," I said. The lie tasted like Asche.

Matei didn't call me out. He just nodded, finished his pasta, and took his plate to the sink.

"Thank you for dinner. It was the best meal I have had in months."

"That's sad."

"Probably. But true."

I sat at the table for a long time after he had gone to the Badezimmer. The Lampe buzzed. The Heizung clicked. Somewhere downstairs, the bakery was closing — I could hear the metal grate being pulled down over the window.

I had come to Berlin to get away from people who knew me. I had come to be anonymous, to start over, to build a version of myself that didn't carry the Gewicht of everything I had left behind. But Matei already knew me. Not the facts — the surface things, the things you could fit into a Nachricht. He knew the shape of me. The lonely parts. The parts that drank black coffee and made pasta from memory and laughed when they were uncomfortable.

I didn't know if that was a good thing or a terrible thing.

I picked up my plate. Walked it to the sink. Rinsed it. Dried it. Put it in the cabinet where I had seen him take plates this morning.

Then I went back to the Sofa and waited for him to come out of the Badezimmer.

He didn't go back to the plastic chair. He sat on the other end of the Sofa — the end that wasn't stained, the end that faced the window. The cushion sank under his weight. He was closer than he had been all night. Not touching. But close.

"Tomorrow, you start at the Café."

"Tomorrow."

"Are you nervös?"

"Terrified."

He nodded like that was the right answer.

"Good. Terror means you care."

"Or it means I have Angst."

"Same thing."

I laughed. He didn't. But his hand was on the cushion between us, close enough that I could see the veins on the back of it, the small scar on his thumb, the way his fingers rested like they were waiting for something.

"Matei."

"What?"

"Why did you really give me the Schlüssel?"

He didn't answer right away. The room was dark except for the Lampe. His profile was sharp against the window — the curve of his jaw, the slope of his nose, the dark hair falling over his forehead.

"Because I wanted you to come back."

"Come back from where?"

"From wherever you were going to go after you left my Wohnung."

I frowned. "I wasn't going anywhere."

"You were." He turned to look at me. His eyes were almost black in the dim light. "You have that look. The look of someone who is always planning their exit. I wanted to give you a reason to stay."

My heart was doing something stupid in my chest. A stutter. A skip. The kind of thing that happened in bad Romanzen and not in real life.

"You don't even know me," I said for the third time that day.

He reached out. His hand covered mine. Warm. Calloused. Real.

"I know you drink your coffee black. I know you laugh when you're uncomfortable. I know you left home because staying hurt more than leaving. I know you make pasta like someone who learned from a Großmutter who loved you. And I know you're still here."

He paused.

"That's enough to start."

I didn't pull my hand away. I should have. I should have made a joke, changed the subject, retreated to the bed and pretended this conversation hadn't happened. But I was tired of retreating. Tired of planning my exit. Tired of being the person who always left first.

"Okay."

"Okay?"

"Okay. That's enough to start."

His thumb moved across my Knöchel. Once. Twice. Then he let go and stood up.

"Gute Nacht Nacht, Yves."

"Gute Nacht Nacht, Matei."

He walked to the Sofa. The one he had given up for me. He lay down with his back to the room, his coat pulled over him like a blanket.

I lay down in the bed. The sheets still smelled like his detergent. The pillow still held the shape of his head.

I stared at the ceiling and listened to him breathe. Stetig. Quiet. Not asleep yet, but close.

And for the first time in years, I didn't feel like running.

Grammar Spotlight

From this chapter: No explicit weil yet, but it is coming. Let me introduce it now because it is essential for B2.

In German, when you use weil (because), the verb goes to the end of the clause.

English order German order

I stayed home because I was tired. Ich blieb zu Hause, weil ich müde war.

I didn't sleep because I was nervous. Ich habe nicht geschlafen, weil ich nervös war.

Key pattern: weil kicks the verb to the end.

Why this matters: Starting in Chapter Four, you will see weil clauses. When you do, notice where the verb goes. After 10-15 examples, you will start to feel when to put the verb at the end — without memorizing a rule.

Tip: Think of weil as a "verb kicker" — it kicks the verb to the end of the sentence.

Writing Prompt

Write Frau Schmidt's first impression of Yves. She's been running Morgenlicht for twenty years. She has seen everything. What does she see when he walks in?

Or: Yves is cooking his grandmother's pasta in Matei's kitchen. Write the smells, the sounds, and the one moment he forgets he is far from home.

Shadowing Script

Practise this exchange for natural café German.

Frau Schmidt: "Was moechten Sie?"

Yves: Einen Kaffee, bitte.

Frau Schmidt: "Schwarz?"

Yves: Ja. Schwarz. Kein Zucker, keine Milch.

Moechten Sie is formal. Later in the book you will hear Yves say it to customers. Notice when the shift happens.

Chapter Four — Morning Light

Before You Read

Five words for this chapter:

der Wecker — alarm clock

verhandeln — to negotiate

die Sturheit — stubbornness

der Rhythmus — rhythm

der Morgennebel — morning haze

Part One is almost over. The almost-moments are getting harder to ignore.

I woke up before my Wecker.

That never happened. I was the kind of person who hit snooze at least three times, who verhandelte with myself about five more minutes, who treated mornings like an enemy to be defeated through sheer Sturheit. But at 7:15 AM, my eyes opened, and I was fully awake, and my first thought was Matei is still asleep on the Sofa.

I lay there for a minute, listening. His breathing was slow and deep. He had fallen asleep on his back last night — I could hear the soft Rhythmus, the occasional pause, the way his breath caught when he turned over. The Sofa creaked. Then silence again.

I got up quietly. The floorboards were cold under my bare feet. I stepped around the creaky spots — I had kartiert them last night, because that was the kind of person I was now — and made my way to the Badezimmer.

The shower was terrible again. Low pressure, lauwarm water, a curtain that tried to attack me every time I moved. But I was getting used to it. That was the thing about terrible things. You learned to live with them.

I dressed in my only clean clothes. Dark jeans. A black sweater that had a small hole in the sleeve. The same boots I had worn on the plane. I looked at myself in the Spiegel. Same face. Same dark circles. Same hair that weigerte sich to do what I wanted.

You are starting a job today, I told my reflection. In a country where you don't speak the language. For a woman you have never met. Because a stranger arranged it for you.

My reflection didn't look beeindruckt.

Matei was still asleep when I came out of the Badezimmer.

I stood over him for a second — not creepy, just observational — and took in the details I hadn't noticed before. The way his dark hair lockte sich at the ends. The small scar on his chin, like he had fallen as a child. The way his hand rested on his chest, fingers curled loosely.

He looked younger when he slept. Less wachsam. Less like a man who remembered everything and more like a boy who hadn't learned to build walls yet.

I turned away before I could do something stupid, like touch his face.

In the kitchen, I found coffee beans, a grinder, and the French press. I had watched him make it yesterday. I kopierte the movements — scoop, grind, pour, wait. The coffee smelled like hope. Or maybe I was just hungry.

I poured two mugs. Black. No sugar. No milk. I set one on the table next to the Sofa, within reaching distance of his hand.

Then I put on my coat, grabbed the Schlüssel — my key, the one he had given me — and left.

The street was different at 8 AM. Brighter. Betriebsamer. People walked with purpose, carrying coffee cups and briefcases and the tired expressions of people who hadn't slept enough. A man ran past me in workout clothes, headphones blaring music I could hear from ten meters away. The bakery on the ground floor was already open, and the smell of fresh bread made my stomach growl.

I walked to Morgenlicht. Three blocks. Past the playground with the screaming toddler — she was there again, same pink coat, same joyful shriek. Past the bench where an old woman fed Tauben. Past the tree with the crooked branch that looked like it was pointing at the Café.

The green awning was out. The chalkboard sign said Heute geöffnet — I didn't know what that meant, but I assumed it was good. Through the window, I could see a woman behind the counter. Grey hair. Kind eyes. The same woman I had seen yesterday through the window.

I stood across the street for a full minute, pretending I wasn't verängstigt.

Then I crossed.

The door made a chiming sound when I opened it. A little bell, the kind you saw in old movies. The woman looked up. She had a round face, red cheeks, and hands that were covered in Mehl.

"Guten Morgen," she said.

I opened my mouth. Closed it. Opened it again.

"Um. Matei sent me."

Her face broke into a smile.

"Ah! Der Freund." She wiped her hands on her apron and came around the counter. She was shorter than me — a lot shorter — and she moved like someone who had been standing behind this counter for decades.

"I'm sorry," I said. "I don't speak German. Not really. A few words. Almost none."

She waved a hand. "Kein Problem. You speak English. I speak a little. We manage."

"You're the owner?"

"I am Frau Schmidt. And you are Yves." She said it Eevs, with a soft V, like she was trying to taste the word. "Matei told me about you."

"What did he tell you?"

She smiled again. "That you need Arbeit. That you are serious. That you make good coffee."

I hadn't made him coffee. He had made me coffee. Twice. But I didn't correct her.

"I can learn. I learn fast."

"Gut." She nodded. "Then you start now."

The next four hours were a blur of coffee cups, plates, and the word bitte.

Frau Schmidt showed me everything. How to work the espresso machine — a brass monster that fauchte like an angry cat. How to arrange the pastries in the display case so they looked like art instead of food. How to say "What would you like?" in German — Was möchten Sie? — and how to smile when I didn't understand the answer.

I dropped a cup. Only one. It shattered on the floor, and Frau Schmidt swept it up without comment, and I wanted to die.

"First time?" she asked.

"First day."

"You will drop more. It's okay."

By noon, I was exhausted. My feet hurt. My back hurt. My face hurt from smiling at strangers. But I had learned four new Phrasen: Bitte schön (here you go), Danke schön (thank you very much), Entschuldigung (sorry/excuse me), and Tschüss (goodbye). I had served twelve customers. I had made eight cappuccinos, three lattes, and one hot chocolate that the customer said was "perfect" in English, which was probably a lie but I took it anyway.

Frau Schmidt made me sit down at a table and eat a Gebäck. Apricot. Warm. Flaky. The best thing I had tasted since I had arrived.

"You did good," she said, sitting across from me.

"I dropped a cup."

"I dropped ten my first day. You will drop more. This is the way."

I ate another bite of the pastry. It was so good I almost forgot to be ängstlich.

"Frau Schmidt?"

"Ja?"

"What did Matei actually say about me? When he told you I needed a job."

She tilted her head. Her grey hair caught the light.

"He said you were a Freund. That you came from far away. That you needed a Chance."

"That's all?"

"That is enough." She reached across the table and patted my hand. Her fingers were warm and floury. "You are here now. The rest is just Arbeit."

I walked back to the Wohnung at 1 PM. The sun was actually out — a pale, watery sun that didn't warm anything but looked nice anyway. The streets were quieter now. Lunchtime. People eating inside, behind windows, their faces blurred by steam.

I had money in my pocket. Not much — Frau Schmidt had paid me cash for the half day, thirty Euro in crumpled bills that smelled like coffee. It was the first money I had earned in a new country. I held it in my hand as I walked, feeling the Gewicht of it.

I stopped at the Supermarkt. Netto again. The same fluorescent lights, the same wonky carts. I bought bread. Cheese. A bag of apples. A bottle of water. I spent seven Euro and felt rich.

The stairs were still siebenunddreißig steps. The Schlüssel still stuck a little. The Wohnung was empty when I opened the door.

Matei wasn't there.

Of course he wasn't. He had a job. A life. Things to do that didn't involve sitting on the Sofa waiting for me to come back. But still. The silence felt louder than it had yesterday.

I put the groceries away. Made myself a sandwich. Sat on the wooden chair and ate it while staring at the wall. The clock on the wall — I hadn't noticed it before — tickte slowly. Tick. Tick. Tick. Like it was counting down to something.

I pulled out my Notizbuch.

Day 2. First day at Morgenlicht.

I dropped one cup. Frau Schmidt didn't fire me.

I learned: Bitte schön, Danke schön, Entschuldigung, Tschüss.

Matei wasn't here when I got back.

I don't know why that bothers me.

I closed the Notizbuch. Stared at the wall some more.

At 2 PM, I couldn't take it anymore. I put on my coat and went out again.

Berlin was different in the afternoon. Less grey. More alive. I walked without a destination, just moving, just seeing. Past a park where kids were playing Fußball. Past a bookstore with a display of books in the window — all German, all incomprehensible, all beautiful. Past a man playing guitar on the corner, singing something slow that I almost recognized.

I found myself at a bridge. A small one, over a Kanal. The water was greenish-brown and moved slowly. I leaned on the Geländer and watched a duck paddle in circles.

This was my city now. My bridge. My duck.

It felt fake. Like I was playing a role in a movie about someone else's life. But I was here. I was really here. And I hadn't run away yet.

My phone buzzed. A message. Unknown number.

How was the first day?

I stared at it. No one had my number. No one except — I scrolled up. The last message was from Matei, two years ago. But this number was different. This was a German number.

Matei? I typed back.

Who else?

How did you get my number?

You gave it to me. Two years ago. In a message.

I laughed out loud. The duck looked at me.

You remember everything, I typed.

I told you. I remember things.

A pause. Then another message.

Did you eat?

I made a sandwich.

That's not food.

It was bread and cheese. That's food.

Come to the bookstore on Karl-Marx-Allee at 7. I will buy you dinner.

I stared at the message. Karl-Marx-Allee. I didn't know where that was. I didn't care.

Okay.

Don't be late.

I'm never late.

You were late at the airport.

The plane was early. That's different.

He didn't respond. But he didn't need to. I could feel him smiling on the other end. Or maybe that was just wishful thinking.

At 6:30, I started getting ready. Which was ridiculous, because I had exactly two outfits and neither of them was impressive. I put on the other sweater — the dark grey one, no holes yet — and tried to do something with my hair. It looked the same. It always looked the same.

I looked at myself in the Badezimmer mirror.

You are going to dinner with a man who gave you a key and a job and said you weren't alone.

That's not a date, I told my reflection.

Then why are you nervös?

I didn't have an answer.

Karl-Marx-Allee was wider than any street I had seen in Berlin. Big buildings on both sides, old and grand, the kind of architecture that looked like it belonged to a different century. There were shops and restaurants and people everywhere, even at 7 PM on a Sunday.

The bookstore was on the corner. Bücher & Co. A sign in the window said Englische Bücher — English books — and I felt a small wave of relief.

Matei was standing outside. He wasn't looking at his phone. He was just standing there, hands in his coat pockets, watching the street. When he saw me, he didn't wave. He just nodded, like he had been expecting me exactly at this moment.

"You're not late."

"I told you."

"You also told me you made a sandwich for lunch. I'm still judging you for that."

We walked into the bookstore. It was warm inside, and it smelled like paper and coffee — there was a small Café in the back. He led me past the shelves, past a table where someone was reading to a child, to a corner table by the window.

"You work here?"

"Sometimes. I help with the events. Poetry readings, book launches. Nothing exciting."

"It's a bookstore. It's automatically exciting."

He looked at me. "You like books?"

"I like stories."

"Same thing."

"No." I sat down across from him. The chair was comfortable. The light was soft. "Books are the containers. Stories are what fill them. You can have a story without a book. You can't have a book without a story."

He was quiet for a moment. Then he said, "What is your story, Yves?"

The question hung between us. I could have deflected. Made a joke. Changed the subject. That was my specialty — talking without saying anything, filling silence with noise.

But I was tired of that. And he had given me a key.

"I don't know yet. That's why I'm here."

He nodded slowly. "Good answer."

A woman came to the table. She asked something in German. Matei answered. She left.

"I ordered for you."

"Bold."

"You don't know the words for the food yet. I saved you the embarrassment."

"How considerate."

"I'm a considerate person."

I laughed. He almost smiled. The fourth time. I was definitely counting.

The food came. Something with potatoes and sausage and a dark Soße that tasted like winter. I ate it slowly, watching him watch the street through the window.

"Matei."

"What?"

"Why do you remember everything?"

He didn't answer right away. His fingers traced the edge of his plate.

"Because most people don't. They forget. They say things and then they move on and they don't think about it again. But the things people say — the small things, the things they think don't matter — those are the things that tell you who they are."

"And you want to know who people are."

"I want to know who you are."

My heart did that stupid thing again. The stutter. The skip.

"You're getting there."

"I know." He looked at me. "That's why I'm still here."

We finished dinner in silence. Not uncomfortable — the good kind, the kind that felt like breathing. When the bill came, he paid before I could even reach for my pocket.

"Tomorrow, you work again."

"9 AM."

"I will be gone before you wake up."

"I noticed."

He tilted his head. "Does that bother you?"

I considered lying. Decided not to.

"A little."

He nodded. "Good."

"Why is that good?"

"Because I would be bothered if you weren't bothered."

We walked back to the Wohnung together. Not touching. But close. Close enough that our shoulders almost brushed. Close enough that I could feel the heat from his arm through both our coats.

The stairs were siebenunddreißig steps. The Schlüssel still stuck. The Wohnung was dark when we opened the door.

"Gute Nacht Nacht, Yves."

"Gute Nacht Nacht, Matei."

I lay down in the bed. He lay down on the Sofa.

I listened to him breathe until I fell asleep.

Grammar Spotlight

From this chapter: "You like books?" (instead of "Do you like books?")

In German, you can ask a yes/no question by putting the verb first — no extra do or does needed.

English German

Do you like books? Magst du Bücher?

Are you nervous? Bist du nervös?

Did you eat? Hast du gegessen?

Do you remember? Erinnerst du dich?

Key pattern: Verb → Subject → Rest of sentence.

From this chapter: "You like Frank Ocean?" would be Magst du Frank Ocean? in German. The question mark does the work.

Why this matters: No do/does/did — just flip the verb to the front.

Write the text Matei sends Yves after his first day at Morgenlicht. Matei uses as few words as possible. What does he choose?

Or: Write the moment Yves realizes he has been counting the stairs without meaning to. What does that feel like from the inside?

Shadowing Script

Read this short exchange — it is a typical Matei-Yves rhythm: short questions, longer answers, then a short Matei line that lands everything.

Matei: How was it?

Yves: I dropped a cup. Frau Schmidt said she dropped ten on her first day.

Matei: Good.

Yves: Good that I dropped it?

Matei: Good that she told you.

Matei's last line is the emotional resolution. Say it quieter than the rest.

Chapter Five — The Space Between

Before You Read

Five words for this chapter:

die Woche — week

abbrennen — to burn down (separable)

die Milch — milk

der Zucker — sugar

die Stille — silence

Watch the space between Yves and Matei. Something is shifting.

The second Woche was harder than the first.

Not because of the work — I was getting better at the espresso machine, and Frau Schmidt had stopped watching me like I might accidentally abbrennen the Café. Not because of the language — I had learned a dozen new words, including Milch (milk), Zucker (sugar), and Rechnung (the bill), which I said wrong every time but people understood anyway.

It was harder because Matei had started to feel like something I could verlieren.

That sounds dramatic. I know. But here is the thing: when you have spent your whole life waiting for people to leave, you start seeing Ausgänge everywhere. A closed door. A missed text. A silence that lasts a few hours too long. Your brain fills in the gaps with the worst possible Geschichte, and then you are already grieving before anyone has even gone.

Matei didn't leave. He went to work. He came home. He made coffee in the morning and left mine on the table. He cooked sometimes — simple things, eggs and bread, a soup that tasted like Rumänien. He sat on the plastic chair and read his books while I wrote in my Notizbuch.

But he didn't touch me again.

Not after that night at the bookstore. Not after his hand had covered mine on the Sofa. He was close — physically, always close — but there was a space between us that felt like a held breath. Like we were both waiting for something. And I didn't know how to ask for it without sounding verzweifelt.

So I didn't ask. I just watched him. Beobachtete. Collected data.

On my eighth day at Morgenlicht, Frau Schmidt taught me how to close the Café.

It was a Ritual. Wipe down the counters. Count the register. Take out the trash. Lock the door. Turn off the lights. The last part was my favorite — standing in the dark Café, the streetlight coming through the window, the smell of coffee and sugar still hanging in the air. It felt like being inside a memory.

"You're doing good," Frau Schmidt said, putting on her coat.

"I dropped a cup yesterday."

"Only one. Yesterday you dropped one. The day before you dropped two. This is Verbesserung."

She patted my cheek — actually patted my cheek, like I was five years old — and left me to lock up.

I stood in the dark for a minute. The bell above the door was silent. The street outside was quiet. Somewhere down the block, someone was playing music — something slow, something sad, something that made me think of Matei.

I locked the door and walked home.

He was already there when I got back. Sitting on the Sofa. His laptop open on the table. He was typing something, his brow gerunzelt, his fingers moving fast.

"You're home early," I said.

"The library closed."

"You work at the library?"

"I work at the bookstore. The library is where I go to write when I don't want to be at home."

"You don't want to be at home?"

He looked up. His eyes were tired.

"I didn't say that."

"You implied it."

"I said I go to the library to write. That's not the same as not wanting to be here."

I sat on the wooden chair. The plastic one was still empty. It was always empty, now. He sat on the Sofa. I sat on the chair. The space between us was two meters and a Lebenszeit.

"What are you writing?" I asked.

He closed the laptop. "Nothing."

"You're a bad liar."

"I'm an excellent liar. I just don't want to lie to you."

That shut me up. He went back to staring at the wall. I went back to watching him.

"Matei."

"What?"

"Why don't you ever sit in the other chair?"

He turned to look at me. The Lampe light caught the side of his face.

"Because I want to sit where you sat."

I blinked. "What?"

"The first night. When you made pasta. You sat on the Sofa. I sat on the wooden chair." He paused. "I have been sitting on the Sofa ever since."

"That doesn't make any sense."

"It makes perfect sense." He leaned back into the cushions. "I wanted to know what it felt like. Where you had been."

My chest did something complicated. A twist. A squeeze. A feeling I didn't have a name for.

"That's the seltsamste thing anyone has ever said to me."

"Probably."

"And also the nicest."

He almost smiled. Almost.

"I'm a nice person."

"You're a strange person."

"Same thing."

I laughed. He didn't. But his hand was on the cushion again, resting where mine had rested that first night. The same spot. The same distance.

I wanted to reach out. I wanted to close the two meters. I wanted to do something other than sit here and pretend I wasn't terrified.

Instead, I stood up. "I'm going to bed."

"It's eight o'clock."

"I'm tired."

He didn't stop me. He just nodded and turned back to his laptop.

I lay in the dark, listening to him type. The keys clicked softly. A Rhythmus. A heartbeat. Something I could almost fall asleep to.

The next morning, he was gone before I woke up.

But there was coffee on the table. And a Notiz.

Yves —

There's bread in the freezer. Don't just eat cheese for breakfast.

— M.

I stared at the note for a long time. His handwriting was small and neat. The kind of handwriting that belonged to someone who thought before they wrote.

I folded the note and put it in my pocket. Next to the Schlüssel.

Work was slow that day. Frau Schmidt sent me home early — something about a doctor's appointment, something I didn't fully understand because she said it in German and I only caught every third word. She patted my cheek again and told me to ausruhen.

I didn't want to rest. I wanted to walk.

Berlin was grey again. The sky was low and heavy, like it was thinking about rain but hadn't committed yet. I walked without a destination. Past the park. Past the bridge with the duck — the duck wasn't there today. Past a church with a bell tower that looked like it hadn't been used in years.

I ended up at the bookstore. Bücher & Co. The sign in the window still said Englische Bücher. I went inside without thinking.

Matei was there.

He was standing behind the counter, talking to a customer. An older woman with a stack of books in her arms. He was explaining something — in German, fast, too fast for me to follow — and the woman was nodding, and his hands were moving, and he looked like he gehörte here. Like this was his place. His language. His life.

I almost left. I didn't want to interrupt. I didn't want him to see me watching.

But he looked up. His eyes found mine through the crowd. He didn't smile. He just nodded, the way he always did, and went back to helping the customer.

I waited by the English section. Browsing. Not browsing. Reading the same book jacket three times without understanding a word.

"You're staring," he said.

I turned. He was standing behind me. Close. Too close for a bookstore, too close for coworkers, too close for two people who were just sharing a Wohnung.

"I'm observing. There's a Unterschied."

"You have used that line before."

"It's a good line."

He took a step closer. I took a step back. My shoulders hit the Bücherregal.

"Why are you here, Yves?"

"I wanted to see you."

The words came out before I could stop them. Honest. Unfiltered. The kind of thing I usually schluckte.

Matei's expression didn't change. But his hand — his right hand — came up and rested on the bookshelf next to my shoulder. Not touching me. Close.

"You see me every day."

"That's not the same."

"What's the difference?"

I looked at his hand. The veins. The scar on his thumb. The way his fingers curled against the shelf.

"Seeing someone is passiv. It just happens. Looking is active. You choose."

"And you chose to look at me?"

"I chose to come here. The looking just happened."

He was quiet for a moment. The bookstore was noisy around us — people talking, pages turning, a child laughing somewhere in the children's section. But in the space between us, there was only silence.

"Yves."

"What?"

"You're doing it again."

"Doing what?"

"Talking without saying anything."

I opened my mouth. Closed it. Opened it again.

"I don't know how to say what I want to say."

"Then don't say it." He leaned closer. His breath was warm on my cheek. "Zeig es mir."

My heart was a disaster. A mess. A stuttering, skipping, out-of-control thing that had no business being this loud.

"I don't know how to do that either," I whispered.

"Then we will figure it out together."

He pulled back. His hand left the shelf. He walked back to the counter like nothing had happened.

I stood there for a full minute, my back against the books, my heart trying to escape my chest.

Then I left the bookstore. Didn't buy anything. Didn't say goodbye.

I walked home in the grey afternoon, and I didn't feel the cold at all.

That night, he came home late.

I was already in the bed — the bed, his bed, the one he had given up for me — but I wasn't asleep. I was staring at the ceiling, replaying the bookstore over and over in my head.

The door opened. His footsteps. He didn't turn on the light.

"You're awake," he said.

"How do you know?"

"Because you're breathing like you're thinking."

I turned over. He was standing by the door, a dark shape against the darker room.

"Matei."

"What?"

"What did you mean? Zeig es mir. What did you want me to show you?"

He was quiet for so long I thought he wasn't going to answer.

Then he walked to the Sofa. Sat down. I heard the cushions sigh under his weight.

"I wanted you to show me that you wanted to stay. Not because you had to. Because you wähltest."

I sat up. The Laken fell to my waist. The room was cold, but I didn't care.

"I'm still here."

"You are."

"I haven't run away."

"No."

"Isn't that enough?"

He turned to look at me. I could just make out his face in the dark — the curve of his jaw, the shadow of his eyes.

"It's a start."

Then he lay down. Pulled his coat over himself. Turned his back to me.

I lay back down. Stared at the ceiling. Listened to him breathe.

And for the second time that week, I didn't feel like running.

I felt like staying.

Grammar Spotlight

From this chapter: "Like he was deciding whether to tell the truth" — this kind of hypothetical often uses würde + infinitive in German.

The Subjunctive II is used for:

· Wishes (I wish I were there → Ich wünschte, ich wäre da)

· Polite requests (Would you help me? → Würdest du mir helfen?)

· Hypothetical situations (If I had a key... → Wenn ich einen Schlüssel hätte...)

Key forms you will see in this book:

English German Subjunctive II

I would ich würde

you would du würdest

he/she would er/sie würde

I would have ich hätte

I would be ich wäre

Why this matters: At B2, you need to recognize subjunctive forms, not produce them perfectly. You will see würde, hätte, and wäre many times in later chapters. Your brain will absorb the pattern.

Writing Prompt

Yves is keeping a list of Matei's almost-smiles in his Notizbuch. Write the first three entries as he would actually write them — including the date, the context, and the feeling he refuses to name.

Or: Write one paragraph in German. Keep it simple. Use only words you have already seen in this book. It doesn't need to be perfect. It needs to be yours.

Shadowing Script

Practise this pair of lines. The rhythm matters — Yves's line is long, Matei's is a single word.

Yves: You sit where I sat to know what it felt like. You bought a notebook because you saw me writing. You made tea the way I drink it from a message two years ago.

Matei: Ja.

That single Ja carries the weight of the whole chapter. Hold it a beat before you say it.

Chapter Six — The Almost

Before You Read

Five words for this chapter:

sich verschieben — to shift (reflexive)

der Schal — scarf

die Rede — speech

leiser — quieter (comparative)

beobachten — to observe

The title is The Almost. The chapter delivers on that promise.

Something verschob sich after the bookstore.

Not dramatically. Not the way it happens in movies, with rain and swelling music and a Rede that fixes everything. It was smaller than that. Leiser. The way light changes when a cloud moves — not suddenly, but when you look up, everything is different.

Matei started leaving things for me.

A Schal on the back of the wooden chair. "It's cold," he said when I asked. "You don't have a scarf." He was right. I wore it every morning.

A Notizbuch — a new one, black, with blank pages — on the table. "You're filling the other one," he said. "I saw it at the bookstore." I didn't tell him I had already bought a replacement. I used his instead.

A small Pflanze on the windowsill. A succulent, the kind that survived Vernachlässigung. "Every Wohnung needs a plant," he said. "Otherwise it's just a box." I named it Matei Jr. He didn't laugh, but his mouth twitched.

These were not grand Gesten. They were not Erklärungen. But they were things. Physical evidence that he was thinking about me when I wasn't there. And I was collecting them like Beweise.

On my twelfth day at Morgenlicht, Frau Schmidt asked me a question.

"Yves. You and Matei. Are you together?"

I dropped the cup I was holding.

It shattered on the floor. Coffee everywhere. Frau Schmidt didn't turn around.

"That's your fourth cup this week," she said calmly.

"I'm sorry."

"You're not sorry. You're vermeidest the question."

I got the broom. Swept up the pieces. My face was hot. I could feel it brennen.

"We're not together."

"Ah." She finally turned. Her grey eyes were kind, but they were also sharp. "So you are just living in his Wohnung. Sleeping in his bed. Wearing his scarf."

"It's not his bed. It's his Sofa."

"His Sofa. His Wohnung. His Schlüssel." She raised an eyebrow. "This is a lot for not together."

I didn't have an answer. I threw the broken cup in the trash and went back to the espresso machine.

"Yves."

"What?"

"He talks about you."

I stopped. Turned.

"What?"

"When he comes in for coffee. He talks about you." She smiled. "He doesn't say much. He never says much. But he mentions you. Yves likes the apricot pastries. Yves learned to say Rechnung today. Yves laughed at something I said." She shrugged. "A man who remembers the pastries you like is a man who is paying Aufmerksamkeit."

I didn't know what to say. So I said nothing. I made a cappuccino for a customer who wasn't there. Frau Schmidt watched me with that sharp, kind look.

"You are both stur," she said. "This is why nothing has happened yet."

"Nothing hasn't happened because nothing is supposed to happen."

"Lie to yourself if you want. But don't lie to me." She patted my cheek. "Now clean the counter. You got coffee everywhere."

That night, I walked home slower than usual.

The streets were wet. It had geregnet while I was working, and the Straßenlaternen reflected off the pavement in orange pools. The air smelled like wet stone and something green. Spring was coming. I could feel it.

I thought about what Frau Schmidt had said. He talks about you. Matei, who spoke in short sentences. Matei, who remembered everything. Matei, who had given me a key and a job and a scarf and a plant.

Matei, who had not touched me since that first week.

I stopped at the bridge. The Kanal was dark. The duck was asleep somewhere, probably. I leaned on the Geländer and stared at the water.

You are both stur.

She was right. I was stur. I was terrified. I had spent my whole life waiting for people to leave, and now someone was staying, and I didn't know what to do with that. My body knew what it wanted. My heart knew what it wanted. But my mouth — my stupid, broken mouth — couldn't form the words.

I pulled out my phone.

Matei.

I typed it. Erased it. Typed it again.

Are you home?

Three dots appeared. Then disappeared. Then appeared again.

Yes.

I'm on my way.

I know.

I stared at the screen. I know. How did he know? Was he watching the window? Did he have a sixth sense for when I was standing on bridges, trying to work up the Mut to say something?

I put my phone away and walked.

The stairs were siebenunddreißig steps. The Schlüssel stuck. The door opened.

Matei was standing by the window. His back was to me. He was looking out at the street — the same street I had just walked down. The same orange lights.

"You're late," he said without turning.

"The Café closed late."

"Frau Schmidt texted me. She said you dropped a cup."

"She texted you about that?"

"She texts me about a lot of things." He turned. His face was half in shadow. "She likes you."

"She told me you talk about me."

He didn't deny it. He just stood there, hands in his pockets, watching me.

"Yves."

"What?"

"Why did you text me?"

I walked to the table. Sat on the wooden chair. The scarf — his scarf — was still around my neck. I unwrapped it slowly, buying time.

"Because I wanted to know if you were here."

"I'm always here."

"Not always. You work. You go to the library. You have a life that doesn't involve me."

He walked to the plastic chair. Sat down across from me. The Lampe was between us, casting a yellow circle on the table.

"You're in every part of my life. You just don't see it."

"Then show me."

The words came out before I could stop them. They hung in the air like smoke.

Matei's expression didn't change. But his hand — his right hand — reached across the table. Palm up. An Einladung.

"Come here."

I didn't move.

"Yves."

"I'm scared."

"I know."

"If I come over there, something is going to happen."

"I know."

"And I don't know if I'm ready."

He didn't pull his hand back. He just waited. His palm was open. His fingers were still.

"You don't have to be ready. You just have to be here."

I stood up. Walked around the table. Sat on the Sofa next to him. Close. Close enough that our knees touched. Close enough that I could smell his coat — cold air, coffee, something underneath that was just him.

He didn't move. He didn't touch me. He just sat there, his hand still on the cushion between us.

"Matei."

"What?"

"Why haven't you kissed me yet?"

The question was stupid. It was also the only question that mattered.

He turned to look at me. His grey eyes were dark in the lamplight. His face was close. Too close. Not close enough.

"Because I wanted you to want it. Not because you felt verpflichtet. Not because I'm the only person who has been nice to you. I wanted you to want it."

"I do want it."

"Then why haven't you kissed me?"

I blinked. "What?"

"You asked why I haven't kissed you. Why haven't you kissed me?"

I opened my mouth. Closed it. Opened it again.

"Because I'm a Feigling."

"You're not a coward."

"I am. I have been running my whole life. From home, from people, from Gefühle. I came to Berlin because I was running."

"And now?"

I looked at his hand. The scar on his thumb. The veins. The way his fingers curled slightly, like he was resisting the urge to reach for me.

"Now I don't want to run anymore. But I don't know how to stay."

He turned his hand over. Palm up again. The Einladung was still there.

"You stay by staying. One day at a time. One moment at a time. You wake up. You make coffee. You go to work. You come home. And you don't leave."

"That's it?"

"That's it."

I looked at his palm. The lines. The warmth.

"And what about you? Are you staying?"

He didn't answer with words. He moved his hand — slowly, so slowly — and placed it on top of mine. His fingers curled around my Knöchel. His palm was warm. His grip was light, like he was holding something fragile.

"I have been staying. I have been staying since the first message. Two years ago. I have been staying since you got off the plane. I will be staying when you finally figure out that you deserve to be here."

My eyes were wet. I didn't know when that had happened.

"That's a lot of Druck."

"No." He squeezed my hand. "It's a lot of Geduld. Pressure is what you put on yourself. Patience is what I'm giving you."

I turned my hand over. Our palms pressed together. His fingers laced through mine.

"Matei."

"Yves."

"I still don't know how to say what I want to say."

"Then don't say it."

He leaned in.

The space between us disappeared.

His forehead touched mine. His breath was warm on my lips. His nose brushed against my cheek. We were so close that I could see the individual lashes of his eyes, the small Muttermal above his eyebrow, the way his mouth was slightly open.

He didn't kiss me.

He just stayed there. Forehead to forehead. Breath to breath. Hands together.

"This is enough. For now."

I closed my eyes.

"Okay."

"Okay."

We stayed like that for a long time. The Lampe buzzed. The Heizung clicked. Somewhere downstairs, someone was playing music — slow, sad, beautiful.

And for the first time, I didn't feel like I was waiting for something to end.

I felt like I was at the beginning.
