Grammar Spotlight

From this chapter: "She said that he talks about you" → Sie sagte, dass er über dich redet.

A dass clause acts as the object of a verb (like "that" in English). In German, dass sends the verb to the end.

English German

I think that he remembers everything. Ich glaube, dass er sich an alles erinnert.

She said that I dropped a cup. Sie sagte, dass ich eine Tasse fallen gelassen habe.

I know that you're scared. Ich weiß, dass du Angst hast.

Key pattern: main clause + dass + subject + ... + verb (at the end).

Why this matters: In later chapters, characters will express thoughts and feelings with dass. Recognizing it will help you understand complex sentences without getting lost.

Tip: When you see dass, look for the verb at the very end of that clause. Everything in between is the content of what someone thinks/says/knows.

Writing Prompt

Zeig es mir — Show me. Write what Yves hears in those three words. Not what Matei means by them. What Yves hears.

Or: Write the conversation Yves has with himself on the walk to the bookstore. He doesn't know yet what he's going to say when he gets there.

Shadowing Script

This is the emotional peak of Part One. Read it as if you don't know what happens next.

Matei: Warum bist du hier?

Yves: Ich wollte dich sehen.

Matei: Zeig es mir.

Zeig es mir: three syllables, falling stress. ZEIG — es — mir. The command form of zeigen. It asks for something that cannot be explained.

Chapter Seven — The Crack

Before You Read

Six words for this chapter:

die Eile — hurry

zerbrechlich — fragile

der Abschied — farewell

wachsam — alert / watchful

eine Stunde — one hour

rau — rough / raw

Part One ends here. The kiss is the climax. Read slowly.

The next morning, Matei was gone before I woke up.

That wasn't neu. But something else was new: he hadn't left coffee on the table.

I stood in the kitchen, staring at the empty space where the mug should have been. The French press was clean. The beans were in the cabinet. But no coffee. No note. Nothing.

He forgot, I told myself. He was in a Eile.

But Matei didn't forget things. That was his whole thing. He remembered everything.

I made my own coffee. It tasted wrong. Too bitter. Too weak. I poured it down the sink and went to work.

Frau Schmidt noticed immediately.

"You look like someone died."

"I'm fein."

"Your face says otherwise." She handed me an apron. "Did you and Matei fight?"

"We didn't fight. He just... wasn't there this morning."

"Ah." She nodded like this explained everything. "The silent treatment. I know it well. My husband did this for forty years."

"We're not together."

"You keep saying that." She walked to the espresso machine. "One day you will stop lying to yourself. Until then, you clean the Badezimmer."

The Badezimmer at Morgenlicht was small and smelled like Bleichmittel. I scrubbed the toilet. I wiped the mirror. I thought about Matei's hand on mine. The way his forehead had touched my forehead. The way he had said this is enough.

If it was enough, why wasn't he here?

I scrubbed harder.

At noon, Frau Schmidt sent me to the bakery down the street to pick up pastries. I walked with my head down, avoiding Augenkontakt with everyone. The bakery was warm and loud. A woman behind the counter shouted orders in German. I waited in line, staring at the floor.

"Yves?"

I looked up. A man was standing at the counter. Dark hair. Grey coat. Not Matei.

"You're Matei's friend, right?"

I blinked. "I'm sorry. Do I know you?"

"Lukas." He smiled. It was a nice smile — easy, confident, nothing like Matei's almost-smiles. "I work at the bookstore. Matei and I have the same Schicht sometimes."

"Oh." I didn't know what else to say.

"He talks about you a lot." Lukas leaned on the counter. "Says you're learning German fast. Says you make better coffee than Frau Schmidt, which I don't believe because her coffee is terrible."

I laughed before I could stop myself. "Her coffee is fine."

"Her coffee is Spülwasser. But she's nice, so no one tells her." He tilted his head. "You okay? You look like someone cancelled your favorite show."

"Just tired."

"Matei keeping you up?"

The question hung in the air. His smile didn't change. But there was something in his eyes — curiosity, maybe. Or something else.

"We're not like that."

"Sure." He pulled out his phone. "What's your number? I'll text you when Matei's being an Idiot at work. You can come laugh at him."

I should have said no. I should have taken my pastries and left. But I was tired. And lonely. And Matei hadn't left me coffee.

I gave him my number.

The pastries were warm. I carried them back to Morgenlicht and didn't think about Lukas's smile.

I thought about it a lot.

That night, Matei came home at nine.

I was sitting on the Sofa, pretending to read a book I had found on his shelf. Something in German, with small print and no pictures. I had been on the same page for an Stunde.

"You're late," I said.

"Work ran long."

"You didn't leave coffee this morning."

He hung his coat on the hook. Didn't look at me.

"I forgot."

"You don't forget things."

He finally turned. His face was blank. The same blank he had worn at the Flughafen. The one that said I'm here but I'm not letting you in.

"I forgot. It happens."

"Matei."

"What?"

"What's wrong?"

He walked to the kitchen. Opened the Kühlschrank. Stared inside like it contained answers.

"Nothing's wrong."

"Something is wrong. You have been komisch since last night."

"I have been weird?" He closed the Kühlschrank. Turned. "You're the one who sat on the Sofa and let me hold your hand and then went to bed like nothing happened."

I stood up. "Nothing did happen."

"Nothing happened because you didn't want anything to happen."

"That's not true."

"Then what did you want, Yves? Tell me. Because I have been patient. I have been waiting. I have been giving you space and time and all the things you said you needed. But I don't know what you actually want."

The room was quiet. The Lampe buzzed. The Heizung clicked.

"I want you to stop being so patient."

He stared at me. "What?"

"I want you to stop waiting. I want you to stop giving me space. I want you to stop acting like I'm going to break." I walked toward him. Stopped a meter away. "I'm not zerbrechlich, Matei. I'm scared. There's a Unterschied."

"Then what do you want me to do?"

"Kiss me. Or don't. But stop standing in the kitchen like you're planning your exit."

His jaw tightened.

"I'm not planning my exit."

"Then why did you leave this morning without saying Auf Wiedersehen Wiedersehen?"

He was quiet for a long moment. Then he said, "Because I didn't trust myself to stay."

The words hit me like cold water.

"What does that mean?"

He ran a hand through his hair. It fell back over his forehead.

"It means that when I'm close to you, I want things. And I don't know if you want the same things. So I put distance between us. To protect you. To protect me. I don't know anymore."

"I'm not good at this." His voice was low. Rau. "I'm good at remembering. I'm good at waiting. I'm not good at... taking."

"Then let me."

He looked up. His grey eyes were dark.

"What?"

I walked to him. Closed the meter. Stood so close I could feel the heat from his chest.

"You have been waiting for me to make a move. I have been waiting for you. That's stupid. We're both stupid."

"Yes."

"So I'm going to do something. And you're going to let me."

He didn't nod. Didn't speak. But he didn't step back.

I reached up. My hand touched his face. His jaw was rough with Stoppeln. His skin was warm.

"Yves."

"Sei still."

I kissed him.

It wasn't gentle. It wasn't the kind of kiss you see in movies, with soft music and perfect lighting. It was messy. Verzweifelt. The kind of kiss that happens when two people have been circling each other for weeks and finally run out of excuses.

His hands found my waist. Pulled me closer. My back hit the kitchen counter. His mouth was hot and tasted like coffee and something else — something bitter and sweet at the same time.

I had imagined this moment a hundred times. On the Sofa in the dark. On the bridge with the duck. In the bed, listening to him breathe. I had imagined it soft and careful, the way Matei did everything else.

But this was not soft.

This was his fingers pressing into my hips. This was my hands fisting in his shirt. This was the sound he made — a small, broken thing — when my teeth grazed his lower lip. This was the way he said my name, not as a question but as an answer.

"Yves."

"I'm here."

"I know."

He broke the kiss first. His forehead rested against mine. His breathing was fast. His hands were still on my waist, shaking slightly.

"That," he said, "was not nothing."

"No. It wasn't."

"What now?"

I laughed. Actually laughed. The sound surprised both of us.

"Now we stop being Idioten. And we figure this out."

"Together?"

"Together."

He kissed me again. Slower this time. Like he was memorierte the shape of my mouth. Like he was trying to remember every detail — the way my breath hitched, the way my fingers curled into his shirt, the way I said his name when he pulled back just enough to look at me.

When he pulled back, his hands were still on my waist. His thumbs traced circles on my hips.

"You're staying tonight. In the bed. With me."

"Are you asking or telling?"

"Both."

I smiled. "Okay."

We didn't sleep much that night.

We lay in the dark, on the bed that had been mine for two weeks but was really his. His arm was under my head. His chest was warm against my back. His breath was slow and even, but I knew he wasn't asleep.

"Matei."

"Hm?"

"Why did you really give me the Schlüssel?"

His arm tightened around me.

"Because I wanted you to have a reason to come back. And because I wanted to know what it felt like to trust someone again."

"Who broke your trust?"

He was quiet for a long time.

"The Ex. The one who left the Frank Ocean album."

"What happened?"

"He left. That's what happened." His voice was flat. "One day he was here. The next day he wasn't. No explanation. Just a note on the table. I can't do this anymore."

I turned over. Faced him in the dark.

"That's awful."

"It was years ago."

"That doesn't make it less awful."

He was quiet. Then he said, "You're not him."

"I know."

"You stay."

"I know."

"You haven't run away yet."

"I'm not going to."

He kissed my forehead. Soft. Kurz.

"Good. Because I don't think I could handle another Abschied."

I held him. He held me. The Heizung clicked. The street was quiet.

And for the first time, I didn't think about leaving.

I thought about staying.

Grammar Spotlight

From this chapter: "Sei still" (Be quiet) and earlier "Komm" (Come).

The imperative is how you tell someone to do something. Different forms for different people.

Forms you will see in this story:

Target German Example

you (singular informal, du) verb stem + (e) Komm her! (Come here)

you (singular, sein / to be) sei Sei still! (Be quiet)

you (plural, ihr) verb stem + t Kommt her! (Come here - to multiple people)

you (formal, Sie) infinitive + Sie Kommen Sie bitte (Please come)

Key irregulars to remember:

Verb du imperative Meaning

sein (to be) sei be

haben (to have) hab have (rare)

werden (to become) werd become

geben (to give) gib give

Why this matters: In later chapters, characters will give direct commands. Recognizing the imperative helps you understand urgency and tone.

What You Have Learned

By now your brain has encountered the following — not memorised, but seen in context many times:

Core vocabulary: der Schluessel (key), die Wohnung (apartment), muede (tired), die Luge (lie), wuetend (angry), bereit (ready), die Tatsache (fact), enttaeuscht (disappointed), die Zukunft (future), das Vertrauen (trust).

Core grammar: dative prepositions (in, aus, von, mit), separable verbs (aufschliessen, abschliessen, anrufen), imperative forms (Sei still, Gib mir, Komm), weil-clauses with verb at the end.

If you can write three sentences, you are exactly where you should be. If you can write five, you are ahead.

Chapter Eight — The Text

Before You Read

Six words for this chapter:

das Vertrauen — trust

verstecken — to hide

die Eifersucht — jealousy

zugeben — to admit (separable)

ehrlich — honest

die Luft — air (and space, breathing room)

Part Two begins. The density increases to 50-70% German. You are ready.

Things were gut for exactly four days.

That's not a Beschwerde. Four days of waking up next to Matei, of his arm around my waist, of coffee that he made and left on the table with notes that said things like Don't burn the milk and You have flour in your hair and — my personal favorite — The plant is watching you. I think it knows.

I had named the succulent Matei Jr. on day three. By day four, I was having full conversations with it.

"You're talking to the plant again," Matei said from the kitchen.

"Matei Jr. is worried about you. He says you work too much."

"The plant doesn't talk."

"He talks to me. We have a deep emotional connection."

Matei walked over with two mugs. Handed me one. Black. No sugar. No milk. Perfekt.

"Does Matei Jr. also tell you that you left your socks on the bathroom floor?"

"He doesn't need to. You already told me. Twice."

"I'm telling you again. Third time's the Charme."

I threw a sugar packet at him. He caught it without looking. Angeber.

Then Lukas texted.

Hey Yves. Matei's being a total Idiot at work today. You should come by the bookstore and witness it. I'll buy you a coffee.

I read the message three times. It was friendly. Lässig. The kind of thing you would send to a friend's Mitbewohner. Nothing weird about it.

But I didn't tell Matei.

That's the thing about trust. It's zerbrechlich. And I had spent my whole life learning to keep things to myself. Not because I was dishonest. Because I was scared. Scared that if I showed someone everything, they would use it against me. Or worse — they would get gelangweilt and leave.

So I put my phone away and didn't mention Lukas.

Then he texted again an hour later.

Seriously, Yves. He just schrie at a customer for pronouncing "Goethe" wrong. It was beautiful. The customer said "Go-eth." Matei's eye started twitching. I thought he was going to levitate.

I laughed. I couldn't help it. The image of Matei losing his cool over a mispronounced dead poet was too good.

What did the customer do? I wrote back.

Left. But not before calling Matei a "pedantisches Arschloch." Which is fair, honestly. Matei then spent ten minutes explaining why Goethe is pronounced "Ger-ta" and not "Go-eth." To no one. The customer was gone. He was explaining it to the empty doorway.

I laughed so hard Frau Schmidt looked up from her tea.

"What's so funny?"

"Matei yelled at a customer."

"That's not funny. That's Tuesday."

"He explained Goethe pronunciation to an empty doorway for ten minutes."

She stared at me. Then she started laughing. A deep, wheezy laugh that turned into a cough that turned back into a laugh.

"That man," she said, wiping her eyes, "is the most Romanian person I have ever met."

I decided to go to the bookstore after my Schicht.

Not because of Lukas. Because I wanted to see Matei. And maybe also because I wanted to see Matei being ridiculous. And maybe also because Lukas said he would buy me coffee, and Frau Schmidt's coffee was free but terrible, and I was curious what actual coffee tasted like again.

"You're going to the bookstore," Frau Schmidt said. It wasn't a question.

"How do you know?"

"You have that look. The look of someone who is about to watch their boyfriend make a fool of himself."

"He's not my —"

"Don't finish that sentence. I will hit you with a broom."

I finished my shift. Changed out of my apron. Walked to Karl-Marx-Allee.

The bookstore was busy when I walked in. A poetry reading in the back room, someone with a loud voice and a guitar that was slightly out of tune. The front was quieter — just a few customers browsing, a woman at the counter buying a stack of children's books.

Lukas was behind the counter. He saw me and waved like we had been friends for years.

"Yves! You came!"

"You said you would buy me coffee."

"I did say that." He poured two cups from a pot behind the counter. Handed me one. "Fair warning: this coffee is terrible. But it's free."

I took a sip. It was worse than Frau Schmidt's. It tasted like someone had washed a coffee bean in dishwater and called it a day.

"This is Spülwasser," I said.

"I know. That's why I'm giving it to you and not drinking it myself." He was drinking tea. Earl Grey. The fancy kind.

"You tricked me."

"I'm a bookseller. Tricking people is in the job description."

I laughed. He grinned.

"So. Matei." He leaned on the counter. "He's in the back. Helping with the reading. He's been in a weird mood all day."

"Weird how?"

"Weird like... happy? It's unsettling. Usually he's just quiet and judgmental. Today he's quiet and smiling. It's like watching a cat purr. You don't trust it."

I felt something warm spread through my chest.

"He's not that bad."

"He's exactly that bad. Last week a customer asked where the self-help section was. Matei said, and I quote, 'On the floor, where you're sitting.' The customer was standing." Lukas shook his head. "He's a menace. But he's our menace."

"Does he know you're texting me?"

Lukas's smile didn't change. But something flickered in his eyes.

"Does he need to?"

The question hung in the air.

"I don't know," I said. "Maybe."

"Matei and I are friends. Work friends. I text everyone. It's not a thing."

"I didn't say it was a thing."

"You didn't have to. Your face said it." He took a sip of his tea. "Look. I'm not trying to cause drama. I just think Matei is funny when he's annoyed, and you seem like someone who would also think that's funny. That's all."

"That's all?"

"That's all." He paused. "Also, he talks about you constantly. It's nauseating. 'Yves learned a new word today. Yves dropped a cup and apologized to it. Yves named my plant after himself.' Do you know how weird that is? He named a plant after himself?"

"I named it after him. Matei Jr."

"That's worse. That's so much worse."

We both laughed. A customer walked up to the counter. Lukas helped her. I stood there, holding my terrible coffee, watching the door to the back room.

Matei came out twenty minutes later.

He was talking to someone — a woman with a notebook and glasses — and he was doing that thing where he listened more than he spoke. Nodding. Asking a question. Nodding again. The woman laughed at something he said. He almost smiled.

Then he saw me.

His expression didn't change. But his shoulders relaxed. Just a little. The kind of shift you wouldn't notice unless you were watching for it.

I was always watching for it.

He said something to the woman. She nodded and walked away. He walked to me.

"You're here."

"Lukas said you yelled at a customer."

"I didn't yell. I corrected."

"He said you explained Goethe to an empty doorway for ten minutes."

Matei's jaw tightened. "Lukas has a big mouth."

"He also said your coffee is terrible. He was right."

I held out my cup. Matei took it. Smelled it. Made a face.

"This isn't coffee. This is hot water that once saw a coffee bean from across the room."

"That's exactly what I said."

"You said it was Spülwasser."

"Same thing."

He almost smiled. Almost. Then he looked at me — really looked — and the almost disappeared.

"Why are you really here, Yves?"

"I wanted to see you."

"You see me every day."

"That's not the same."

"What's the difference?"

I looked at his hand. The scar on his thumb. The way his fingers curled around the cup.

"Seeing you is passive. It just happens. Coming to see you is a choice."

He was quiet for a moment. Then he said, "You're quoting yourself. From the last time we had this conversation."

"It's a good line."

"It's an okay line."

"You liked it the first time."

"I was being polite."

"You're never polite."

"I'm always polite. I'm Romanian."

I laughed. He didn't. But his hand — his right hand — reached out and touched mine. Just for a second. Just a brush of fingers.

"Lukas texted you, didn't he?"

"How do you know?"

"Because he's been smiling at his phone all day. And now you're here. Two plus two."

"That's not how math works."

"It's how my math works."

I didn't deny it. I was tired of denying things.

"He said you explained Goethe pronunciation to an empty doorway."

"The doorway was not empty. I was in the doorway. The customer had left. I was finishing my thought."

"For ten minutes."

"It was a complex thought."

I laughed so hard a woman browsing nearby shushed me. Matei looked at her. She looked away.

"You're dangerous," I said.

"I'm thorough."

"Same thing."

He almost smiled. That was the fifth one I had counted since I arrived in Berlin. I was keeping a list in my Notizbuch. Page fourteen. Almost-smile #5: Bookstore, after Goethe incident.

I stayed for another hour.

Matei worked the counter. I sat at a table near the window and pretended to read a book. Actually, I watched him. The way he explained things to customers — patient, precise, never condescending. The way he handled a stack of books like they were zerbrechlich. The way he looked up every few minutes, just to check if I was still there.

Lukas brought me another coffee. It was still terrible.

"You're staring at him," Lukas said.

"I'm observing."

"You're staring. It's fine. He stares at you too. It's disgusting."

"We're disgusting."

"At least you own it."

Lukas went back to the counter. I went back to watching.

At 6 PM, Matei's shift ended. He walked to my table. Put on his coat.

"Ready?"

"For what?"

"Dinner. You're cooking."

"Why am I cooking?"

"Because I bought groceries yesterday. And you're better at it."

"You bought groceries? Voluntarily?"

"Lukas made me."

"Lukas made you buy groceries?"

"He said, and I quote, 'If you don't feed that boy something other than coffee and regret, I'm calling social services.'"

I laughed. "Lukas is weird."

"Lukas is a lot of things. Weird is one of them."

We walked home together. The streets were dark. The Straßenlaternen cast orange light on the pavement. His hand brushed mine. Then held it.

"Matei."

"What?"

"Lukas texts me sometimes. About you. About work. It's nothing."

He was quiet for a step. Then two.

"I know."

"You're not jealous?"

"I didn't say that."

"Are you jealous?"

He stopped walking. Turned to look at me.

"I'm jealous of everyone who gets to see you when I'm not there."

I stared at him.

"That's the most romantic thing you have ever said."

"It's not romantic. It's territorial."

"Same thing."

He kissed my forehead. Soft. Kurz.

"Just tell me next time. When he texts you. I don't care what he says. I care that you don't hide it."

"Okay."

"Okay."

We walked home. His hand was in mine. The stairs were siebenunddreißig steps. The Schlüssel stuck. The door opened.

That night, after dinner, my phone buzzed.

Lukas: You two are disgustingly cute. I hate it. Also, Matei almost smiled today. Almost. I’ve worked with him for two years and never seen him get that close. What did you do?

I typed back: I exist.

Lukas: Rude. But fair.

I put my phone away. Matei was on the Sofa, reading. His glasses were on — the ones he only wore at home, the ones that made him look like a Professor from a black-and-white movie.

"Lukas says you almost smiled today."

He didn't look up from his book.

"I smile."

"He says he’s never seen you get that close."

"He's not paying attention."

"He's been paying attention for two years."

Matei looked up. His grey eyes caught the light.

"Then he wasn't paying attention to the right things."

I sat next to him. Leaned my head on his shoulder.

"What were you smiling about?"

He turned a page.

"You."

"What about me?"

"You told Frau Schmidt that Matei Jr. needed more sunlight. She asked if Matei Jr. was your child. You said yes."

I laughed. "She believed me."

"She believes everything you say. You could tell her the sky is green and she would say 'ah, the light is different in Berlin.'"

"That's because she likes me."

"Everyone likes you. It's annoying."

"You like me."

He closed his book. Set it on the table. Turned to look at me.

"I like you more than I have liked anyone. And that's terrifying."

"Why?"

"Because now I have something to lose."

I kissed him. Soft. Slow.

"You're not going to lose me."

"You don't know that."

"I'm choosing to stay. Every day. That's not nothing."

He pulled me closer.

"No," he said. "It's not nothing."

Grammar Spotlight

From this chapter: "Das ist ja Spülwasser" (That's so dishwater) — ja as a modal particle softens or emphasizes.

What are modal particles? Small words that add tone, feeling, or attitude to a sentence. They don't translate directly to English. Very common in spoken German.

Key particles you will encounter:

Particle Effect Example

ja statement of obvious fact Das ist ja schön! (That's beautiful, as you can see)

doch contradiction / reminder Komm doch mit! (Just come with me — you know you should)

halt resignation / acceptance Das ist halt so. (That's just how it is)

eben same as halt Dann geh eben nicht. (Then just don't go)

schon reassurance / qualification Das wird schon gut gehen. (It'll be fine — don't worry)

mal softening / casual (short for einmal) Komm mal her. (Come here for a sec)

Example from this chapter (paraphrased): "Ich hab dir doch gesagt" (I told you — remember?) — doch reminds the listener of something they should know.

Why this matters: Modal particles are the secret sauce of natural German. You don't need to produce them at B2, but recognizing them will make you understand tone much better. And they're very funny when you start noticing them.

Writing Prompt

Write the text Yves should have sent Matei instead of hiding the Lukas conversation. Not the perfect text — the honest one.

Or: Matei admits he shuts down when he's angry because he learned it from his father. Write what Yves does with that information in the three seconds after Matei says it.

Shadowing Script

Formal register practice — write and say this sentence aloud, which appears in a different form in the chapter:

Deine Aufgabe ist es, mir zu vertrauen. — Your job is to trust me.

Then try the informal version: Vertrau mir einfach. — Just trust me.

Notice: formal German uses mehr Worte. Informal German gets to the point faster. Both are correct. Context decides.

Here is Chapter Nine — The Morning After (with humor baked in).

Chapter Nine — The Morning After

Before You Read

Five words for this chapter:

der Morgen danach — the morning after

das Schweigen — silence (the noun form of schweigen, to be silent)

unbeholfen — awkward

vertraegt sich — gets along (with)

die Geste — gesture

After the fight comes the quiet. This chapter is mostly body language.

I woke up alone.

Not ungewöhnlich. Matei was an early riser. He liked to be out of the Wohnung before the city got loud, before the bakery downstairs started selling out of the good bread, before I had to drag myself out of bed and pretend to be a funktionierender human being.

But this time felt different.

The space beside me was cold. No lingering Wärme. No dent in the pillow where his head had been. He had gotten up hours ago, and he hadn't come back.

I sat up. The Wohnung was quiet. Too quiet.

On the table, there was coffee. Black. No sugar. No milk. And a note.

Yves —

I need some Luft. I'll be back tonight.

— M.

P.S. There are pastries in the freezer. Not the apricot ones. Those are mine. Yours are the ones that look like someone stepped on them. Sorry.

P.P.S. I'm not actually sorry.

I stared at the note for a long time. His handwriting was small and neat. The kind of handwriting that belonged to someone who thought before they wrote — and then thought again, and then added a postscript about pastries.

I folded the note and put it in my pocket. Next to the Schlüssel.

"You absolute weirdo," I said to the empty room.

The empty room did not respond. Matei Jr. sat on the windowsill, judging me silently.

Work was a Katastrophe.

I dropped two cups before noon. Frau Schmidt didn't say anything, but she watched me with those sharp grey eyes, and at 11:30, she pulled me aside.

"Sit."

"I have to clean the Badezimmer."

"The Badezimmer can wait. Sit."

I sat. She sat across from me. The Café was empty except for a man in the corner reading a newspaper and ignoring us.

"What happened?"

"Nothing."

"You dropped two cups. Last week you dropped four total. This is Rückschritt."

"I'm tired."

"You're lying." She folded her arms. "Did you and Matei fight?"

I stared at the table. The wood was scratched. Someone had carved a heart into it, years ago, with two initials inside. T + M. Not Matei. Someone else. Probably two people who also had terrible taste in furniture.

"He left a note," I said. "He said he needed Luft."

"Ah." Frau Schmidt nodded. "The Luft note. My husband wrote that note forty-three times."

"Forty-three?"

"I counted. The first thirty times, I panicked. The last thirteen, I ate his pastries while he was gone."

"Did he ever actually leave?"

"Once. He got as far as the U-Bahn station. Then he remembered he left his wallet on the kitchen table." She smiled. "He came back. He always came back."

"That's not advice."

"It's not advice. It's a Geschichte. And a warning: hide the pastries."

I laughed. I couldn't help it.

"You're terrible."

"I'm practical. There's a Unterschied."

I left work early. Frau Schmidt shooed me out the door with a bag of pastries — the stepped-on kind, Matei's warning had been accurate — and a warning not to drop the bag.

I walked to the bridge. The one with the duck.

The duck was there today, paddling in circles like it had nowhere to be and all day to get there. It was a small duck. Unremarkable. But it had a quality I admired: it never seemed worried about anything.

"You have it easy," I told the duck.

The duck quacked. I chose to interpret this as agreement.

I leaned on the Geländer and ate a pastry. It was good. Flaky. Too sweet. I ate another one.

My phone buzzed.

Matei: Where are you?

I stared at the message. He hadn't texted me all day. Now he was asking where I was.

Bridge, I wrote back. The one with the duck.

I know which one. Stay there.

Why? Are you coming to push me in?

Tempting. But no.

Then why?

A pause. Then:

Because I need to apologize. And I can't do it over text. My thumbs are not emotionally available.

I laughed. The duck looked at me.

"He's an idiot," I told the duck.

The duck quacked. I chose to interpret this as obviously.

Twenty minutes later, Matei appeared at the end of the bridge.

He was wearing the same grey coat. His hands were in his pockets. His hair was messy, like he had been running his hands through it. He looked like someone who had spent the morning walking halfway across Berlin and regretting every step.

He walked to me. Stopped a meter away. Didn't touch me.

"You came," I said.

"I said I would."

"You also said you needed Luft."

"I got Luft. A lot of Luft. I walked to Tiergarten and back."

"That's like ten kilometers."

"I know."

"Did it help?"

"No. My feet hurt."

I looked at his shoes. They were nice shoes. Expensive. Completely wrong for a ten-kilometer walk of shame.

"You wore your good shoes."

"I wasn't planning to walk to Tiergarten. I was planning to walk to the bakery. Then I kept going."

"Because you were angry."

"Because I was stupid."

"Same thing."

He almost smiled. Almost.

"I'm not good at this."

"At what?"

"At being angry. When I'm angry, I schalte ab. I leave. I don't talk. It's what I learned. From my father. From the Ex. From all the people who taught me that anger is dangerous."

"It is dangerous."

"Not when it's honest." He took a breath. "I was angry last night. Not because of Lukas. Because you didn't trust me."

"I do trust you."

"You hide things. Small things. Things that don't matter. And every time you hide something, I wonder what else you're hiding."

I wanted to argue. I wanted to say I'm not hiding anything. But that wasn't true. I had been hiding my whole life. Hiding my fear. Hiding my Einsamkeit. Hiding the fact that I didn't know who I was or what I wanted.

Also hiding that I had eaten his apricot pastries yesterday. But that felt like a separate issue.

"I'm scared," I said.

"I know."

"I'm scared that if you know everything about me, you'll leave."

He stepped closer. Close enough that I could smell his coat. Cold air. Coffee. Him. And something else. Slightly burnt.

"Did you set something on fire?" I asked.

"I tried to make coffee. At a Späti. I burned my hand."

"You burned your hand making coffee at a convenience store?"

"The machine was complicated."

"It's a coffee machine. You press a button."

"This one had dials."

I laughed so hard the duck looked up.

"You're an idiot," I said.

"I'm your idiot."

He said it like a Tatsache. Not a question. A fact.

"That's not an apology."

"I'm getting there." He reached out. His hand touched my face. His thumb traced my Wange. His burned finger was bandaged with what looked like a piece of paper towel and electrical tape.

"Is that electrical tape?"

"It's what the Späti had."

"You're going to get an infection."

"Then you can take care of me."

"That's not romantic. That's just medical negligence."

He almost smiled again. Then he said, quietly:

"I'm sorry. For leaving this morning. For not leaving coffee. For being bad at feelings. For wearing my good shoes on a ten-kilometer walk of shame."

"The shoes are unforgivable."

"I know."

"But I forgive the rest."

He kissed me. On the bridge. In front of the duck. In front of a family with a dog, who whistled and said something in German that I didn't understand but sounded zustimmend.

When he pulled back, his hand was still on my face.

"No more hiding," he said.

"No more hiding."

"And no more running."

"I'll try."

"That's all I ask."

"Also, I ate your apricot pastries."

He stared at me.

"You what?"

"Yesterday. After you left for work. I ate both of them."

"Both?"

"They were good."

"They were mine."

"Sharing is caring."

"That's not —" He stopped. Shook his head. Then he laughed. A real laugh. The first one I had heard from him that wasn't an almost.

"You're terrible," he said.

"I'm practical. There's a Unterschied."

"That's Frau Schmidt's line."

"I'm learning from the best."

He kissed my forehead. "Come on. Let's go home."

"Only if we stop at the bakery. I need to replenish your pastry supply."

"You're just going to eat those too."

"Probably. But I'll feel bad about it."

"You won't."

"I'll feel slightly guilty. For at least three seconds."

He took my hand. We walked home. The duck quacked behind us.

I chose to interpret this as goodbye.

Grammar Spotlight

From this chapter: "Ich schaltete ab" (I shut down) — the prefix goes to the end, the verb stem is conjugated in the middle.

You have seen separable verbs (abschließen, aufschließen, auspacken, abschalten). In the present tense, the prefix goes to the end. In the simple past (preterite/imperfect), the same rule applies — the prefix stays at the end, and the verb stem is conjugated.

Examples from the story (present vs. past):

Verb Present Simple Past (Imperfect)

auspacken (to unpack) Ich packe aus Ich packte aus

abschalten (to shut down) Ich schalte ab Ich schaltete ab

aufschließen (to unlock) Ich schließe Auf Wiedersehen Ich schloss Auf Wiedersehen

ankommen (to arrive) Ich komme an Ich kam an

Key pattern: Conjugated verb stem + prefix at the end. Same word order as present tense!

Why this matters: As German density increases, you will see more simple past forms. Knowing they behave like present tense separable verbs (prefix at the end) helps you parse sentences faster. Also, Matei's internal monologue becomes much funnier in past tense. Trust me.

Writing Prompt

Write the morning after from Matei's side: what he makes for breakfast, what he doesn't say, and the one small thing he does that Yves doesn't notice.

Or: The duck at the bridge becomes important in this book. Write why Yves keeps going back to it. Not the funny answer. The real one.

Shadowing Script

Practise this short exchange for casual spoken German rhythm:

Yves: Guten Morgen.

Matei: Morgen.

Yves: Schon wach?

Matei: Schon lange.

Schon lange — already a long time. No subject, no verb. Spoken German drops them constantly. Practise being comfortable with incomplete sentences.

Chapter Ten — The Call

Before You Read

Six words for this chapter:

der Anruf — phone call

die Mutter — mother

verschweigen — to keep secret (separable)

die Vergangenheit — the past

erwaehnen — to mention

das Schweigen brechen — to break the silence

Lagos calls. Yves has to decide how much of his new life to share.

The week after the bridge was different.

Not perfekt. Nothing was perfekt. Matei still forgot to buy groceries. I still dropped cups at work. We still had moments where the silence between us felt like a held breath, waiting to be released.

But we were trying. Both of us. And trying, it turned out, was most of the Arbeit.

Also, Matei had started leaving me notes with drawings. Bad drawings. The first one was a stick figure next to a coffee cup with the caption "This is you. This is your third cup. Please stop."

The second one was a duck wearing a tiny crown. No caption. Just a duck with a crown.

"What is this supposed to mean?" I asked.

"It means you spend too much time at the bridge."

"The duck has a crown."

"He's the king of the bridge."

"You gave the duck a backstory?"

"Everyone has a backstory. Even ducks."

I kept the drawing. It was in my Notizbuch now, between the vocabulary lists and the count of Matei's almost-smiles. Page nineteen. King Duck, ruler of the Kanal.

Then Frau Schmidt didn't show up for work.

It was a Tuesday. I arrived at Morgenlicht at 8:45, ten minutes early, because Matei had started walking me to work in the mornings. He didn't say it was romantic. He just said, "It's on my way." It wasn't. He worked in the opposite Richtung.

"You know I can walk alone," I said.

"I know."

"You don't have to escort me like I'm a child."

"You dropped three cups yesterday."

"That's not related."

"You also walked into a door."

"The door was very clean. I didn't see it."

"That's my point."

The Café was dark. The green awning was still closed. The chalkboard sign was blank.

I stood outside, verwirrt. Frau Schmidt was always here before me. She opened at 8:30. She had a Routine — unlock the door, turn on the lights, start the espresso machine. The old brass one that hissed like a cat. She said the hiss woke her up.

"That's weird," I said.

"What's weird?"

"The lights are off. She's always here by now."

"Maybe she's late."

"Frau Schmidt is never late. She told me once that being late is 'a moral failure.' Then she looked at you."

"She looked at me?"

"For a really long time. Uncomfortably long."

"I was late once. One time."

"You were late three times last week."

"The U-Bahn was —"

"The U-Bahn was fine. You just wanted to finish your chapter."

He didn't deny it. Which was basically an admission of guilt.

I called Frau Schmidt's phone. No answer.

I texted. Nothing.

I waited fifteen minutes. Then I called Matei.

"She's not here."

"Who?"

"Frau Schmidt. The Café is closed. She's not answering her phone."

He was quiet for a moment. Then: "Stay there. I'm coming."

"You don't have to —"

"Yves."

"What?"

"Don't argue. Just stay there."

"I wasn't arguing. I was expressing a differing opinion."

"That's arguing."

"That's discussion."

"Stay there."

He hung up.

He arrived in a Taxi.

That's how I knew he was worried — Matei never took Taxis. He walked everywhere, even when it was raining, even when it was freezing, even when I offered to pay for the bus. He said walking was "better for the soul." I said walking was better for his Sturheit. He said those were the same thing.

"You took a Taxi," I said.

"I ran."

"You don't run."

"I ran today. My soul can recover tomorrow."

"Did you pay the Taxi driver?"

"I gave him a book."

"A book?"

"It was a good book. He seemed happy."

I stared at him. "You paid a Taxi driver with a book?"

"It was a first edition."

"That's not how money works."

"It worked. He drove me here."

"You're insane."

"Probably. Did you try the back door?"

"There's a back door?"

He walked around the building. I followed. The Gasse behind the Café was narrow and smelled like old grease and regret. Matei knocked on a metal door. No answer. He knocked again. Harder.

"Frau Schmidt? It's Matei."

Silence.

"Maybe she's not here," I said.

"Her car is in the back."

"She has a car?"

"A 1998 Volvo. It's beige. She calls it 'the tank.'"

"Of course she does."

He tried the handle. It was nicht abgeschlossen. The door opened into a small Wohnung. A kitchen. A table. A sink full of dishes.

Frau Schmidt was on the floor.

She was bewusstlos.

Not dead — her chest was moving, slow but steady — but her face was pale, and her lips were grey, and there was a phone on the floor next to her hand like she had tried to call someone and dropped it.

"Oh no," I said. "Oh no no no."

Matei was on his knees next to her in half a second. His hand was on her wrist, checking her Puls. His face was calm, but I could see the Zittern in his fingers.

"Call an ambulance."

"I don't know the number."

"112. Call. Now."

"Why is it 112? Why not 911? Why does Germany have to be different about everything?"

"Yves."

"Right. Sorry. Calling."

I called. My German was bad. The operator asked questions I couldn't understand. Something about "Wo ist der Notfall?" and "Atmet sie?" I handed the phone to Matei.

"They want to talk to you."

"Everyone wants to talk to me."

He took the phone. Spoke in rapid German. Answered everything. Hung up.

"They're coming." He hadn't moved from her side. His hand was still on her wrist.

"Is she going to be okay?"

He didn't answer.

"Matei."

"I don't know."

"You're supposed to say yes. You're supposed to lie to me."

"I don't lie to you."

"This would be a good time to start."

He looked at me. His grey eyes were tired.

"She's going to be okay."

"That was a terrible lie. You sounded like a robot."

"I'm not good at lying."

"You're not good at a lot of things."

"Thank you for your support."

"That's what I'm here for."

The ambulance came in seven minutes.

I know because I counted. It was something to do besides panic. The Sanitäter were fast and efficient and spoke to Matei like he was family. They loaded Frau Schmidt onto a Trage. One of them asked something in German. Matei answered. The paramedic nodded and looked at me.

"You come too. She would want."

"How do you know what she would want?"

"She talks about you. Both of you. You're the 'coffee boys.'"

I looked at Matei. "Coffee boys?"

"I'm going to kill her."

"She's unconscious."

"After she wakes up."

I got in the ambulance. Matei stayed behind to lock the Café.

"I'll meet you there."

"Don't take a book this time. Use money."

"I know how money works."

"You paid a Taxi driver with a first edition."

"It was a good first edition."

The doors closed. The Sirenen started. I held Frau Schmidt's hand and tried not to cry. Her hand was warm. Her nails were painted — a soft pink, slightly chipped.

"Your nail polish is chipped," I told her unconscious body. "Matei is going to make fun of you."

She didn't respond. But her hand twitched. I chose to interpret this as I don't care.

The hospital was white and loud and smelled like Antiseptikum.

They took Frau Schmidt to a room. A doctor spoke to me in English. Her English was better than my German, but not by much.

"She had a Schlaganfall. Small. We caught it early."

"Is she going to be okay?"

"She will need Rehabilitation. Therapy. She cannot work for several weeks. Maybe months."

"Months?"

"The brain needs time to heal. Like a muscle."

"The brain isn't a muscle."

"It's like a muscle. Metaphorically."

"That's not how metaphors work."

She smiled. "You must be Yves."

"How did you know?"

"Frau Schmidt talks about you. The 'coffee boy who asks too many questions.'"

"I'm going to kill her."

"After she wakes up."

"That's what Matei said."

"Great minds."

She left. I sat in the waiting room. The chairs were plastic. Uncomfortable. The same plastic as Matei's chair at home. The one no one sat in.

The plastic chair of shame, I called it in my head.

Matei arrived an hour later.

He had closed the Café, turned off the lights, locked the door. He had also called the bakery down the street and told them to cancel the morning pastry delivery.

"You called the bakery?"

"Someone had to."

"You spoke German on the phone?"

"I speak German every day."

"To me. You speak slow German to me. Like I'm a toddler."

"You are a toddler. Emotionally."

"That's fair."

He sat down next to me. His hand found mine.

"How is she?"

"Schlaganfall. Small. They say she'll recover, but it will take time."

"How much time?"

"Weeks. Months. The doctor was vague. She used a bad metaphor about muscles."

"Doctors are like that."

"That's not a metaphor. That's just a statement."

"I know."

We sat there for a moment. The waiting room was quiet. A vending machine hummed in the corner. It sold coffee that probably tasted like Spülwasser.

"The Café," I said. "She can't work. For months."

"I know."

"She doesn't have anyone. No family. Just the Café."

"And us."

"Us?"

He looked at me. His grey eyes were steady.

"We run it."

I stared at him.

"We what?"

"You know how to make the coffee. You know the customers. You know the Routine."

"I dropped four cups last week."

"You dropped three. Frau Schmidt told me."

"That's not better."

"It's better." He squeezed my hand. "I'll help in the mornings. Before work. And I know people. We can find someone to cover the afternoons."

"Matei, I can't run a Café. I can barely order food in German. Last week I asked for 'a glass of cow.' The waitress brought me milk."

"You asked for a glass of cow?"

"Milch** means milk. I said Kuh. Cow. It was one letter off."**

"That's four letters off."

"I was close."

He almost smiled. Almost.

"You don't have to run it alone. You just have to keep it alive. Until she comes back."

"What if I burn it down?"

"You won't."

"What if I forget to order supplies and we run out of coffee?"

"Then we sell tea."

"What if I accidentally poison someone?"

"Then we learn to make poison taste better."

"That's not comforting."

"It's honest."

I looked at him — this man who had given me a key and a job and a reason to stay — and I thought about Frau Schmidt on the floor, reaching for her phone, alone.

"Okay."

"Okay?"

"Okay. I'll do it. But if the Café burns down, it's your fault."

"How is it my fault?"

"You encouraged me."

"That's not how responsibility works."

"It's how my responsibility works."

He kissed my forehead. Right there in the hospital waiting room, with Leuchtstoffröhren and the smell of Antiseptikum and a vending machine that hummed like it was judging us.

"Good. Because I already told the bakery you would be there at 6 AM tomorrow."

"You did not."

"I did."

"You're insane."

"Probably."

"I hate you."

"You love me."

"That's not mutually exclusive."

I leaned my head on his shoulder. He put his arm around me.

We sat like that until a nurse came to tell us Frau Schmidt was awake.

She looked smaller in the hospital bed.

The fluorescent light made her grey hair look white. Her eyes were open, though. They were still sharp. Still slightly judgmental.

"You're here," she said. Her voice was weak.

"Where else would we be?" Matei sat in the chair next to her bed. I stood behind him.

"The Café. I didn't open."

"We took care of it," I said. "It's closed. The pastries are canceled. The lights are off. Also, Matei paid a Taxi driver with a book."

She looked at Matei.

"A first edition," he said.

"Which book?"

"The Trial. Kafka."

"That's a good book."

"That's what I said."

"You overpaid."

"The driver was happy."

"The driver doesn't know what a first edition is worth."

"Ignorance is bliss."

"Ignorance is expensive."

I looked between them. "Are you two negotiating right now? She's in a hospital bed."

Frau Schmidt smiled. A small smile. Tired. Real.

"The Café," she said. "It's my life. If it closes..."

"It won't close," Matei said.

"We'll keep it open," I said. "Until you come back."

She looked at me. Really looked.

"You can't. You don't speak German. You asked for a glass of cow."

"How did you know about that?"

"The waitress is my neighbor."

"Everyone in this city knows each other."

"It's a small city."

"It's not. It's huge. You just all have a gossip network."

She laughed. Then coughed. Then laughed again.

"You're ridiculous," she said.

"I'm practical. There's a Unterschied."

"That's my line."

"You taught me well."

She reached out. Her hand found mine. Her fingers were cold.

"The keys are in the drawer. Behind the counter. There's a blue notebook. The Passwörter. The supplier numbers. Everything."

"I'll find it."

"The espresso machine hates you. Be firm with it."

"I'm always firm."

"You're not. You're gentle. That's why it hisses at you."

"It hisses at everyone."

"It doesn't hiss at me."

"Because it's afraid of you."

"That's how you get results."

Matei cleared his throat.

"Can we focus?"

Frau Schmidt looked at him. "You. Take care of him. He asks too many questions and he's bad at German."

"I noticed."

"Also, he eats all the apricot pastries."

"I noticed that too."

"Hide them."

"I will."

I threw my hands up. "I'm right here. I can hear you."

"Good," Frau Schmidt said. "Then you know what we expect."

That night, we sat on the Sofa.

The Lampe was on. The Heizung clicked. Matei Jr. sat on the windowsill, still alive, still thriving, somehow.

"You're scared," Matei said.

"Terrified."

"Good. Terror means you care."

"Or it means I'm about to ruin someone's life."

"Frau Schmidt trusted you. Do you know why?"

"Because you vouched for me?"

"No. Because you stayed. When she gave you a chance, you didn't leave. You came back the next day. And the next. And the next." He put his hand on my knee. "That's not nothing, Yves. That's everything."

"What if I fail?"

"Then you fail. And you try again." He squeezed my knee. "That's what staying means."

"What if I set the Café on fire?"

"Then we open a Café called Burnt. It will be ironic. People will love it."

"You're ridiculous."

"I'm supportive."

"Same thing."

He kissed me. Soft. Slow.

"You're going to be fine."

"You don't know that."

"I know you."

"That's not the same."

"It's enough to start."

I leaned into him. His arm went around my shoulders.

"Matei."

"What?"

"I'm glad you're here."

"I'm not going anywhere."

"Even if I burn down the Café?"

"Especially then. Someone has to identify the bodies."

"That's dark."

"That's love."

We sat like that until the Lampe flickered and the street went quiet.

Tomorrow, I would open the Café at 5:45 AM. I would make coffee. I would drop cups. I would apologize to the floor. I would learn the German words for supplier and invoice and please pay within thirty days or I will find you.

But tonight, I was just here.

And for now, that was enough.

Grammar Spotlight

From this chapter: "If it closes, she would lose more than money" — implied hypothetical.

The Konjunktiv II is used for:

· Hypothetical situations (If I were rich...)

· Polite requests (Would you help me?)

· Wishes (I wish I had more time)

The three most important forms for B2:

English German Konjunktiv II

I would (do something) ich würde + infinitive

I would have ich hätte

I would be ich wäre

Examples from the story (adapted):

English German

She would lose more than money. Sie würde mehr als Geld verlieren.

If I had a key, I would stay. Wenn ich einen Schlüssel hätte, würde ich bleiben.

If he were here, he would help. Wenn er hier wäre, würde er helfen.

Key pattern for würde: würde + infinitive at the end. The main verb doesn't change — würde does all the work.

Why this matters: Starting now, you will see würde, hätte, and wäre in every chapter. Recognizing them means you understand when something is hypothetical, not real. Also, Matei uses them to make dark jokes about burning down the Café. Pay attention.

Writing Prompt

Yves calls his mother from Berlin. She asks how he is. He says he is fine. Write what he doesn't say — in German, using only words you have already encountered in this book.

Or: Write the conversation Yves has with Matei after the call — the version where Yves tells the truth instead of saying 'It was fine.'

Shadowing Script

Formal phone German. Read aloud and memorise:

Hallo, hier ist Yves. — Hello, this is Yves.

Kann ich bitte mit [Name] sprechen? — Can I please speak with [Name]?

Ich rufe wegen [Thema] an. — I am calling about [topic].

Danke fuer Ihren Rueckruf. — Thank you for returning my call.

These four phrases will cover 80% of professional phone calls in your Ausbildung. Say them until they are automatic.

Chapter Eleven — The First Day

Before You Read

Five words for this chapter:

der erste Tag — the first day

die Bewerbung — application

der Ausbilder — trainer / supervisor

das Netzwerk — network

die Firewall — firewall

IT vocabulary begins here in earnest. These words will recur through Part Three and beyond.

I opened the Café at 5:45 AM.

That's not a Tippfehler. Five forty-five. In the morning. Before the sun. Before the birds. Before any vernünftiger Mensch should be allowed to operate heavy machinery like an espresso machine that hissed like it wanted to kill me.

"You and me," I told the espresso machine, "we're going to have a conversation. And by conversation, I mean you will work, or I will throw you into the Kanal."

The espresso machine hissed.

"That's what I thought."

The blue notebook was exactly where Frau Schmidt said it would be. Behind the counter, in the drawer, next to a bag of spare change and a photograph of a man I didn't recognize. Her husband, probably. The one who had packed a bag three times. He looked tired. I understood.

The notebook had everything. Passwörter. Supplier numbers. Instructions for the espresso machine written in a mix of German and English that made my eyes cross. Turn the red knob. Wait for the green light. Do not overfill the filter or you will bereuen it.

I regretted it anyway.

The first espresso shot was pure Holzkohle. I dumped it. The second was slightly less burnt. I dumped that too. By the fifth attempt, I had something that resembled coffee and not liquid asphalt.

"Progress," I told Matei Jr., who was not there. I had left him at home. Talking to a plant in public felt like a step too far. Even for me.

At 6:15, I unlocked the front door.

The green awning rolled out with a sound like a dying accordion. The chalkboard sign said Heute geöffnet in Frau Schmidt's handwriting. I didn't have the heart to change it. Also, my handwriting looked like a spider had fallen into an inkwell and had a seizure.

The first customer arrived at 6:30.

An old man with a newspaper and a Limp. He ordered something in German. I understood the word Kaffee and nothing else.

"Black?" I asked.

He looked at me like I had grown a second head.

"Schwarz?" I tried.

He nodded. I made him a black coffee. He took a sip. Made a face that said this is terrible but I am too polite to say so. Drank it anyway.

"Danke," he said, and left a two-Euro tip.

"Thank you," I said. "Come back tomorrow. I'll be better. Probably. Maybe."

He walked out. I put the tip in my pocket. Frau Schmidt had said tips were for the Personal. I was the staff. I was also the manager, the dishwasher, and the person who had almost cried four times before 7 AM.

By 8 AM, I had made sixteen coffees, dropped one cup, and learned the German word for receipt — Quittung — from a woman who yelled it at me three times before I understood.

"Quittung," I repeated.

"Ja. Quittung."

"That's a terrible word. It sounds like something you cough up."

She did not laugh. She took her receipt and left.

"Tough crowd," I told the espresso machine.

The espresso machine hissed.

Matei showed up at 8:15.

He was supposed to be at the bookstore. Instead, he was standing in the doorway, holding a bag of pastries from the bakery down the street. He was also wearing a shirt that said I'm silently judging you in German. I didn't know he owned that shirt. I didn't know that shirt existed.

"You look terrible," he said.

"I feel terrible."

"How many cups?"

"One."

"That's good."

"I also burned my hand on the Dampfstab."

He walked behind the counter. Took my hand. Examined the burn. It was small. A red mark on my thumb. He kissed it.

"That doesn't help."

"It helps me."

"You're not the one who is burned."

"Emotionally, I am."

He put the pastries in the display case. Took over the espresso machine while I handled the register. Together, we got through the morning rush. It was still Chaos. But it was shared Chaos.

At 9:30, the Café emptied. I collapsed into a chair. Matei sat across from me.

"You're not at work."

"I called in sick."

"You're not sick."

"I'm emotionally sick. Watching you struggle is exhausting."

I threw a sugar packet at him. He caught it without looking.

"Angeber."

"I've been doing this longer than you."

"That's not a flex. That's just sad."

He almost smiled. Almost. Then the bell above the door chimed, and a woman walked in.

She was young. Maybe thirty. Dark hair. A red coat that looked expensive. She carried a leather bag and walked like she owned the room. Also like she had never dropped a single cup of coffee in her entire privileged life.

"Guten Morgen," she said. Then she looked at me. Her eyes narrowed.

"Yves?"

I froze.

"Do I know you?" I asked.

She smiled. It was a strange smile. Not warm. Not cold. Something in between. Like she knew something I didn't. Which was annoying, because I was already having a bad day.

"You don't remember me. That's okay. It was a long time ago." She walked to the counter. "I'll have a latte. Hafermilch. Extra hot."

Matei made the latte. I stood there, trying to place her face. The dark hair. The sharp cheekbones. The way she said my name like she had a right to it.

She paid. Took her latte. Sat at a table by the window. She did not sit at the table with the carved heart. She sat at the table next to it. The one with the wobbly leg.

"Who was that?" Matei asked quietly.

"I don't know."

"She knew your name."

"I noticed."

"She also knew you worked here."

"I noticed that too."

"Do you want me to go ask her?"

"And say what? 'Excuse me, strange woman, why do you know my boyfriend's name?' That's not creepy at all."

"I can be charming."

"You're Romanian. That's not the same thing."

He made a face. I watched the woman from behind the counter. She wasn't looking at me. She was looking at her phone, typing something, smiling at the screen.

My phone buzzed.

Unknown number: You look good, Yves. Berlin suits you.

I looked at the woman. She looked at me. She smiled again.

"Who is she?" Matei asked.

"I told you. I don't know."

"She just texted you."

"I saw that."

"Are you going to respond?"

"And say what? 'Thanks, stranger who knows my name and my location'? That's how you get murdered."

"You're not going to get murdered."

"You don't know that."

"I know you. You're too annoying to murder. No one would want to listen to you that long."

"That's romantic."

"I'm a romantic person."

I did not respond to the text. I put my phone away. Made another coffee for a customer who wasn't there. The woman finished her latte, stood up, walked to the counter.

"Same time tomorrow?" she asked.

"I don't even know your name."

"No. You don't."

She left. The bell chimed. The door closed.

"That was seltsam," Matei said.

"You think?"

"Do you have any idea who she is?"

I thought about it. The dark hair. The sharp cheekbones. The way she said my name.

"No. But I think she knows me."

"That's not comforting."

"Welcome to my life."

The rest of the day was a blur.

More customers. More coffee. More dropped cups — two more, because my hands were shaking and I couldn't stop thinking about the woman in the red coat.

"That's three cups today," Matei said.

"I know."

"That's a record."

"Thank you for keeping track."

"Someone has to."

At 3 PM, Matei left for his shift at the bookstore. He kissed my forehead and told me to lock the door behind me.

"Text me if she comes back."

"She won't."

"How do you know?"

"Because she said 'same time tomorrow.' That means she's planen something. People who are planning something don't come back the same day. They wait. It's dramatic."

"You know a lot about dramatic people."

"I live with one."

"You live with me."

"Exactly."

He left. I locked the door. Cleaned the counters. Counted the register. Turned off the lights. The espresso machine hissed one last time, like it was saying goodbye.

"See you tomorrow," I told it. "Don't be a jerk."

It hissed. I chose to interpret this as no promises.

At 4 PM, I walked home.

The streets were grey. The duck wasn't at the bridge. I didn't care. I was too busy thinking about the woman in the red coat. The way she had said my name. The way she had smiled. The way she had texted me like she had a right to my Aufmerksamkeit.

My phone buzzed again.

Unknown number: You're wondering who I am. That's cute. See you tomorrow, Yves.

I did not respond. I blocked the number.

Then I unblocked it. Because if she was going to be weird, I wanted to know about it.

"This is how people get murdered," I told myself.

Myself did not respond. Myself was busy being annoyed.

Matei was already home when I got there.

He was sitting on the Sofa, his laptop open, not typing. Just staring at the screen. The screen was blank.

"You're home early," I said.

"The bookstore was slow."

"You're lying."

"I'm worried." He closed the laptop. "Who was that woman?"

"I don't know."

"You don't know, or you don't want to tell me?"

I sat on the wooden chair. The plastic one was still empty. It was always empty. I was starting to feel bad for it.

"I don't know. I have never seen her before. But she knew my name. And she knew I was in Berlin. And she knew I worked at the Café."

"That's not nothing."

"I know."

"Yves." He leaned forward. "Did you leave behind something in Nigeria? Someone? A situation?"

I thought about it. My Großmutter. My coworkers. The friends who had stopped calling. The people I had ghosted because I couldn't handle their questions about why I was leaving.

"No. Nothing like that."

"Then why is she here?"

"I don't know."

"Did you maybe... I don't know... accidentally become famous and not tell me?"

"I'm a barista who once asked for a glass of cow. I'm not famous."

"You're famous in my heart."

"That's not helpful right now."

"It's always helpful to know you're famous in my heart."

He stood up. Walked to the window. Stared out at the street.

"I don't like this."

"Neither do I."

"What are we going to do?"

I stood up. Walked to him. Put my hand on his back.

"We're going to open the Café tomorrow. And if she comes back, we're going to ask her who she is and what she wants."

"And if she doesn't tell us?"

"Then we call the Polizei."

"And say what? 'A woman knows my boyfriend's name'? That's not a crime."

"It should be."

"I'll write to my congressman."

"You don't have a congressman. You're Romanian."

"I'll write to someone."

He turned. His face was close to mine.

"You're taking this very calmly."

"I'm not calm. I'm pretending to be calm. There's a Unterschied."

"You've said that before."

"It's still true."

He kissed me. Hard. Brief.

"Okay. Tomorrow. We figure it out."

"Together."

"Together."

"And if she tries to kidnap me, you have to do something heroic."

"Like what?"

"I don't know. You're creative."

"I'll throw a book at her."

"A good one?"

"A first edition."

"Not the Kafka."

"The Kafka is mine. I'll throw something else."

"You're ridiculous."

"I'm prepared."

That night, I didn't sleep.

I lay in bed, staring at the ceiling, listening to Matei breathe. His arm was around my waist. His chest was warm against my back.

I thought about the woman in the red coat. The way she had said my name. The way she had smiled. The way she had texted me like she had a right to my Aufmerksamkeit.

I had spent my whole life running from people who knew me. People who wanted things from me. People who reminded me of who I used to be.

But I didn't know who I used to be anymore. I was Yves. Berlin. Coffee. Matei.

That was supposed to be enough.

My phone buzzed. I had forgotten to block the number again.

Unknown number: I know you blocked me. That's fine. I'll see you tomorrow anyway. Sleep well, Yves.

"Creepy," I said.

"What's creepy?" Matei murmured.

"Nothing. Go back to sleep."

"You're thinking too loud."

"Sorry."

"Don't be sorry. Just sleep."

I tried. I really did.

But somewhere in the city, a woman in a red coat was walking through the dark, and she knew my name, and she wasn't finished with me yet.

"If I get murdered," I whispered, "you have to avenge me."

"I'll throw a book at her."

"A good one."

"The best one."

"I love you."

"I love you too. Now sleep."

I closed my eyes.

The phone buzzed again.

I ignored it.

Grammar Spotlight

From this chapter: "Sei still" (Be quiet) — but more relevant: "Sei vorsichtig" (Be careful) and the implied "Werd nicht wütend" (Don't become angry).

You have already seen sei (be) in Chapter Seven. The imperative of sein is irregular:

Target Imperative of sein

Verb du form Meaning

Why this matters: Imperatives are everywhere in spoken German — giving directions, warnings, advice. Recognizing them helps you understand urgency and tone. Also, Matei uses them to tell Yves not to do stupid things. Which is often.

Writing Prompt

Write Yves's first internal monologue at the Betrieb. He is sitting in orientation. He understands about 60% of what is being said. What does he do with the other 40%?

Or: Write a formal email from Yves to his Ausbilder requesting clarification on an assignment. Keep it under six sentences. Use the formal Sie.

Shadowing Script

Formal email register — read and practise. This is the template for every professional email you will write during your Ausbildung:

Sehr geehrte/r [Name], — Dear [Name],

Ich schreibe Ihnen bezueglich [Thema]. — I am writing to you regarding [topic].

Koennen Sie mir bitte [Bitte] mitteilen? — Could you please let me know [request]?

Fuer Ihre Unterstuetzung bedanke ich mich im Voraus. — Thank you in advance for your support.

Mit freundlichen Gruessen, — Kind regards,

Yves [Nachname] — Yves [Surname]

This structure is not optional in German professional life. It is expected. Learn it once, use it always.

Chapter Twelve — Lucky

Before You Read

Five words for this chapter:

das Glueck — luck / happiness

unverdient — undeserved

die Narbe — scar

das Gestaendnis — confession

aufatmen — to breathe easy (separable)

Ada appears. Someone from before Berlin who knew Yves before he knew himself.

She came back the next day.

Same red coat. Same leather bag. Same Lächeln that wasn't warm or cold but somewhere in between — the kind of smile that said I know something you don't, and I'm going to enjoy watching you figure it out.

She ordered the same thing — latte, Hafermilch, extra hot — and paid with the same crisp Euro. The bills were so new they crackled.

I made her drink. My hands were steady. I was proud of that.

"You didn't sleep well," she said. Not a question.

"How would you know?"

"Your eyes. They're tired. Also, you have a stain on your shirt. Coffee, I think. From yesterday."

I looked down. There was a stain. Right over my heart. Of course.

"That's not coffee. That's my soul. It leaks."

She laughed. It was a vertrautes laugh. Something from a long time ago, buried under years of forgetting.

"You always had a comeback. Even when you were little. Your Großmutter would yell at you, and you would just stand there with your arms crossed, waiting for her to finish so you could say something smart."

"I don't remember that."

"I do. I remember everything."

"Great. Another person who remembers everything. That's not annoying at all."

"Who's the other person?"

"My boyfriend. He's a human calendar. It's exhausting."

She tilted her head. "Boyfriend?"

"Matei. The one who made your latte yesterday. The one you ignored."

"I didn't ignore him. I was observing."

"That's what I say."

"Great minds."

"Or creepy minds."

"Same thing."

She took a sip of her latte. Her eyes didn't leave mine.

"You've changed," she said.

"That's what happens when you leave home and start a new life. You change."

"Not everyone changes. Some people just get older."

"That's profound. Did you read that on a candle?"

She laughed again. "You're still funny."

"I'm still alive. That's the same thing for me."

I stared at her.

"Who are you?"

She set her cup down. Looked at me. Really looked. The way you look at someone when you're trying to decide if they're worth the trouble.

"You don't recognize me, do you?"

"I told you. No."

"Not even a little?"

"Should I?"

She leaned forward. Her face was close to mine. Close enough that I could see the small scar on her eyebrow. Close enough that I could smell her perfume — something floral, expensive, the kind of thing you buy when you have money and want everyone to know it.

"Adaeze," she said. "But you knew me as Ada."

The name hit me like a door slamming.

Ada. Ada with the braids. Ada who lived down the street. Ada who used to sneak me food from her mother's kitchen when my Großmutter forgot to cook. Ada who I had kissed once, behind the church, just to see what it felt like.

Ada who I had stopped talking to when I realized I was kissing boys in secret and couldn't look her in the eye anymore.

"No," I said.

"Yes."

"You're lying."

"I'm not."

"Ada had braids. And she was shorter. And she —"

"I grew. People do that. It's called aging."

"I know what aging is. I just didn't expect you to —"

"To what? Exist? In Berlin? In your Café? With a better haircut?"

"Your haircut is fine."

"Thank you."

"That wasn't a compliment."

"I'm taking it as one."

"Why are you here, Ada?"

"I live here now. Moved to Berlin last month. For work." She took another sip. "I saw you through the window. I couldn't believe it. Lucky, in Berlin, making coffee. I had to come in."

"Don't call me that."

"Call you what?"

"Lucky. That's not my name anymore."

"What is your name now?"

"Yves."

"Yves." She said it slowly, like she was tasting it. "French. Fancy. You always wanted to be somewhere else."

"I wanted to be somewhere I wasn't known."

"And now I'm here. So much for that."

"You're here. For now. You could leave."

"I could. But I won't."

"Why not?"

"Because I want to see what happens."

"Nothing is going to happen."

"Something is always happening, Lucky. That's the problem."

She smiled. The warm kind this time. The kind that reminded me of sitting on her porch, sharing a mango, pretending we had nowhere to be.

"You kissed me once," she said.

"I was eight."

"I was nine. I thought about that kiss for years."

"That's concerning."

"It's not concerning. It's honest."

"Honest is overrated."

"That's what someone who is bad at honesty would say."

The bell chimed. Matei walked in.

He was wearing his grey coat. His hair was messy. His eyes went straight to Ada, then to me, then back to Ada. His expression didn't change. But his jaw tightened. Just a little. The kind of thing you wouldn't notice unless you were watching for it.

I was always watching for it.

"Yves," he said. "Who's this?"

I opened my mouth.

Nothing came out.

This was the moment. I could introduce her as Ada, an old friend from Nigeria. I could tell the truth — that she was someone I had kissed once, someone who knew me before I knew myself. I could be honest, the way Matei had asked me to be.

But I was scared. Scared of what Matei would think. Scared of the questions he would ask. Scared of the boy I used to be, the one who kissed girls behind churches and pretended he was normal.

"An old friend," I said. "Ada."

Matei looked at her. Then at me.

"Nice to meet you," he said. His voice was flat. The same flat he used when a customer asked a stupid question. "I'm Matei."

"The boyfriend," Ada said.

"The roommate," I said.

The word hung in the air.

Roommate.

I had said it. I had actually said it.

Matei's expression didn't change. But his hands — his hands curled into fists at his sides.

"Roommate," he repeated.

"That's what I said."

"That's what you said."

"Yes."

"Okay."

He walked behind the counter. Didn't touch me. Didn't look at me. Started cleaning the espresso machine. The brass one that hissed. It hissed at him. He didn't flinch.

The silence was loud.

Ada finished her latte. Stood up. Sling her bag over her shoulder.

"I'll be around, Lucky. We should catch up properly. Maybe dinner?"

"Maybe," I said.

"Bring your roommate."

She left. The bell chimed. The door closed.

Matei didn't look up from the espresso machine.

"Roommate," he said again.

"Matei —"

"Roommate. That's what I am. A roommate."

"You don't understand."

"Then explain it to me."

I walked to him. Put my hand on his arm. He didn't pull away, but he didn't lean in either.

"That's Ada. I knew her when I was a kid. In Nigeria. She called me Lucky. That was my name before Yves."

"I don't care what your name was."

"I kissed her once. Behind a church. I was eight. She was nine. I didn't know what I was doing."

"I don't care about that either."

"Then what do you care about?"

He finally looked at me. His grey eyes were hard.

"I care that you introduced me as your roommate. I care that you lied. I care that you're still hiding."

"I'm not hiding."

"You just hid me."

The words hit like a punch.

"I was scared."

"Of what?"

"Of her. Of what she would think. Of what she would say. She knew me before. Before I knew myself. She thought I was straight. She thought — she thought I was going to grow up and marry her or someone like her. And I couldn't — I couldn't just —"

"You couldn't tell her the truth."

"I couldn't."

"Why not?"

"Because I'm still scared, okay? I'm still scared of people knowing. I'm still scared of what they'll think. I'm still the same person who ran away from Nigeria because I couldn't handle being seen. I haven't magically become brave just because I have a boyfriend who makes good coffee."

"I make excellent coffee."

"That's not the point."

"It's part of the point."

"Matei."

"Yves."

He pulled his arm away. Walked to the window. Stared out at the street.

"I'm not asking you to come out to everyone. I'm asking you not to hide me."

"I wasn't hiding you."

"You called me your roommate. In my own Wohnung. The Wohnung where you sleep in my bed. Where you named my plant after me. Where you keep a list of my almost-smiles in your Notizbuch."

"How do you know about the list?"

"You left it on the table. Page nineteen."

"You read my Notizbuch?"

"It was open. The duck was wearing a crown."

"That's an invasion of privacy."

"That's called being in a relationship. People read each other's notebooks. It's in the contract."

"There's no contract."

"There should be."

"You're impossible."

"I'm Romanian. Same thing."

I laughed. I couldn't help it.

"You're not funny."

"I'm hilarious. You're just stressed."

"I am stressed. A strange woman from my past just showed up at my Café, and I introduced you as my roommate, and now you're angry, and I don't know how to fix it."

"I'm not angry."

"You look angry."

"I look Romanian. There's a Unterschied."

"Is there?"

"No. But I'm working on it."

He walked back to me. Put his hands on my shoulders. His thumbs pressed into the tense muscles of my neck.

"I'm not angry, Yves. I'm tired. I'm tired of being hidden. I'm tired of being the secret. I'm tired of being the roommate when I'm the person who loves you."

"I love you too."

"Then act like it."

"How?"

"Next time, introduce me as your boyfriend. Or your partner. Or your annoying Romanian who steals your pastries. I don't care what you call me. Just don't call me your roommate."

"What if I call you my emotional support Eastern European?"

He almost smiled. Almost.

"That's worse."

"What if I call you my personal coffee artist?"

"That's not a thing."

"It could be."

"No."

"What about der Freund? Just der Freund."

He was quiet for a moment. Then: "That works."

"Okay. Next time. Der Freund."

"Next time."

"I'm sorry."

"I know."

"I'll do better."

"I know."

"Also, I ate your apricot pastries again."

"I know. I saw the crumbs."

"You're not going to yell at me?"

"I'm saving it for later. For when you really mess up."

"That's ominous."

"That's love."

He kissed my forehead. Soft. Brief.

"Now call Ada. Invite her to dinner. And this time, introduce me properly."

"What if she doesn't like you?"

"Everyone likes me."

"That's not true."

"It's true enough."

"You're impossible."

"You love me."

"Unfortunately."

He kissed me again. This time on the mouth. The espresso machine hissed. I chose to interpret this as approval.
