Grammar Spotlight

From this chapter: "my Notizbuch" → mein Notizbuch, "your boyfriend" → dein Freund, "his apartment" → seine Wohnung.

Possessive pronouns change endings based on the gender/case of the noun they modify.

The base forms (nominative, masculine, no ending):

Person German English

I mein my

you (du) dein your

he / it sein his / its

she / it ihr her / its

we unser our

you (ihr) euer your (plural)

they / Sie ihr / Ihr their / your (formal)

Example endings you have seen:

· meiner Großmutter (dative feminine → -er)

· seine Hand (nominative feminine → -e)

· deinen Namen (accusative masculine → -en)

Why this matters: Possessives appear constantly. Instead of memorizing the case ending table, notice the patterns as you read. The most common endings are -e (nominative feminine/plural), -en (accusative masculine / dative plural), and -er (dative feminine).

Practical tip: When you see mein, look at the noun after it. If the noun has an ending like -e or -en, the possessive will match. Your brain will absorb this naturally. Also, Matei uses possessives to claim things. Mein Kaffee. Mein Yves. Mein Notizbuch. It's cute. Annoying. But cute.

Writing Prompt

Ada arrives from Lagos. She knew Yves before Berlin. Write her first impression of Matei — not what she says to Yves, but what she thinks and keeps to herself.

Or: Yves has to introduce Matei to Ada properly. Write the sentence he practices in his head three times before he says it out loud.

Shadowing Script

Introductions in German — formal and informal. Read both versions aloud.

Informal: Das ist Matei. Er wohnt hier. Wir... kennen uns. — This is Matei. He lives here. We... know each other.

Formal: Darf ich vorstellen — das ist Matei. — May I introduce — this is Matei.

Notice the ellipsis in the informal version. Wir kennen uns is technically 'we know each other' but Yves uses it because he doesn't have a better word yet. By the end of this book, he will.

Chapter Thirteen — The Dinner

Before You Read

Five words for this chapter:

das Abendessen — dinner

der Strom — electricity / current

die Kaffeemaschine — coffee machine

der Passwort — password

die Verantwortung — responsibility

Yves takes over the café. This chapter is about what it means to stay.

Ada picked a Restaurant in Neukölln.

Something trendy with exposed brick and candles in wine bottles and a Speisekarte written in German that I couldn't read. The kind of place where the portions were small and the prices were large and the waiters looked like they had never dropped a single cup of coffee in their entire perfect lives.

"This place looks expensive," I said.

"It is," Ada said.

"Why did you pick an expensive place?"

"Because you owe me. Twelve years of silence. Interest has accrued."

"That's not how friendship works."

"It's how my friendship works."

She was already there when we arrived, sitting at a table by the window, her red coat draped over the back of her chair like a superhero cape. She had changed into a black dress. She looked like she was about to close a business deal or attend a funeral. Possibly both.

"You look nice," I said.

"I know."

"That was supposed to be a compliment."

"I took it as one."

She stood up. Hugged me. Held on too long.

"You came," she said.

"I said I would."

"You also said you'd write me when you left Nigeria. You didn't."

"I'm not good at goodbyes."

"You never were."

She pulled back. Looked at Matei. He was standing behind me, hands in his coat pockets, face neutral. He had changed into a clean shirt. The one without the coffee stain. I had ironed it for him. He had complained that I was ironing wrong. I had threatened to iron his face. We had compromised.

"You brought your roommate," Ada said.

Matei's jaw tightened. Just a little.

"He's not my roommate."

Ada raised an eyebrow. "No?"

I took a breath. Matei's hand found the small of my back. A touch. A reminder.

"This is Matei. He's my Freund."

The word hung in the air. Freund. I had never said it out loud before. Not about anyone. Not about him. It felt strange in my mouth. Foreign. Like speaking a language I had only just learned.

Ada's expression didn't change. She looked at Matei. Then at me. Then back at Matei.

"The boyfriend," she said.

"The boyfriend," I confirmed.

"Not the roommate."

"Not the roommate."

"The one who makes your coffee."

"Among other things."

"What other things?"

"That's private."

"I'm asking."

"And I'm not answering."

She smiled. "Okay."

"Okay?"

"Okay." She sat back down. Picked up her wine glass. "Sit. I ordered for us already. I hope you still like spicy food."

"What if I don't?"

"Then you should have written me back."

We sat.

Matei pulled out my chair. I blinked at him.

"What are you doing?"

"Being polite."

"You're never polite."

"I'm always polite. I'm Romanian."

"You said that last time. It's not a get-out-of-jail-free card."

"It's working so far."

Ada watched us with the expression of someone who was enjoying herself way too much.

"You two are weird," she said.

"We're in love," Matei said.

"Same thing."

"That's what I keep telling him."

"You're not helping," I said.

"I'm not trying to help. I'm trying to be charming."

"You're failing."

"I'm Romanian. Failing at charm is our national pastime."

Ada laughed. It was the same laugh from twelve years ago, the one that used to make me feel safe. It still worked.

The food came.

It was good. Spicy, like Ada remembered. Rice. Vegetables. Some kind of chicken that made my eyes water. I ate without tasting. I was too busy watching Matei and Ada watch each other.

"So," Ada said, twirling noodles around her fork. "Freund."

"Yes."

"How long?"

"A few weeks. But we've known each other longer."

"How much longer?"

"Two years. Online."

She nodded slowly. "And you moved to Berlin for him?"

"I moved to Berlin because I needed to leave. He was part of it. Not all of it."

"What was the rest of it?"

"Myself."

"That's vague."

"I'm a vague person."

"You're not. You're specific. You just pretend to be vague so people don't ask questions."

"That's not true."

"It's exactly true. You've been doing it since you were eight. I'd ask what you were thinking, and you'd say 'nothing,' and then you'd go write it in your notebook."

"You remember my notebook?"

"You had a notebook. You wrote everything in it. You wrote about your Großmutter. You wrote about the boys you liked but couldn't name. You wrote about wanting to be somewhere else." She set her fork down. "I read it once. You left it open on the porch."

I stared at her. "You read my notebook?"

"It was open."

"That's an invasion of privacy."

"That's what friends do. They invade each other's privacy."

"That's not —"

"It's a little bit true," Matei said.

"Stay out of this."

"I'm just saying. You left your notebook open on the table. Page nineteen. The duck with the crown."

"You're both terrible."

"We're honest," Ada said.

"Same thing," Matei said.

"I hate both of you."

"No, you don't," they said together.

I threw my napkin at Matei. He caught it without looking. Angeber.

Ada put her fork down. Looked at me.

"You kissed me once."

The table went quiet.

"I was eight."

"You were eight. I was nine. I thought about that kiss for years."

"That's concerning."

"It's not concerning. It's honest."

"Honest is overrated."

"You said that already. At the Café."

"It's still true."

"I thought you liked me."

"I did like you."

"Not the way I liked you."

I didn't know what to say. Matei's hand found mine under the table. His fingers laced through mine.

"Ada. I didn't know who I was back then. I barely know now."

"So you kissed me to figure it out?"

"I kissed you because I was trying to be someone I wasn't."

She was quiet for a long moment. The restaurant was loud around us — people laughing, glasses clinking, a waitress shouting orders in rapid German. I caught the word Rechnung and felt a small surge of pride. Then I realized she was yelling at a customer who hadn't paid. So maybe not the best context.

"I'm not angry," Ada said finally. "I was. For a long time. When you stopped talking to me, I thought I had done something wrong. I thought you hated me."

"I didn't hate you."

"I know that now." She looked at Matei. "You're lucky. He's handsome. In a quiet, judgmental way."

"Thank you," Matei said.

"That wasn't a compliment."

"I'm taking it as one."

"You two really are the same person."

"We're not," we said together.

She laughed. "See?"

The rest of dinner was easier.

Ada asked Matei questions. Real ones. Not the polite kind. The kind that made him pause before answering.

"What do you do?"

"I work at a bookstore."

"Do you like it?"

"I like books. Customers are optional."

"Do you want to work there forever?"

"No. I want to write."

"What do you write?"

"Poetry. Bad poetry. I throw most of it away."

"Can I read some?"

"No."

"Why not?"

"Because it's bad. And because Yves would make fun of me."

"I would not," I said.

"You would."

"I would only make fun of you a little."

"That's what I said."

Ada looked between us. "You're disgusting."

"We know."

She turned back to Matei. "Do you love him?"

"Yes."

"Why?"

He looked at me. His grey eyes were soft. The kind of soft he only let me see.

"Because he's the first person who didn't run away when I was quiet. Because he talks to plants. Because he drops cups and apologizes to the floor. Because he made me pasta on the third day and it was the best meal I had had in months." He paused. "Because he's trying. Every day. Even when it's hard."

Ada stared at him. Then at me.

"He's a keeper."

"I know."

"Don't mess it up."

"I'm trying not to."

"Try harder."

After dinner, we walked Ada to the U-Bahn station.

The streets were dark. The Straßenlaternen cast orange light on the pavement. A man played guitar on the corner. He was bad. Really bad. But he was having a great time.

"I'm glad you found someone," Ada said, hugging me.

"I'm glad you found Berlin."

"I'm not going anywhere." She pulled back. Looked at Matei. "You too. Don't let him run."

"I won't."

"And don't let him eat all the pastries."

"Too late."

"Then hide them better."

She waved. Walked down the stairs. Disappeared into the station.

The bad guitarist switched to a song I almost recognized. He was still bad. But he was committed.

"That wasn't so bad," Matei said.

"I thought she was going to cry."

"She almost did."

"So did I."

"You cry at everything."

"I do not."

"You cried at the duck last week. The duck was just sitting there."

"He looked lonely."

"He's a duck. He doesn't have feelings."

"You don't know that."

"I know a lot of things."

"You know everything. It's exhausting."

He put his arm around my shoulders.

"You did good."

"I introduced you as my boyfriend."

"You did."

"Out loud. In front of another person."

"I was there."

"I know. I'm just... processing."

"Take your time."

"I love you."

"I love you too."

"Even though I'm a mess."

"Especially because you're a mess. It's more interesting."

"That's not romantic."

"It's honest. Same thing."

We walked home through the dark streets.

The Kanal was black. The duck was asleep somewhere, probably dreaming of bread. The U-Bahn rumbled beneath us. The city hummed. Berlin at night was different. Quieter. Less judgmental.

"Matei."

"What?"

"Thank you for coming."

"Where else would I be?"

"I don't know. Somewhere else. Angry."

"I'm not angry."

"You're not?"

"No. I'm tired. There's a Unterschied."

"Is there?"

"No. But I'm working on it."

He squeezed my hand. I squeezed back.

"Also, I ate the rest of the apricot pastries. While you were in the bathroom."

"I know. I saw the crumbs on your shirt."

"That's why you're not angry?"

"That's why I'm saving it for later."

"You're impossible."

"You love me."

"Unfortunately."

The next morning, I opened the Café at 6 AM.

I didn't drop any cups. I didn't burn the milk. I made sixteen coffees and remembered to smile at every customer. The espresso machine hissed. I hissed back. It shut up.

At 9 AM, Matei showed up with pastries. The good kind. The apricot ones. He kissed me behind the counter. A customer whistled. I flipped them off. Matei laughed.

"You're getting comfortable," he said.

"I'm getting tired."

"Same thing."

He helped me through the morning rush. At 11, the Café emptied, and we sat at the table with the heart carved into it. T + M. Not us. Someone else. But maybe one day.

"Frau Schmidt called," I said.

"How is she?"

"Better. She wants to come back next week. Just for a few hours. To help."

"That's good."

"She also said I'm not allowed to quit."

"Are you going to?"

I looked around the Café. The green awning. The chalkboard sign. The espresso machine that hissed like a cat. The blue notebook with all the Passwörter.

"No. I think I'm going to stay."

He almost smiled. Almost.

"Good. Because I already told the landlord you're taking over the lease."

"You did not."

"I did."

"You're insane."

"Probably."

"What if I'd said no?"

"You didn't."

"What if I burn it down?"

"Then we open a Café called Burnt. I told you this."

"You're ridiculous."

"I'm supportive."

"Same thing."

I kissed him. In the Café. In the morning light. With the bell above the door silent and the street outside waking up.

"Yves."

"What?"

"You're not running anymore."

"No. I'm not."

"Good. Because I'm out of pastries to bribe you with."

"You still have the plant."

"Matei Jr. is not a bargaining chip."

"He could be."

"Leave the plant out of this."

I laughed. He kissed my forehead.

"Now make me a coffee. Black. No sugar. No milk."

"You know how to make coffee."

"Yours is better."

"That's a lie."

"It's a compliment. Take it."

I made him a coffee. It was perfect. I hated that it was perfect.

"You're getting good at this," he said.

"I'm getting good at a lot of things."

"Like what?"

"Like staying."

He almost smiled. Almost.

Then he drank his coffee, and I drank mine, and we sat at the table with the carved heart, and the morning light came through the window, and the city woke up around us.

And for the first time, I didn't feel like I was pretending.

Grammar Spotlight

From this chapter: "I ate because I was hungry" — in German: Ich aß, weil ich hungrig war.

You have seen subordinate conjunctions like weil (because) and dass (that). They send the verb to the end.

Examples from this chapter (adapted into German):

English German

I ate because I was hungry. Ich aß, weil ich hungrig war.

She said that she wasn't angry. Sie sagte, dass sie nicht wütend sei.

I think that we're good. Ich glaube, dass wir gut sind.

Key pattern: Main clause + conjunction + subject + ... + verb at the end.

Other common conjunctions that send the verb to the end:

· ob (whether)

· wenn (if/when)

· als (when — past)

· bis (until)

· bevor (before)

· nachdem (after)

Why this matters: In high-density German (80%+), you will see these structures constantly. Train your eye to look for the verb at the end after weil, dass, wenn.

Tip from the method: Don't memorize the rule. Just notice it every time it appears. After 50+ examples, your brain will expect the verb at the end. Also, Matei uses weil to explain why he's right. Which is always.

Writing Prompt

Frau Schmidt calls Yves from the hospital. She tells him not to quit. Write the four sentences she doesn't say — the ones underneath the ones she does.

Or: Yves decides to stay. Write what that decision feels like at 5:45am, standing in an empty café that is now his responsibility.

Café German — customer service phrases. Read aloud, memorise, use:

Chapter Fourteen — The Ex

Before You Read

Six words for this chapter:

der Ex — ex-partner

der Verrat — betrayal

das Schweigen — silence (review)

erklaeren — to explain

blass — pale

die Rueckkehr — return / comeback

Sebastian arrives. Everything Matei has protected himself against walks through the door.

Things were fein for exactly one week.

Then the Ex showed up.

I was closing the Café. Wiping down the counter. Counting the register. The usual Routine. Frau Schmidt had come by earlier that morning — her first day back, just for two hours, just to sit at the table and drink coffee and tell customers she was fein. She wasn't fine. Her left hand shook when she held the cup. But she was here. That was something.

Also, she had brought her own mug. It said World's Okayest Boss. I had bought it for her as a joke. She had cried. Then she had threatened to fire me. Then she had cried again.

"It's fine," she had said. "I'm just emotional."

"You're never emotional."

"I'm old. Old people get emotional about mugs."

"That's not a thing."

"It is now."

The bell above the door chimed.

"Wir haben geschlossen," I said without turning around. It was my new phrase. I had practiced it in the mirror. My pronunciation was still terrible, but I was committed.

"Then why is the door open?"

A man was standing in the doorway. Tall. Blonde. Expensive coat. The kind of Lächeln that said he knew he was handsome and had been told so many times that it had become a personality trait. He looked like he had never dropped a cup of coffee in his life. He probably had people for that.

"We're closed," I said.

"I can see that."

"Then why are you here?"

"I'm looking for Matei."

"He's not here."

"I know. His Wohnung was empty. I tried there first."

"You tried his Wohnung? At 7 PM? Without calling first?"

"I don't have his number anymore."

"That's not a coincidence."

He smiled. It was a nice smile. Annoyingly nice. The kind of smile that made you want to punch someone, but also maybe buy them a drink so you could figure out what was wrong with them.

"You must be Yves."

"And you must be the guy who leaves without saying goodbye."

His smile faltered. Just a little. Good.

"Matei told you about me."

"He mentioned you. Once. Briefly. In the context of 'my ex left and took the Frank Ocean album.'"

"It was a limited edition."

"It was a gift. From him. To you. And you took it when you left. That's not just breaking up. That's theft with emotional damage."

He stared at me.

"You're funny."

"I'm not funny. I'm angry on behalf of my boyfriend. There's a Unterschied."

"He's your boyfriend now?"

"He's been my boyfriend. He's my boyfriend. He will continue to be my boyfriend. Possibly forever. We're thinking about matching sweaters."

"Matei doesn't wear matching sweaters."

"Matei will do a lot of things he doesn't do because he loves me. Including matching sweaters. Including learning to like apricot pastries. Including not murdering me when I eat his."

Sebastian laughed. It was a beautiful laugh. I hated that it was beautiful.

"You're different than I expected."

"What did you expect?"

"Someone... quieter."

"I'm quiet. When I want to be. Right now I don't want to be."

"I can see that."

He walked inside. Looked around the Café like he was bewertete it. His eyes landed on the blue notebook, the espresso machine, the heart carved into the table. T + M. Not them. Someone else.

"This place is cute."

"It's not cute. It's functional."

"Same thing."

"It's not."

"You and Matei really are similar."

"We're not."

"You finish each other's sentences?"

"No."

"You argue about semantics?"

"That's not arguing. That's clarifying."

"Same thing."

"You're impossible."

"I'm an architect. Same thing."

He walked to the counter. Leaned on it. Close enough that I could smell his Parfüm — expensive, too strong, the kind that announced itself before you did.

"What do you want?" I asked.

"To talk to Matei. I've been trying to reach him for weeks. He won't answer my calls. He won't reply to my texts."

"Maybe there's a reason for that."

"Maybe. Or maybe he's just being dramatisch. He was always dramatic."

"He's not dramatic. He's Romanian. There's a Unterschied."

"Is there?"

"No. But I'm working on it."

Sebastian laughed again. "I like you."

"I don't care."

"You should. I'm very likable."

"You left your boyfriend with a seven-word note and took his favorite album. You're not likable. You're a cautionary tale."

His smile finally disappeared.

"You don't know the whole story."

"Then tell me."

"It's not your story to know."

"Then leave. And don't come back."

"I can't."

"Can't or won't?"

"Both."

He pulled a card out of his pocket — a business card, white with black text — and set it on the counter.

Sebastian Bauer. Architekt.

"Tell him I stopped by."

"I'll think about it."

"No, you won't."

"You're right. I won't. I'll tell him tonight. Over dinner. Which I will cook. Because I'm good at things."

"Like what?"

"Like pasta. Like coffee. Like not leaving people without explanation."

He looked at me for a long moment. Then he smiled again. The annoying one.

"You're good for him."

"I know."

"Don't mess it up."

"I'm trying not to."

"Try harder."

He walked to the door. Stopped. Turned.

"You're different than I expected."

"You said that already."

"I meant it more the second time."

"That's not how words work."

"It's how my words work."

He left. The bell chimed. The door closed.

I stood there for a long time, staring at the business card.

Sebastian Bauer. Architekt.

"Architect of what?" I muttered. "Bad decisions?"

The espresso machine hissed. I chose to interpret this as obviously.

My phone buzzed.

Matei: Where are you?

Café, I typed back.

You were supposed to close an hour ago.

I know. A customer came in.

At 7 PM?

He said the door was open.

Was it?

Maybe. I'm bad at locking doors. It's a character flaw.

Who was the customer?

I stared at the screen. I could lie. I could say no one or a man who wanted directions or someone who thought we were open for dinner. But I was tired of lying. Tired of hiding. Tired of being the person who always said the easy thing instead of the true thing.

Sebastian, I typed.

A long pause. Three dots appeared. Then disappeared. Then appeared again.

I'll be home in twenty minutes.

Okay.

Don't eat the pastries.

Too late.

Which ones?

All of them.

All of them?

There were only three.

There were six.

...I'll buy more.

You'll make more. From scratch. With your hands.

I don't know how to make pastries.

Then you'll learn. It's in the relationship contract.

There's no contract.

There should be. I'll draft one.

You're impossible.

I'm Romanian. Same thing.

I locked the Café. Double-checked. Triple-checked. Walked home.

The stairs were siebenunddreißig steps. The Schlüssel stuck. The Wohnung was dark.

Matei was on the Sofa. His laptop was open. He wasn't typing. He was staring at the screen. The screen was blank.

"You're home," I said.

"I'm home."

"Are you angry?"

"I'm processing."

"That's not an answer."

"It's the only answer I have."

I sat next to him. Didn't touch him. The plastic chair was empty. It was always empty. I was starting to think it had feelings.

"What did he want?" Matei asked.

"To talk to you. He said you won't answer his calls."

"I won't."

"He said he's been trying for weeks."

"I know."

"He said you're being dramatic."

"I'm not dramatic. I'm Romanian."

"That's what I told him."

"Good."

"I also told him he's a cautionary tale."

Matei looked at me. His grey eyes were tired. But there was something else there. Something that looked like relief.

"You said that?"

"I said a lot of things. I told him we're thinking about matching sweaters."

"We're not."

"He doesn't know that."

"You're terrible."

"I'm protective. There's a Unterschied."

"Is there?"

"No. But I'm working on it."

He almost smiled. Almost.

"What else did you say?"

"I told him you wouldn't murder me when I eat your pastries."

"That's not true. I would definitely murder you."

"You would not."

"I would think about it. For a long time. While making new pastries. That you wouldn't be allowed to eat."

"That's fair."

He leaned back into the Sofa. I leaned into him. His arm went around my shoulders.

"He asked if there was a chance," Matei said quietly.

"A chance for what?"

"For us. For him and me. He said he made a mistake. He said he's sorry. He said he's been thinking about me for years."

"What did you say?"

"I said no."

"Just no?"

"I said no. And then I hung up."

"You hung up on him?"

"I hung up on him."

"That's cold."

"That's what happens when you leave someone with a seven-word note and take their favorite album."

"The Frank Ocean one?"

"The Frank Ocean one."

"That's unforgivable."

"That's what I said."

"Good."

I kissed his cheek. His jaw was rough with Stoppeln. He hadn't shaved. He always shaved when he was stressed.

"Are you okay?" I asked.

"I will be."

"That's not an answer."

"It's the only answer I have."

"You already used that line."

"It's a good line."

"It's an okay line."

"You liked it the first time."

"I was being polite."

"You're never polite."

"I'm always polite. I'm Nigerian."

"That's not a thing."

"It is now."

He laughed. A real laugh. Short. Tired. Real.

"I love you," he said.

"I love you too."

"Even though I'm a mess."

"Especially because you're a mess. It's more interesting."

"That's my line."

"I'm borrowing it."

"Pay me back."

"How?"

"Make me pasta. The good kind. With the expensive cheese."

"You bought the cheese?"

"Yesterday. Before all of this."

"You planned ahead."

"I'm always planning ahead."

"You forgot to buy groceries last week."

"That was different. I was distracted."

"By what?"

"By you. You were singing in the shower. Badly. It was adorable."

"I don't sing badly."

"You sing like a dying cat. It's charming."

"That's not a compliment."

"It is from me."

We made pasta together.

He chopped the onions. I cried. Not from the onions. The Soße came together the way it always did — slow, steady, familiar. The kitchen got hot. The windows fogged up. The whole Wohnung smelled like garlic and something else. Something that felt like home.

"Matei."

"What?"

"Are you going to be okay? With Sebastian being back?"

"I don't know."

"That's honest."

"I'm trying to be."

"It's working."

He stirred the sauce. Didn't look at me.

"He asked if we could be friends. I said I would think about it."

"Will you?"

"I don't know. Maybe. In a year. In five years. Not now."

"That's fair."

"Is it?"

"You're allowed to take time. You're allowed to be angry. You're allowed to not know."

"That's a lot of permission."

"You have it. All of it. Unlimited."

He finally looked at me. His eyes were wet.

"You're too good for me."

"Probably. But I'm keeping you anyway."

He kissed me. Right there in the kitchen, with the sauce bubbling and the pasta water boiling and the whole world outside not mattering at all.

"The pasta is burning," I said.

"Let it."

"That's expensive cheese."

"I'll buy more."

"You said that yesterday."

"I'll say it again tomorrow."

"You're ridiculous."

"I'm in love. Same thing."

We ate at the table. The two mismatched chairs — me on the wooden one, him on the plastic one. The Lampe cast a yellow circle of light over our Teller. The pasta was good. Not great. The sauce had simmered a little too long. But it was ours.

"Yves."

"What?"

"Thank you."

"For what?"

"For being there. For not running. For eating all my pastries so I have a reason to make more."

"You're welcome."

"Also, you have flour in your hair."

"I always have flour in my hair."

"I know. It's cute."

"That's not a compliment."

"It is from me."

I laughed. He almost smiled.

Then we cleaned the kitchen, and he held my hand, and the Heizung clicked, and the street was quiet, and the plant on the windowsill — Matei Jr. — was still alive.

"Matei."

"What?"

"I'm glad you didn't say yes to him."

"Me too."

"I'm glad you chose me."

"I didn't choose you. I kept choosing you. Every day. There's a difference."

"Is there?"

"No. But I'm working on it."

He kissed my forehead. Soft. Brief.

"Gute Nacht Nacht, Yves."

"Gute Nacht Nacht, Matei."

We went to bed. He held me. I didn't sleep.

I stared at the ceiling and thought about Sebastian's smile, his expensive coat, the way he had said "You're good for him" like he was giving me permission.

He wasn't. He didn't get to give permission. He had given up that right when he left.

I turned over. Pressed my face into Matei's back.

"I love you," I whispered.

"I know," he said. "Now sleep. You have to open the Café tomorrow."

"What if I burn it down?"

"Then we open Burnt. I told you this."

"What if I forget to order coffee?"

"Then we sell tea."

"What if I accidentally poison someone?"

"Then we learn to make poison taste better."

"You're not taking this seriously."

"I'm taking you seriously. That's enough."

He was warm. He was here. He was staying.

For now, that was enough.

Grammar Spotlight

From this chapter: Not directly, but Sebastian is described as handsome — implied comparative: "You're different than I expected. Someone... quieter" — the comparative would be leiser (quieter).

Comparative adjectives in German are formed by adding -er to the base adjective. Some take an umlaut (a → ä, o → ö, u → ü).

Common comparatives you will need:

Positive Comparative English

hübsch hübscher pretty → prettier

groß größer big → bigger (umlaut)

klein kleiner small → smaller (no umlaut)

gut besser good → better (irregular)

gern lieber gladly → rather

viel mehr much/many → more

leise leiser quiet → quieter

Example from this chapter: "You're different than I expected. Someone... quieter." → Du bist anders, als ich erwartet habe. Jemand... leiser.

Using als for than: Mein Kaffee ist besser als deiner. (My coffee is better than yours.)

Why this matters: As you read more German, you will need to compare things. The comparative -er is regular for most adjectives, and you will recognize it easily once you have seen it a few times. Also, Matei uses comparatives to compliment Yves. Dein Kaffee ist besser als meiner. It's cute. Annoying. Cute.

Writing Prompt

Sebastian comes back. Write the seven-word note he left when he left. The master prompt says he left it. What seven words?

Or: Write what Yves wants to say to Sebastian and what he actually says. They don't have to be different. But they probably are.

Shadowing Script

Practise these two lines — one formal, one emotional. The contrast is the point.

Sebastian: Es tut mir leid." — I'm sorry.

Matei: Ich weiss." — I know.

Es tut mir leid is the formal, complete apology. Matei's response — Ich weiss — accepts it without offering absolution. Four words total. Enormous weight. Say both lines without rushing.

Review — Part Two: Roots (Chapters 8-14)

Part Two is finished. The past has arrived in Berlin — Sebastian, Ada, the first real tests. Everything that was easy is now complicated. Everything that is complicated is becoming real.

What You Have Learned

New vocabulary that should now feel familiar: das Vertrauen (trust), die Eifersucht (jealousy), der Verrat (betrayal), die Zukunft (future, review), das Gestaendnis (confession), erklaeren (to explain), trotzdem (nevertheless).

New grammar: genitive case in formal writing (des, der), reported speech with dass-clauses, modal verbs deepening (mussen, konnen, wollen, sollen in context).

Production Challenge

Write a short paragraph in German about what has happened between Yves and Matei since the kiss. Five sentences. Use at least three new words from Part Two.

Or: Write the text Yves should have sent Matei about Lukas — the honest version. In German. Max three sentences.

Formal Register Check

You have now seen formal German appearing in café receipts, job listings, and Frau Schmidt's notes. Translate these without help:

1. Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren,

2. Mit freundlichen Gruessen

3. Ich bewerbe mich um die Stelle als...

4. Fuer Ihre Unterstuetzung bedanke ich mich im Voraus.

Translations: 1. Dear Sir or Madam, 2. Kind regards, 3. I am applying for the position as... 4. I thank you in advance for your support.

If these feel natural, your formal register is developing. If they feel strange, re-read the shadowing scripts from Chapters 10 and 11.

Recall Challenge

From memory:

1. What seven-word note did Sebastian leave when he left?

2. Where does Ada come from?

3. What is the name of Matei's plant?

4. What does Lukas do for work?

5. What was Frau Schmidt's diagnosis?

Answers: 1. The master prompt says seven words — the book leaves you to wonder what they were. 2. Lagos — she and Yves grew up together. 3. Matei Jr. 4. He works at the bookstore with Matei. 5. A small stroke, caught early — she will recover.

Part Three is 70-85% German. The story carries you. Trust it.

Chapter Fifteen — The Decision

Before You Read

Five words for this chapter:

die Entscheidung — decision

der Mut — courage

sich bewerben — to apply (reflexive)

die Qualifikation — qualification

der Lebenslauf — CV / resume

Part Three begins. The Ausbildung becomes real. So does everything else.

Four months in Berlin. That was the number I couldn't stop thinking about.

Four months of waking up in Matei's bed. Four months of burning milk and dropping cups and apologizing to the floor. Four months of Frau Schmidt's sharp eyes and Ada's weekly visits and the duck at the bridge — the duck who was definitely judging me, I didn't care what Matei said.

Four months of not running.

And still, every morning, I woke up wondering when it would end.

"You're thinking too loud," Matei said. He was in the kitchen, making coffee. His back was to me. His shoulders were relaxed. He was wearing the shirt that said I'm silently judging you in German. It was 7 AM. He had been awake for an hour.

"I'm always thinking too loud."

"This morning is louder than usual."

"That's not a thing."

"It is now. I invented it. You're thinking about the Ausbildung."

I sat up. The Laken fell to my waist. "How do you know?"

"Because you've been thinking about it for four months. You think about it in your sleep. Last night you said 'I need more Lebenslauf' in your sleep. In German."

"I don't speak German in my sleep."

"You do now. It's adorable. Also concerning."

He walked over with two mugs. Handed me one. Black. No sugar. No milk. Perfekt.

"You're avoiding the topic," he said.

"I'm not avoiding. I'm delaying."

"Same thing."

"No, delaying is strategic. Avoiding is cowardly. There's a Unterschied."

"Is there?"

"No. But I'm working on it."

He sat on the edge of the bed. The mattress dipped. I spilled coffee on my hand. Didn't care.

"Yves. Talk to me."

"What if I'm not good enough?"

"For what?"

"For the Ausbildung. For Germany. For you. For any of this."

He took my coffee. Set it on the table. Took his coffee. Set it next to mine. Then he took my face in his hands. His palms were warm. His thumbs traced my cheekbones.

"Listen to me. You are the most stubborn person I have ever met. You arrived in Berlin with one suitcase and a key. You didn't speak the language. You dropped cups. You cried at a duck."

"I did not cry at the duck."

"You teared up. It counts. You said 'he looks lonely.'"

"He did look lonely."

"He's a duck. Ducks don't have feelings."

"You don't know that."

"I know a lot of things."

"You know everything. It's exhausting."

He kissed my forehead.

"You're going to be fine. You're going to apply. You're going to get rejected. You're going to apply again. And then you're going to get in. And then you're going to be an Azubi. And then you're going to be a Fachinformatiker. And then you're going to buy me a house with a garden."

"That's a lot of pressure."

"That's a lot of confidence. There's a Unterschied."

"Is there?"

"No. But I'm working on it."

The Ausbildung conversation had started three months ago, when Frau Schmidt was still in the hospital.

"What do you actually want?" she had asked. Not what do you want to do or what are your plans — just what do you actually want.

"I don't know," I had said.

"Then find out. Before you waste more time."

"That's harsh."

"That's honest. There's a Unterschied."

"Everyone keeps saying that."

"Because it's true."

I had thought about it for weeks. Lying in bed. Walking to work. Sitting on the bridge, watching the duck paddle in circles. What did I actually want?

Not the café. Not forever. I loved Frau Schmidt and the espresso machine and the regulars who pretended my German was getting better. But the café wasn't mine. It would never be mine. It was hers.

Not the bookstore. Not Matei's world. I loved watching him recommend books to strangers, loved the way his face lit up when someone asked for something unexpected. But I didn't belong behind that counter.

So what?

"IT," I had said one night, out of nowhere.

Matei looked up from his book. "What?"

"IT. Computers. Cybersecurity. That's what I want."

"Okay."

"That's it? Just 'okay'?"

"What do you want me to say?"

"I don't know. Something supportive. Something like 'Yves, that's a great idea, you're very smart, you'll be amazing, let me make you a celebratory coffee.'"

"You're very smart. You'll be amazing. Make your own coffee. I'm reading."

"You're impossible."

"I'm supportive. Same thing."

He had gone back to his book. But the next morning, there was a notebook on the table. A new one. Black. On the first page, in his small, neat handwriting:

IT Ausbildung in Berlin — Resources

· Bundesagentur für Arbeit website

· IHK Berlin — Ausbildung listings

· German IT vocabulary list (I'll help)

· Practice interviews (I'll be the mean interviewer)

· Frau Schmidt knows someone at a Betrieb in Wedding

I had stared at the list for a long time.

"You made me a list," I said.

"I make lists."

"You made me a list about my future."

"I make lists about everything. The plant has a list. Water on Mondays. Sunlight. Don't let Yves talk to it too much."

"You made a list for the plant?"

"Matei Jr. has needs."

"You're insane."

"I'm organized. Same thing."

Now, four months in, I was still staring at that list.

It was on the kitchen table, tucked under the sugar bowl. The sugar bowl was empty. We kept forgetting to buy sugar. Neither of us used it. But it felt wrong to throw it away.

"You're staring at the list again," Matei said.

"I'm not staring. I'm contemplating."

"Same thing."

"No, contemplating is deeper. There's more eye contact with the paper."

"You're ridiculous."

"You love me."

"Unfortunately."

He sat across from me. The plastic chair. It was still empty most days. But today he sat in it. I blinked.

"You're sitting in the plastic chair."

"It's a chair. Chairs are for sitting."

"You never sit in that chair."

"I'm sitting in it now. Don't make it weird."

"You're making it weird by sitting in it."

"You're making it weird by commenting on it."

"This is a stupid conversation."

"This is a necessary conversation. You're avoiding the list."

"I'm not avoiding. I'm —"

"If you say 'delaying,' I'm going to throw this sugar bowl at you. It's empty. It won't hurt. But it will be embarrassing for both of us."

I looked at the list.

Bundesagentur für Arbeit website. I had visited it. Twelve times. The German was too hard. I had cried. Not a lot. A little.

IHK Berlin — Ausbildung listings. I had found three possible programs. I had bookmarked them. I had not applied.

German IT vocabulary list. Matei had made flashcards. I had used them twice. The flashcards were now being used as coasters.

Practice interviews. We had done one. I had said "Ich bin gut mit Computern" and Matei had said "That's not a sentence, that's a cry for help" and I had thrown a pillow at him.

Frau Schmidt knows someone. She did. His name was Herr Köhler. He owned a small IT Betrieb in Wedding. He was looking for Azubis. He had asked for my Lebenslauf. I had not sent it.

"I'm scared," I said.

"I know."

"What if I'm not good enough?"

"Then you get better. That's what Ausbildung is for."

"What if my German is too bad?"

"Then you learn more. That's what living here is for."

"What if they laugh at me?"

"Then they're idiots. And I will write them a strongly worded letter. In Romanian. They won't understand it. But they'll know they're being judged."

"You'd do that?"

"I'd do worse. I'd send them a copy of my poetry."

"That's cruel."

"I'm protective. Same thing."

I picked up the list.

"Okay. Today. I'm going to do it."

"Do what?"

"Send my Lebenslauf to Herr Köhler. Apply for the Ausbildung. Stop being a coward."

"You're not a coward."

"I've been avoiding this for four months."

"You've been preparing. There's a Unterschied."

"Is there?"

"No. But I'm proud of you anyway."

He stood up. Walked to the kitchen. Came back with a pen. The good pen. The one he used for his poetry. The one he said had "creative energy." I thought it was just a pen. He thought it was magic.

"Here. Use this."

"It's a pen."

"It's a creative pen. It has energy."

"Pens don't have energy."

"This one does. I wrote a poem about you with it."

"What poem?"

"I'm not telling you."

"Why not?"

"Because it's bad. And because you'll make fun of me."

"I would not."

"You would."

"I would only make fun of you a little."

"That's what I said."

I took the pen. It was warm from his hand. Or maybe that was the creative energy. Or maybe pens just got warm when you held them. I didn't know. I wasn't a pen scientist.

"Okay. Here goes nothing."

I wrote an email. In German. Bad German. Matei stood behind me, reading over my shoulder.

"That's not how you spell Bewerbung."

"Yes it is."

"It has two 'b's. And an 'u'. And no 'e' after the 'w'."

"German spelling is stupid."

"German spelling is logical. You're just bad at it."

"You're not helping."

"I'm helping by correcting you. That's what help looks like."

"Help looks like encouragement. Not criticism."

"Encouragement is just criticism with a smile. Now fix the spelling."

I fixed the spelling. I wrote the email. I attached my Lebenslauf. The one Matei had helped me write. The one Frau Schmidt had corrected. The one Ada had read and said "This makes you sound like a robot. Add something about your personality." I had added "I make good pasta." She had said "That's not a qualification." I had said "It should be."

My finger hovered over the send button.

"Do it," Matei said.

"What if I regret it?"

"Then you regret it. And you try something else. That's what life is."

"That's very philosophical for 8 AM."

"I'm a very philosophical person. Now press the button."

I pressed it.

The email sent.

"Oh no," I said.

"Oh yes," he said.

"I just sent my Lebenslauf to a stranger."

"You sent your Lebenslauf to a potential employer. There's a Unterschied."

"Is there?"

"Yes. One is terrifying. The other is also terrifying. But one might lead to a job."

"You're not helping."

"I'm making coffee. That's helping."

He made coffee. I stared at the screen. The email was gone. Sent. Irreversible.

"I need to sit down."

"You're already sitting down."

"I need to lie down."

"It's 8:15 AM."

"I'm tired."

"You're dramatic."

"Same thing."

Three days later, Herr Köhler replied.

I was at the Café. Frau Schmidt was at her table, drinking tea, pretending not to watch me refresh my email every thirty seconds.

"You're going to break the computer," she said.

"Computers don't break from refreshing."

"This one might. It's from 2008."

"Then it's your fault for not upgrading."

"It's my fault for hiring someone who refreshes his email like a teenager waiting for a text back."

"I'm not —"

"You are. It's fine. It's cute. Annoying, but cute."

My phone buzzed.

Matei: Check your email.

Why?

Just check it.

I checked it.

There it was. An email from Herr Köhler. In German. Formal German. The kind that made my eyes cross.

Sehr geehrter Herr Yves,

Vielen Dank für Ihre Bewerbung. Ich würde Sie gerne zu einem Vorstellungsgespräch einladen. Können Sie nächsten Donnerstag um 14 Uhr?

Mit freundlichen Grüßen,

Herr Köhler

"Oh no," I said.

"What?" Frau Schmidt asked.

"He wants an interview."

"That's good."

"That's terrifying."

"That's the same thing. Now call Matei. He's probably waiting."

I called Matei.

"You got the email," he said.

"How do you know?"

"Because you called me. You only call when something happens. You text when nothing happens. It's a pattern. I noticed."

"You notice everything."

"I know. It's a curse. What did he say?"

"He wants an interview. Next Thursday. At 2 PM."

"That's six days."

"I know."

"That's enough time to prepare."

"That's not enough time to learn German."

"You don't need to learn German. You need to learn interview German. It's a different language. Smaller vocabulary. More sweating."

"You're not helping."

"I'm going to help you practice. Every night. For six days. You're going to be sick of me by the end."

"I'm already sick of you."

"Good. Then you'll be prepared."

The next six days were a blur of flashcards and fake interviews and Matei being the meanest interviewer in the history of interviews.

"Tell me about yourself," he said, for the thirtieth time.

"My name is Yves. I am from Nigeria. I live in Berlin. I like coffee and ducks and —"

"Stop. That's terrible."

"You told me to tell you about myself."

"Not like that. Like a professional. 'Ich bin Yves, ich komme aus Nigeria, ich lebe seit vier Monaten in Berlin. Ich habe Erfahrung im Kundenservice und interessiere mich für IT und Cybersecurity.' Say it."

"That's too many words."

"That's six words more than you just said. You can do it."

"Ich bin Yves, ich komme aus Nigeria, ich lebe seit vier Monaten in Berlin. Ich habe Erfahrung im Kundenservice und interessiere mich für IT und Cybersecurity."

"Good. Now say it without sounding like a robot."

"That's how I sound."

"Then sound like a different robot. A friendly one. One that drinks coffee and has emotions."

"Robots don't have emotions."

"This one does. Now say it again."

By the fifth night, I could say it in my sleep. By the sixth night, I was dreaming in German. Bad German. German where the verbs were in the wrong place and the nouns had the wrong gender. But German.

"You're ready," Matei said, the night before the interview.

"I'm not ready."

"You're ready."

"What if I freeze?"

"Then you freeze. And then you unfreeze. And then you keep going. That's what staying means."

"That's very philosophical for 11 PM."

"I'm a very philosophical person. Now sleep. You have a big day tomorrow."

"What if I oversleep?"

"I'll wake you."

"What if I forget how to speak German?"

"You'll remember. Your brain knows more than you think."

"What if I accidentally say something stupid?"

"Then you say something stupid. And then you move on. Everyone says stupid things. I said stupid things. Yesterday I told a customer that the book they wanted was 'in the back, probably under something.' I don't even know what's in the back."

"That's not stupid. That's just vague."

"Same thing."

He kissed my forehead.

"Now sleep. Or I'll tell Matei Jr. to keep you awake."

"The plant doesn't have that power."

"The plant has many powers. You just don't know them yet."

I closed my eyes.

The next morning, I woke up before my Wecker. I put on my best shirt. The one without the coffee stain. I drank coffee. Black. No sugar. No milk. I kissed Matei goodbye.

"Break a leg," he said.

"That's for actors."

"Then break a keyboard. Or a router. Something IT-related."

"That's not a thing."

"It is now. I invented it. Now go."

I went.

The interview was in Wedding. The building was grey. The office was small. Herr Köhler had a beard and glasses and a poster of a server rack on his wall. He asked me questions in German. I answered. Sometimes correctly. Sometimes not. But I kept going.

"Why do you want this Ausbildung?" he asked.

I thought about it. About Matei. About the duck. About the key in my pocket. About four months of not running.

"Because I want to stay," I said. "In Berlin. In Germany. And I need something to stay for. Something that's mine."

Herr Köhler looked at me for a long moment.

"That's a good answer," he said.

"Thank you."

"Your German is bad."

"I know."

"But it's better than it was four months ago."

"How do you know that?"

"Frau Schmidt told me. She also told me you drop cups and talk to plants."

"She talks too much."

"She talks the right amount. You'll hear back from us in two weeks."

I stood up. Shook his hand.

"Thank you for your time."

"Thank you for not crying. Frau Schmidt said you might."

"I save my crying for ducks."

He laughed. I left.

I walked to the bridge. The duck was there. Paddling in circles. Looking lonely. Or maybe not. Maybe he was just paddling. Maybe ducks didn't have feelings. Maybe Matei was right.

"I don't know if I got the job," I told the duck.

The duck quacked.

"That's not helpful."

The duck quacked again.

I sat on the Geländer. Pulled out my phone.

Matei: How did it go?

I don't know. He said my German is bad.

That's not news.

He said it's better than it was four months ago.

That's good.

He also said Frau Schmidt warned him I might cry.

Did you?

No. I saved it for the duck.

How is the duck?

Lonely. Or maybe just wet. I can't tell.

Come home. I bought pastries.

The good ones?

The apricot ones. And I hid half of them.

Where?

If I told you, they wouldn't be hidden.

You're impossible.

I'm in love. Same thing.

I walked home. The stairs were siebenunddreißig steps. The Schlüssel stuck. The door opened.

Matei was on the Sofa. The pastries were on the table. Half of them. The other half were somewhere else. I didn't ask where.

"Well?" he said.

"Well what?"

"How do you feel?"

"Terrified. Hopeful. Nauseous. Hungry."

"That's four things."

"I'm a complex person."

"You're a simple person who uses big words to seem complex."

"That's rude."

"That's accurate."

He handed me a pastry. I ate it. It was perfect. I hated that it was perfect.

"Matei."

"What?"

"Thank you."

"For what?"

"For making me do the scary thing."

"I didn't make you. You chose. There's a Unterschied."

"Is there?"

"No. But I'm proud of you anyway."

He kissed me. Pastry crumbs and all.

"Now eat another pastry. You earned it."

"What if I get rejected?"

"Then we try again. That's what staying means."

"What if I get accepted?"

"Then we celebrate. And then you start the Ausbildung. And then you become a Fachinformatiker. And then you buy me that house with the garden."

"You're really committed to this garden thing."

"I want to grow tomatoes. And herbs. And maybe a tree."

"You've never gardened in your life."

"I'll learn. That's what staying means."

I laughed. He almost smiled.

Then we ate the rest of the pastries, and he told me about his day, and I told him about the interview, and the Heizung clicked, and the street was quiet, and the plant on the windowsill — Matei Jr. — was still alive.

Two weeks later, the email came.

Sehr geehrter Herr Yves,

Wir freuen uns, Ihnen mitteilen zu können, dass wir Sie für die Ausbildung zum Fachinformatiker ausgewählt haben.

I read it four times.

Then I called Matei.

"I got it."

"I know."

"How do you know?"

"Because you called. You only call when something happens."

"I got the Ausbildung."

"I know."

"Aren't you going to say something?"

"I bought champagne. It's in the fridge. It's been there for two weeks."

"You bought champagne before I got the answer?"

"I'm optimistic. There's a Unterschied."

"Is there?"

"No. But I was right. Now come home. We're celebrating."

"What if I had been rejected?"

"Then we would have drunk the champagne anyway. To your courage. To trying. To staying."

"You're ridiculous."

"I'm in love. Same thing."

I walked home. The stairs were siebenunddreißig steps. The Schlüssel stuck. The door opened.

Matei was standing in the kitchen. Two glasses. Champagne. The good kind. The expensive kind. The kind he had bought with his book money.

"To staying," he said, handing me a glass.

"To staying," I said.

We drank.

It was cold. Bubbly. Perfect.

I hated that it was perfect.

But I didn't hate anything else.

Grammar Spotlight

From this chapter: "I couldn't stop thinking about" → Ich konnte nicht aufhören zu denken.

You have seen modal verbs in present tense (kann, muss, will, darf, soll, mag). In past tense (imperfect/preterite), they are even more common in written German.

The six modal verbs in simple past:

Infinitive Meaning Simple Past (ich)

können can, to be able to ich konnte

müssen must, to have to ich musste

wollen to want to ich wollte

dürfen may, to be allowed to ich durfte

sollen should, to be supposed to ich sollte

mögen to like ich mochte

Examples from this chapter (adapted):

English German

I couldn't stop thinking. Ich konnte nicht aufhören zu denken.

I wanted to stay. Ich wollte bleiben.

He was supposed to help. Er sollte helfen.

Why this matters: In narratives (like this novel), the simple past of modals appears constantly. Recognizing konnte, musste, wollte helps you understand what characters could, had to, or wanted to do. Also, Matei uses wollte a lot when talking about Yves. Ich wollte dich nicht verlieren. (I didn't want to lose you.) Romantic. Annoying. Romantic.

Or: Write a paragraph in German — no English allowed — describing what Yves wants from the Ausbildung. Not the professional answer. The real one.

Chapter Sixteen — Die Bewerbung

Before You Read

Six words for this chapter:

das Anschreiben — cover letter

die IHK — Chamber of Commerce (Industrie- und Handelskammer)

der Betrieb — company / firm

typisch — typical

ehrlich — honest (review)

die Vorbereitung — preparation

Writing a Bewerbung in German is its own skill. Watch how Matei rewrites Yves's draft.

The champagne was empty. The celebration was over. Now came the hard part: actually applying.

"You already applied," Matei said. We were sitting at the kitchen table. The laptop was open. The screen was bright. It was 7 PM. We had been at this for two hours.

"I applied to one place. Herr Köhler. He said yes. That's one."

"That's the only one you need."

"What if I fail the Ausbildung? What if I hate it? What if Herr Köhler turns out to be a secret villain who locks me in the server room?"

"Why would he lock you in the server room?"

"I don't know. Villains do things like that. It's in the handbook."

"There's no handbook."

"There should be. I'll write one. Chapter one: 'How to Avoid Being Locked in Server Rooms by Potential Employers.'"

"You're ridiculous."

"I'm prepared. Same thing."

He closed the laptop. I reached for it. He moved it out of reach.

"We're taking a break."

"We just took a break. You ate a pastry. I watched you eat a pastry. It was very stressful for me."

"You're stressed by watching me eat?"

"You eat aggressively. It's concerning."

"I eat with passion. There's a Unterschied."

"Is there?"

"No. But I'm working on it."

The truth was, I had already sent out four applications. Four. To four different Betriebe. Three had said no. One — Herr Köhler — had said yes. But Matei kept insisting I should apply to more.

"Options are good," he said.

"Options are stressful."

"Options are security. If one falls through, you have another."

"That's very German of you."

"I'm Romanian. We're also practical. Just with more complaining."

"You don't complain."

"I complain internally. It's more efficient."

He opened the laptop again. Pulled up the IHK website. The one with all the Ausbildung listings. The one that made my eyes cross and my hands sweat.

"Here," he said. "This one. In Neukölln. Small Betrieb. They specialize in cybersecurity."

"Cybersecurity is hard."

"That's why it pays well."

"I don't care about pay. I care about not embarrassing myself."

"You're going to embarrass yourself. That's part of learning. The question is whether you keep going after you embarrass yourself."

"That's very philosophical for 7 PM."

"I'm a very philosophical person. Now write."

We worked on the Bewerbung for three evenings.

The first evening, I wrote a draft. It was terrible. Matei read it in silence. His face did not change. That was how I knew it was bad.

"Say something," I said.

"I'm processing."

"Your face isn't moving."

"My face is thinking."

"Faces don't think."

"My face does. It's a very smart face."

"Just tell me. Is it bad?"

"It's not bad."

"You're lying."

"I'm being polite. There's a Unterschied."

"Is there?"

"No. It's terrible. But we can fix it."

He took the laptop. Started typing. His fingers moved fast. He deleted whole paragraphs. Rewrote sentences. Changed words I didn't know.

"What are you doing?"

"Making it better."

"You're changing everything."

"I'm improving everything. There's a Unterschied."

"You keep saying that."

"Because it keeps being true."

When he was done, he turned the laptop back to me. The screen was different. The words were better. They sounded like me — but a more professional me. A me who knew what he was doing. A me who had never dropped a cup of coffee in his life.

"This isn't me," I said.

"It's you. Just with better grammar."

"I don't talk like this."

"You will. In interviews. On paper. The rest of the time, you can talk like a normal person who says 'glass of cow.'"

"I'm never going to live that down, am I?"

"No. It's my favorite story. I tell it at parties."

"We don't go to parties."

"When we do, I'll tell it then."

The second evening, we worked on the Lebenslauf.

Matei had opinions. Strong opinions. About fonts.

"Times New Roman is for essays and funerals," he said.

"It's a classic font."

"It's a boring font. Use something else. Something with personality."

"My resume doesn't need personality. It needs to get me a job."

"Personality gets you the job. Boring gets you ignored."

"What font do you use?"

"Garamond. It's elegant. It says 'I read books and I have feelings.'"

"Resumes don't have feelings."

"This one will. Now change it."

I changed it. Garamond. It looked the same as Times New Roman. I did not say this out loud. Matei could sense font indifference. It was one of his many talents.

"Now the photo," he said.

"I don't have a photo."

"Take one."

"Now?"

"Yes. Smile."

"I don't smile on command."

"Smile like you just ate the last apricot pastry and I don't know about it."

"That's a very specific direction."

"I'm a very specific person."

I smiled. He took the photo with his phone. He looked at it. Nodded.

"Good. You look mischievous. Employers like that."

"They do not."

"They will. Trust me."

"I trust you. But I also think you're making this up."

"I'm not making it up. I'm intuiting. There's a Unterschied."

"Is there?"

"No. But the photo is staying."

The third evening, we worked on the Anschreiben — the cover letter.

This was the worst part. The part where you had to explain why you wanted the job without sounding desperate. Why you were qualified without sounding arrogant. Why they should pick you without sounding like you were begging.

"I hate this," I said.

"Everyone hates this."

"How do people do this?"

"They lie. A little. They make themselves sound better than they are. It's expected."

"I'm not good at lying."

"You're excellent at lying. You told me you were 'fine' for three weeks when you first arrived. You were not fine. You were a disaster."

"A charming disaster."

"A disaster. The charming part came later."

"That's rude."

"That's honest. Now write. 'Dear Herr Köhler, I am writing to apply for the IT Ausbildung position at your company.'"

"That's how you start?"

"That's how everyone starts. It's boring. But it's safe."

"What if I start with something interesting? Like 'I once asked for a glass of cow, but I promise my IT skills are better than my German.'"

"That's a terrible idea."

"It's memorable."

"It's memorable for the wrong reasons. Don't."

"You're no fun."

"I'm practical. There's a Unterschied."

"You're just saying that now."

"I'm always saying it. You're not listening."

I wrote the boring opening. Then I wrote the middle. Then I wrote the end. Matei read it. Made a face. Made changes. Read it again. Made more changes. Read it a third time.

"It's good," he said.

"You're lying."

"I'm not. It's good. Not great. But good. And good is enough."

"Good is not enough. Good gets you ignored."

"Good gets you an interview. Great gets you the job. You'll be great in the interview. The letter just needs to open the door."

"That's a lot of pressure on the interview."

"That's why we're going to practice. Every night. Until you're sick of me."

"I'm already sick of you."

"Good. Then you'll be prepared."

He pressed send.

"You just sent it."

"I did."

"Without asking me?"

"You would have said no."

"Because I'm not ready!"

"You're ready. You've been ready. You're just scared."

"I'm not scared. I'm —"

"If you say 'delaying,' I'm going to throw this pen at you. It's the creative pen. It has energy. It might hurt."

"Pens don't hurt."

"This one does. I wrote sad poetry with it. It's full of emotion."

"That's not how physics works."

"That's how my physics works. Now stop arguing. The email is sent. It's done. You're going to be fine."

I stared at the screen. The email was gone. Sent. Irreversible.

"I need to lie down."

"It's 9 PM."

"I'm tired."

"You're dramatic."

"Same thing."

The next morning, there was a reply.

Not from Herr Köhler — from a different Betrieb. One I had applied to days ago. The one that had said no. They had changed their mind? No. They had a different position. One that opened up suddenly. Someone had quit. Or been fired. Or locked in a server room. I didn't ask.

Sehr geehrter Herr Yves,

Wir haben Ihre Bewerbung erhalten und möchten Sie gerne zu einem Vorstellungsgespräch einladen.

"Oh no," I said.

"What?" Matei asked. He was in the kitchen. Making coffee. His back was to me.

"Another interview."

"That's good."

"That's two."

"That's options."

"That's stressful."

"That's life. Now drink your coffee. You have applications to write."

"I already wrote them."

"You have more to write. Options, remember?"

"I hate you."

"You love me."

"Same thing."

He handed me my coffee. Black. No sugar. No milk. Perfekt.

"Matei."

"What?"

"Thank you."

"For what?"

"For making me do the thing."

"You did the thing. I just watched."

"You watched and judged and corrected my font."

"Someone had to. You were going to use Times New Roman. That's a crime against typography."

"You're ridiculous."

"I'm supportive. Same thing."

He kissed my forehead.

"Now drink your coffee. You have interviews to prepare for. And I have a list of questions to ask you. And I'm going to be mean. Really mean. The meanest interviewer you've ever met."

"Worse than Herr Köhler?"

"Worse than anyone. I'm going to ask you questions in German so fast you won't understand them. I'm going to interrupt you. I'm going to frown at your answers. I'm going to make you sweat."

"That sounds terrible."

"That's preparation. There's a Unterschied."

"Is there?"

"No. But you're going to be ready."

He was right. I wasn't ready. But I was going to be.

I drank my coffee. He made his list. The plant sat on the windowsill, watching, judging, surviving.

Matei Jr. didn't say anything.

But I knew what he was thinking.

Finally.

Grammar Spotlight

From this chapter: Not explicitly, but let's introduce the genitive because it appears in formal German — like in Bewerbungen and official letters.

The genitive case shows possession. It answers "whose?" In English, we use 's or of. In German, the article changes.

Definite article declension (genitive):

Gender Article Example

masculine des das Haus des Mannes (the man's house)

neuter des das Buch des Kindes (the child's book)

feminine der die Farbe der Blume (the flower's color)

plural der die Arbeit der Leute (the people's work)

Common genitive prepositions you will see:

· wegen (because of)

· trotz (despite)

· während (during)

· anstatt (instead of)

Examples from the IT world (relevant for your Ausbildung):

English German

the company's server der Server des Betriebs

the applicant's qualifications die Qualifikationen des Bewerbers

during the interview während des Vorstellungsgesprächs

Why this matters: In everyday conversation, Germans often use von + dative instead of genitive (das Haus von dem Mann). But in formal writing — emails, letters, applications — the genitive is expected. You need to recognize it, even if you don't fully produce it.

Tip from the method: Don't memorize the table. Just notice that des appears before masculine/neuter nouns, and the noun often adds -s or -es. Your brain will absorb the pattern.

Writing Prompt

Write the bad version of Yves's Bewerbung — the one Matei reads in silence. What is wrong with it? Be specific. What does Yves say about himself that is technically true but professionally wrong?

Or: Write a short formal email in German — max six sentences — applying for an Ausbildung position. Use the vocabulary from this chapter. Use Sie throughout.

Shadowing Script

Formal written German — practise the opening and closing of a professional letter:

Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren, — Dear Sir or Madam,

Hiermit bewerbe ich mich um die ausgeschriebene Ausbildungsstelle als Fachinformatiker. — I hereby apply for the advertised apprenticeship position as an IT specialist.

Ich freue mich Auf Wiedersehen ein persoenliches Gespraech. — I look forward to a personal meeting.

Mit freundlichen Gruessen — Kind regards

Hiermit (hereby) and Mit freundlichen Gruessen (kind regards) are not optional in formal German. They signal that you know the register. Use them.

Chapter Seventeen — Die Ablehnung

Before You Read

Five words for this chapter:

die Ablehnung — rejection

die Enttaeuschung — disappointment

weitermachen — to continue / carry on (separable)

der Rueckschlag — setback

trotzdem — nevertheless / anyway

The first rejection arrives. How Yves handles it matters more than the rejection itself.

The first rejection arrived on a Tuesday.

I was at the Café. Frau Schmidt was at her table. The espresso machine was hissing. The morning rush was over. I was wiping the counter, thinking about nothing, when my phone buzzed.

Betreff: Ihre Bewerbung bei IT-Solutions Berlin

I didn't recognize the name. I had applied to so many Betriebe that they had started to blur together. This one was in Kreuzberg. Small. Specialized in network security. The interview had gone okay. Not great. Okay.

I opened the email.

Sehr geehrter Herr Yves,

Vielen Dank für Ihre Bewerbung und Ihr Interesse an einer Ausbildung bei IT-Solutions Berlin.

Leider müssen wir Ihnen mitteilen, dass wir uns für einen anderen Kandidaten entschieden haben.

Wir wünschen Ihnen für Ihre weitere Suche viel Erfolg.

Mit freundlichen Grüßen,

IT-Solutions Berlin

"Oh," I said.

Frau Schmidt looked up. "What?"

"Nothing."

"You said 'oh.' That's not nothing."

"It's a small thing."

"Your face says otherwise."

"My face is fine."

"Your face looks like someone ate your pastries."

"Someone did. Matei. Yesterday. He didn't even apologize."

"That's not why you're upset."

"It's part of it."

"Yves."

I handed her my phone. She read the email. Her face didn't change. She handed it back.

"That's one," she said.

"That's one rejection."

"That's one Ablehnung. There will be more. And then there will be an acceptance. That's how this works."

"What if there aren't more acceptances?"

"Then you try again. Next year. Or you find a different path. That's how life works."

"That's very philosophical for 11 AM."

"I'm a very philosophical person. Now stop moping. The bathroom needs cleaning."

"The bathroom always needs cleaning."

"That's because you do a bad job. Clean it better this time."

I cleaned the bathroom.

Then I cleaned it again.

Then I sat on the toilet lid and stared at the wall and thought about the word Ablehnung. Rejection. It sounded like what it was. Sharp. Final. The kind of word that didn't leave room for argument.

My phone buzzed.

Matei: How's work?

Fine.

You're lying.

How do you know?

You said "fine." You only say "fine" when something is wrong. When things are actually fine, you say "it's okay" or "not terrible" or "I only dropped one cup."

I only dropped one cup.

What's wrong?

I got a rejection.

Which one?

IT-Solutions Berlin.

Their office is ugly anyway.

You've never been to their office.

I don't need to. I can tell from their website. It's beige. Beige is the color of people who don't have personalities.

That's not a thing.

It is now. I invented it. Come home early. I bought pastries.

The good ones?

The apricot ones. And I'm not hiding them. You can have as many as you want.

That's suspicious.

I'm being nice.

You're never nice.

I'm always nice. I'm Romanian.

That's not an excuse.

It's not an excuse. It's an explanation.

I left work early. Frau Schmidt waved me out the door.

"Go. Eat pastries. Feel sorry for yourself. Tomorrow you try again."

"What if I don't want to try again?"

"Then you don't. And you find something else. But you do it tomorrow. Not today. Today you eat."

"You're a good boss."

"I know. Now go before I change my mind and make you clean the bathroom again."

I went.

Matei was on the Sofa when I got home.

The pastries were on the table. All of them. Six. Apricot. Glazed. Perfect.

"You didn't hide any," I said.

"I told you. I'm being nice."

"Why?"

"Because you got rejected. And rejection sucks. And pastries help. Scientifically proven."

"By whom?"

"By me. I'm a scientist. Of pastries."

"That's not a real job."

"It could be. I'll write a book about it. The Pastry Scientist: How Baked Goods Heal Emotional Wounds."

"That's the worst title I've ever heard."

"That's the best title you've ever heard. You're just jealous."

I sat next to him. Ate a pastry. Then another.

"I'm going to eat all of these," I said.

"I know."

"And I'm not going to feel bad about it."

"Good."

"And tomorrow I'm going to apply to more places."

"Good."

"And I'm going to get rejected again."

"Probably."

"And then I'm going to apply again."

"Good."

"You're not saying much."

"I'm listening. There's a Unterschied."

"Is there?"

"Yes. Listening means I hear you. Saying means I interrupt you. I'm trying not to interrupt."

"That's very mature of you."

"I'm a very mature person. Now eat another pastry. You're still sad. I can tell."

"How can you tell?"

"You're eating aggressively again. It's your sad-eating face."

"I have a sad-eating face?"

"You have many faces. It's one of them."

We sat in silence for a while. The Heizung clicked. The Lampe buzzed. The plant sat on the windowsill, alive, judging, surviving.

"Matei."

"What?"

"What if I never get an Ausbildung?"

"Then you do something else."

"Like what?"

"I don't know. You're creative. You'll figure it out."

"What if I don't figure it out?"

"Then I'll help you."

"What if you can't help me?"

"Then we'll both be confused together. That's better than being confused alone."

"That's very romantic."

"I'm a very romantic person."

"You're not. You're just saying that because I'm sad."

"I'm saying it because it's true. Now eat another pastry."

"I can't. I'm full."

"That's never stopped you before."

"I'm also feeling sick. From the rejection. And the pastries."

"That's called a sugar crash. Drink water."

He handed me water. I drank it.

"Matei."

"What?"

"Thank you."

"For what?"

"For not saying 'I told you so.'"

"I told you so."

"You just said it."

"I know. I waited until after you thanked me. It's polite. There's a Unterschied."

"Is there?"

"No. But I feel better."

"You're impossible."

"You love me."

"Unfortunately."

The next morning, I woke up early.

Matei was still asleep. His breathing was slow. His face was soft. He looked younger when he slept. Less like a person who remembered everything and more like a person who forgot things sometimes — like groceries, and birthdays, and the fact that he had promised to fix the crack in the ceiling.

I got up quietly. Made coffee. Black. No sugar. No milk. Made a second cup for him. Left it on the table.

Then I opened my laptop.

The IHK website. The Ausbildung listings. The same ones that had made me cry two weeks ago. I scrolled through them. Found a new one. In Wedding. Close to Herr Köhler's office. Different specialty — more systems administration, less cybersecurity.

"You're up early," Matei said. He was standing in the doorway. His hair was a mess. His eyes were half-closed. He was wearing the shirt that said I'm silently judging you in German.

"I couldn't sleep."

"Nightmares about rejections?"

"No. I was thinking."

"About what?"

"About applying again."

"Good."

"To this one." I turned the laptop toward him. He read the listing. Nodded.

"Good choice."

"You don't know anything about it."

"I know it's in Wedding. I know you can walk there. I know the name sounds reliable. 'SecureNet Systems.' That's a good name. It says 'we know what we're doing.'"

"That's not how company names work."

"It is now. I'm a naming expert."

"You're a bookseller."

"Booksellers know names. We sell things with names on them."

"That's not —"

"Are you going to argue with me, or are you going to write the Bewerbung?"

I wrote the Bewerbung.

It was better this time. Faster. Less crying. Fewer typos. I still spelled Bewerbung wrong twice, but Matei caught it. He was reading over my shoulder. His breath was warm on my neck.

"That's not how you spell 'qualifications.'"

"Yes it is."

"It has two 'f's. And no 'c'."

"German spelling is —"

"If you say 'stupid,' I'm going to delete this entire email and make you start over."

"You wouldn't."

"Try me."

I fixed the spelling.

I attached my Lebenslauf. The one with the Garamond font. The one with the mischievous photo. The one that Matei had said was "full of personality" and Frau Schmidt had said was "fine, I guess" and Ada had said was "very you, whatever that means."

I wrote the subject line: Bewerbung als Azubi — Yves

"That's boring," Matei said.

"Subject lines are supposed to be boring."

"No, they're supposed to be clear. Boring is fine. Clear is better. Yours is both. Good job."

"Was that a compliment?"

"It was an observation. Don't get used to it."

I hovered over send.

"Do it," he said.

"What if they reject me?"

"Then they reject you. And you try again."

"What if I run out of places to try?"

"Then you move to a different city. Or a different country. Or you start your own IT company. Or you become a professional pastry eater. I don't know. But you don't give up. That's not who you are."

"That's exactly who I am. I'm a runner. I run from things."

"You used to run. Now you stay. There's a Unterschied."

"Is there?"

"Yes. You're still here. You're still trying. You're still eating my pastries. That's not running. That's being annoying. And I love you for it."

"That's not romantic."

"It's honest. Same thing."

I pressed send.

The reply came four days later.

I was at the bridge. The duck was there. Paddling. Judging. Being a duck.

My phone buzzed.

Betreff: Ihre Bewerbung bei SecureNet Systems

I opened it.

Sehr geehrter Herr Yves,

Vielen Dank für Ihre Bewerbung.

Wir würden Sie gerne zu einem Vorstellungsgespräch einladen.

"Oh," I said.

The duck quacked.

"I got an interview."

The duck quacked again.

"That's not helpful, but I appreciate the enthusiasm."

I called Matei.

"I got an interview."

"I know."

"How do you know?"

"Because you called. You only call when something happens."

"It's with SecureNet Systems. The one in Wedding."

"The one with the reliable name."

"The one with the reliable name."

"When is it?"

"Next Thursday. At 10 AM."

"That's seven days."

"I know."

"That's enough time to prepare."

"I know."

"I'm going to be mean again. Really mean. The meanest interviewer you've ever met."

"You said that last time."

"I meant it last time. I mean it more this time."

"That's not how intensity works."

"It is now. I invented it. Now come home. We're celebrating."

"What are we celebrating? I haven't gotten the job yet."

"We're celebrating the interview. And the fact that you didn't give up. And the fact that you only cried a little."

"I didn't cry."

"You teared up. At the bridge. The duck saw you."

"The duck doesn't have feelings."

"The duck has feelings. You taught him."

"I hate you."

"You love me."

"Same thing."

I walked home. The stairs were siebenunddreißig steps. The Schlüssel stuck. The door opened.

Matei was in the kitchen. Not making coffee. Making something else. Something that smelled like garlic and tomatoes and home.

"What are you making?"

"Pasta. Your grandmother's recipe."

"You learned it?"

"I watched you make it. Fifty times. Maybe more."

"That's creepy."

"That's love. Same thing."

He handed me a fork. I tasted the sauce. It was perfect. I hated that it was perfect.

"You're getting good at this."

"I'm getting good at a lot of things."

"Like what?"

"Like staying. Like being patient. Like not murdering you when you eat my pastries."

"That's three things."

"I'm a complex person."

"You're a simple person who uses big words to seem complex."

"That's my line."

"I'm borrowing it."

"Pay me back."

"How?"

"Help me with the interview prep. Be mean. Really mean. Make me sweat."

"I can do that."

"I know. That's why I keep you around."

We ate pasta. Drank wine. The cheap kind. The one that came in a box. Matei said it was "vintage." I said it was "box wine." He said "same thing."

After dinner, we sat on the Sofa. The Lampe buzzed. The Heizung clicked. The plant sat on the windowsill. Alive. Thriving. Judging.

"Matei."

"What?"

"What if I get this job?"

"Then you start the Ausbildung. And you learn. And you struggle. And you get better. And then you're a Fachinformatiker."

"And then?"

"And then you buy me that house with the garden."

"You're really committed to this garden thing."

"I want to grow tomatoes. And maybe a duck."

"You can't grow a duck."

"You can grow anything if you try hard enough."

"That's not how biology works."

"That's how my biology works."

"You're impossible."

"You love me."

"Unfortunately."

He kissed me. Soft. Slow.

"You're going to be fine."

"You don't know that."

"I know you. That's enough."

I leaned into him. His arm went around my shoulders.

"Matei."

"What?"

"Thank you. For not letting me give up."

"You didn't give up. You just paused. There's a Unterschied."

"Is there?"

"No. But I'm proud of you anyway."

We sat like that until the Lampe flickered and the street went quiet.

Tomorrow, I would prepare for the interview. I would practice with Matei. I would sweat. I would stumble. I would get better.

But tonight, I was just here.

And for now, that was enough.
