Grammar Spotlight

From this chapter: "Trotz der Ablehnung" (Despite the rejection) — trotz takes the genitive.

Common genitive prepositions you will see in formal writing and interviews:

Preposition Meaning Example

wegen because of wegen der Ablehnung (because of the rejection)

trotz despite trotz des Fehlers (despite the mistake)

während during während des Vorstellungsgesprächs (during the interview)

anstatt instead of anstatt einer Pause (instead of a break)

außerhalb outside of außerhalb der Arbeitszeit (outside of work hours)

innerhalb inside of innerhalb einer Woche (within a week)

Examples from this chapter (adapted):

English German

Because of the rejection, I was sad. Wegen der Ablehnung war ich traurig.

Despite the rejection, I applied again. Trotz der Ablehnung habe ich mich wieder beworben.

During the interview, I was nervous. Während des Vorstellungsgesprächs war ich nervös.

Why this matters: In everyday conversation, many Germans use von + dative instead (wegen von der Ablehnung). But in written German — emails, applications, formal letters — the genitive is correct. You need to recognize it, especially when reading emails from potential employers.

Tip from the method: Don't memorize the prepositions. Just notice that after wegen, trotz, während, the following article often changes (der → des for masculine/neuter, die → der for feminine/plural). Your brain will absorb the pattern.

Writing Prompt

Write Yves's reply to the rejection email. Not the one he sends. The one he writes first, before Matei reads it over his shoulder and tells him to delete the last paragraph.

Or: Three rejections in. Write the conversation Yves has with the duck at the bridge. The duck, as always, says nothing. But Yves keeps talking anyway.

Shadowing Script

Rejection and persistence vocabulary — say these with conviction:

Vielen Dank fuer Ihre Rueckmeldung. — Thank you very much for your response.

Ich werde meine Bewerbungsunterlagen ueberarbeiten. — I will revise my application documents.

Ich bleibe an diesem Thema dran. — I will keep working on this.

Trotzdem — nevertheless / anyway

Trotzdem is one of the most useful words in the German language. It means: I know what you said, and I am continuing anyway. Use it.

Chapter Eighteen — The Architect

Before You Read

Five words for this chapter:

der Architekt — architect (here: the person who designed something)

das System — system

konfigurieren — to configure

das Betriebssystem — operating system

analysieren — to analyse

IT work gets specific here. These words will appear in your Ausbildung exams.

Sebastian came back three days after my interview with SecureNet Systems.

I was closing the Café. Wiping the counter. Counting the register. The usual Routine. Frau Schmidt had gone home early. Her hand was shaking again. She didn't say anything, but I saw her hide it in her pocket.

"You're staring," she had said.

"I'm observing."

"You're worried. It's fine. I'm old. Old people shake."

"That's not a thing."

"It is now. I invented it."

"That's my line."

"I'm borrowing it. Pay me back by not burning down my Café."

I had promised not to burn down the Café. She had looked at me like she didn't believe me. Fair.

The bell above the door chimed.

"Wir haben geschlossen," I said without turning around. My pronunciation was getting better. Almost intelligible.

"I know."

I turned.

Sebastian. Same blonde hair. Same expensive coat. Same smile that made me want to punch something. He was holding a bouquet of flowers. Sunflowers. The kind you buy when you want to say I'm sorry without actually saying I'm sorry.

"What are those for?" I asked.

"They're for Matei."

"Matei is allergic to sunflowers."

"He's not."

"He is now. I invented it. He breaks out in hives. It's very dramatic. He cries."

"Matei doesn't cry."

"He cries at commercials. The ones with dogs. And soldiers coming home. It's very moving. You should see it."

"You're lying."

"I'm protecting. There's a Unterschied."

"Is there?"

"No. But the flowers are staying outside."

I took the flowers. Walked to the door. Set them on the sidewalk. Came back inside.

"That was rude," he said.

"That was boundary-setting. There's a Unterschied."

"You keep saying that."

"Because you keep crossing boundaries. Now what do you want?"

He walked to the table with the carved heart. Sat down. The chair creaked. He crossed his legs. Looked around the Café like he was appraising real estate.

"I wanted to see him. To apologize. Properly. Not over the phone."

"You already apologized. Over the phone. He told me. He said it was 'fine.' That's Matei for 'I'm still angry but I don't want to talk about it.'"

"I know."

"Then why are you here?"

"Because I want to try again. Not with him. With being... not a terrible person."

"That's a low bar."

"I know."

"You're not helping your case."

"I'm aware."

I stared at him. He stared at me. The espresso machine hissed. I chose to interpret this as get on with it.

"Matei isn't here. He's at work. The bookstore. He'll be there until six."

"I know."

"Then go there."

"I can't."

"Why not?"

"Because he told me not to. He said he needs space. He said he'll call me when he's ready."

"Then wait."

"I'm tired of waiting."

"That's too bad. Waiting is what you do when you hurt someone. You wait. You don't show up with flowers and expect forgiveness."

"I don't expect forgiveness."

"Then what do you expect?"

He was quiet for a long moment. The Lampe buzzed. The Heizung clicked. Somewhere downstairs, the bakery was closing.

"I expect nothing. I just wanted to see if he was okay."

"He's okay. He's better than okay. He's happy. Annoyingly happy. He smiles now. Real smiles. Not the almost ones."

"The almost smiles." Sebastian's voice was soft. "I remember those."

"Good for you. He doesn't almost smile anymore. He smiles. Because of me. Because I make him coffee and eat his pastries and talk to his plant."

"You talk to his plant?"

"Matei Jr. is a very good listener."

"You named the plant Matei Jr.?"

"It was either that or 'The Green One.' He chose Matei Jr."

"He didn't choose."

"He didn't say no. That's consent."

Sebastian laughed. It was a sad laugh. The kind that said I miss this without saying it.

"You're good for him."

"I know."

"He deserves someone good."

"I know."

"I wasn't good."

"I know."

"You say that a lot."

"Because it keeps being true."

He stood up. Walked to the counter. Pulled out his wallet.

"I'll take a coffee. Black. No sugar. No milk."

"That's Matei's order."

"I know."

"You're copying him."

"I'm remembering him. There's a Unterschied."

"Is there?"

"No. But I'm trying."

I made him the coffee. Black. No sugar. No milk. My hands were steady. I was proud of that.

He took a sip. Made a face.

"It's good."

"You look surprised."

"I am. Matei said you were bad at coffee."

"Matei is a liar. I'm excellent at coffee. I'm excellent at a lot of things."

"Like what?"

"Like staying. Like not leaving seven-word notes. Like not stealing limited-edition Frank Ocean albums."

He flinched. Good.

"You're not going to let that go, are you?"

"No. It's my favorite story. I tell it at parties."

"You don't go to parties."

"When I do, I'll tell it then."

He finished his coffee. Set the cup down. Looked at me.

"Tell Matei I stopped by."

"He knows."

"How?"

"Because I'm going to tell him. Tonight. Over dinner. Which I will cook. Because I'm good at things."

"You said that already."

"It's still true."

He walked to the door. Stopped. Turned.

"Yves."

"What?"

"Thank you. For taking care of him."

"I'm not taking care of him. I'm loving him. There's a Unterschied."

"Is there?"

"Yes. One is a job. The other is a choice. I choose him. Every day. Even when he's annoying. Even when he corrects my German. Even when he steals the last pastry and pretends he didn't."

"He does that?"

"He's a monster. A lovable monster. But a monster."

Sebastian smiled. A real smile. Sad. Tired. Real.

"Goodbye, Yves."

"Goodbye, Sebastian."

He left. The bell chimed. The door closed.

I stood there for a long time, staring at the empty cup.

That night, I told Matei.

We were on the Sofa. The Lampe was on. The Heizung clicked. Matei Jr. sat on the windowsill, alive, thriving, judging.

"Sebastian came to the Café today."

Matei didn't look up from his book.

"I know."

"How do you know?"

"Because you have that look. The look of someone who had a conversation they didn't want to have."

"That's not a thing."

"It is now. I invented it. What did he want?"

"To apologize. To see if you were okay. To drink your coffee order and pretend it was his."

"Did you give him coffee?"

"I gave him coffee. Black. No sugar. No milk. He said it was good."

"It is good."

"I know. I made it."

"You're getting good at things."

"I'm getting good at a lot of things."

"Like what?"

"Like staying. Like not running. Like not punching your ex in the face even though he deserves it."

"He doesn't deserve it."

"He does. A little."

"Maybe a little."

Matei closed his book. Set it on the table. Turned to look at me.

"What else did he say?"

"He said he wants to try again. Not with you. With being a better person."

"That's good."

"Is it?"

"Yes. People should try to be better. Even people who hurt you."

"That's very forgiving of you."

"I'm not forgiving him. I'm acknowledging that people change. There's a Unterschied."

"Is there?"

"Yes. Forgiving means letting go. Acknowledging means I see it but I don't have to do anything about it."

"That's very philosophical for 9 PM."

"I'm a very philosophical person. Now eat your pastry. You're stress-eating with your face again."

"I don't have a stress-eating face."

"You do. It's the same as your sad-eating face. But with more intensity."

"You're impossible."

"You love me."

"Unfortunately."

We ate pastries. Drank coffee. Sat in silence. The good kind. The kind that didn't need words.

"Matei."

"What?"

"Are you okay?"

"I will be."

"That's not an answer."

"It's the only answer I have."

"You used that line already."

"It's a good line."

"It's an okay line."

"You liked it the first time."

"I was being polite."

"You're never polite."

"I'm always polite. I'm Nigerian."

"That's not a thing."

"It is now. I invented it."

He almost smiled. Almost.

"I love you," he said.

"I love you too."

"Even though I'm a mess."

"Especially because you're a mess. It's more interesting."

"That's my line."

"I'm borrowing it."

"Pay me back."

"How?"

"Make me pasta. The good kind. With the expensive cheese."

"You bought the cheese?"

"Yesterday. Before all of this."

"You planned ahead."

"I'm always planning ahead."

"You forgot to buy groceries last week."

"That was different. I was distracted."

"By what?"

"By you. You were practicing interview questions in the shower. In German. You said 'Ich bin gut mit Computern' seventeen times. It was adorable."

"I said it seventeen times?"

"I counted."

"That's creepy."

"That's love. Same thing."

We made pasta. He chopped the onions. I cried. Not from the onions. The Soße came together. The kitchen got hot. The windows fogged up.

"Matei."

"What?"

"Are you going to see him? Sebastian? When he calls?"

"I don't know. Maybe. Someday. Not now."

"That's fair."

"Is it?"

"You're allowed to take time. You're allowed to be angry. You're allowed to not know."

"That's a lot of permission."

"You have it. All of it. Unlimited."

He looked at me. His eyes were wet.

"You're too good for me."

"Probably. But I'm keeping you anyway."

He kissed me. Right there in the kitchen, with the sauce bubbling and the pasta water boiling and the whole world outside not mattering at all.

"The pasta is burning," I said.

"Let it."

"That's expensive cheese."

"I'll buy more."

"You said that yesterday."

"I'll say it again tomorrow."

"You're ridiculous."

"I'm in love. Same thing."

After dinner, we sat on the Sofa. The Lampe buzzed. The Heizung clicked. The plant sat on the windowsill. Alive. Thriving. Judging.

"Matei."

"What?"

"Thank you."

"For what?"

"For not running. For staying. For being here."

"I'm not going anywhere."

"You say that a lot."

"Because you need to hear it."

"I do."

"I know."

He kissed my forehead. Soft. Brief.

"Gute Nacht Nacht, Yves."

"Gute Nacht Nacht, Matei."

We went to bed. He held me. I didn't sleep.

I stared at the ceiling and thought about Sebastian's flowers, his sad smile, the way he had said "You're good for him" like he was giving me permission.

He wasn't. He didn't get to give permission. That wasn't how love worked.

Love was choosing. Every day. Even when it was hard. Even when your ex showed up with sunflowers and apologies.

I turned over. Pressed my face into Matei's back.

"I love you," I whispered.

"I know," he said. "Now sleep. You have to open the Café tomorrow."

"What if Sebastian comes back?"

"Then you give him coffee. Black. No sugar. No milk. And you tell him I'm busy."

"What if he brings more flowers?"

"Then you put them outside. With the others."

"What if he asks about the plant?"

"Tell him Matei Jr. is allergic to architects."

"That's not a thing."

"It is now. I invented it."

"You're impossible."

"You love me."

"Unfortunately."

He was warm. He was here. He was staying.

For now, that was enough.

Grammar Spotlight

From this chapter: "He was warm. He was here. He was staying." — In German: Er war warm. Er war hier. Er blieb.

You have seen the present tense of sein (to be) and haben (to have). In written German — especially narratives — the simple past (imperfect/preterite) is used instead of the present perfect.

Simple past of sein (to be):

Person German English

ich war I was

du warst you were

er/sie/es war he/she/it was

wir waren we were

ihr wart you (plural) were

sie/Sie waren they/you (formal) were

Simple past of haben (to have):

Person German English

ich hatte I had

du hattest you had

er/sie/es hatte he/she/it had

wir hatten we had

ihr hattet you (plural) had

sie/Sie hatten they/you (formal) had

Examples from this chapter (adapted):

English German

He was tired. Er war müde.

She had a key. Sie hatte einen Schlüssel.

We were happy. Wir waren glücklich.

They had coffee. Sie hatten Kaffee.

Why this matters: In spoken German, you will hear ich bin gewesen (present perfect) more often. But in written German — novels, emails, formal writing — the simple past is standard. Recognizing war and hatte will help you read faster. Also, Matei uses war when talking about the past. Früher war ich anders. (I was different before.) It's sad. But honest.

Writing Prompt

Write Yves's internal monologue during his first IT task at the Betrieb. He knows what he's doing — technically. But he's watching himself from the outside. Write that split.

Or: Write a short technical explanation in German — how does a firewall work? Use simple sentences. You don't need perfect German. You need clear German.

Shadowing Script

IT workplace German — say these aloud until natural:

Ich habe das Problem identifiziert. — I have identified the problem.

Das System muss neu gestartet werden. — The system needs to be restarted.

Ich schicke Ihnen die Dokumentation. — I will send you the documentation.

Koennen Sie das kurz erklaeren? — Can you explain that briefly?

Koennen Sie das kurz erklaeren is the sentence that will save you more times than any other in your first year. Say it without embarrassment. Asking for clarification is professional.

Chapter Nineteen — Die Schwester

Before You Read

Five words for this chapter:

die Schwester — sister

die Entfremdung — estrangement

die Versoehnnung — reconciliation

Schuld haben — to be at fault / to owe

schweigen — to be silent (verb form)

Andreea comes to Berlin. The wound between siblings is not so different from any other wound.

The woman walked into the Café on a Thursday.

Not Ada. Not Sebastian. Someone new. Dark hair, tired eyes, a coat that had seen better winters. She looked like she had been traveling for days. She looked like she hadn't slept in years.

"Guten Morgen," I said. My German was getting better. Almost confident.

"Sprechen Sie Englisch?" she asked.

"Yes. Unfortunately."

She almost smiled. Almost.

"I'm looking for Matei."

"Everyone is looking for Matei."

"I'm his sister."

I stopped wiping the counter.

"Andreea."

"You know me."

"He mentioned you. Once. Briefly. In the context of 'my sister told me to come home after Sebastian left and I didn't.'"

"That's not how it happened."

"That's how he told it."

"He left out the part where I was trying to protect him."

"Protection feels different on the receiving end."

She looked at me for a long moment. Then she sat down at the table with the carved heart. The chair creaked. She didn't seem to notice.

"You're Yves."

"I'm Yves."

"He talks about you."

"Everyone says that."

"He doesn't talk about anyone. That's how I know you're important."

"I'm not important. I'm just loud."

"Same thing."

I made her a tea. Chamomile. She held the cup with both hands. Her fingers were cold. The Café was warm, but she was shivering.

"How long have you been in Berlin?" I asked.

"Three days."

"Three days? And you're just now coming to the Café?"

"I was waiting. For courage."

"It takes courage to see your brother?"

"It takes courage to face someone you failed."

I didn't know what to say to that. So I made her another tea. And another pastry. The apricot ones. Matei would be angry. I didn't care.

"He's at work. The bookstore. He'll be there until six."

"I know."

"Then go there."

"I can't."

"Why not?"

"Because he won't see me. He's been ignoring my calls for years. My emails. My letters. Everything."

"That's a long time to ignore someone."

"I know."

"What did you do?"

She was quiet for a moment. The Lampe buzzed. The espresso machine hissed.

"I told him to come home. After Sebastian left. I said, 'Berlin isn't your home. Romania is. Come back. Start over. Forget him.'"

"That's not terrible advice."

"It's not the advice that was terrible. It's that I didn't listen when he said no."

"He said no?"

"He said, 'This is my home now. I'm not leaving.' And I said, 'Then you're making a mistake.' And he hung up. And he didn't call back. For years."

"That's a long time to be angry."

"He's not angry. He's hurt. There's a Unterschied."

"Is there?"

"Yes. Anger passes. Hurt stays. Until someone apologizes."

"Did you apologize?"

"I tried. He wouldn't listen."

"Maybe he wasn't ready."

"Maybe. But I'm here now. And I'm not leaving until he talks to me."

We sat in silence. The Café was empty. The morning rush was over. The afternoon rush hadn't started. It was just us and the hissing espresso machine and the ghost of Frau Schmidt's judgment from her table in the corner.

"He's happy," I said.

"What?"

"Matei. He's happy. Annoyingly happy. He smiles now. Real smiles. Not the almost ones."

"The almost smiles," she said. "I remember those."

"Everyone remembers those. It's a thing. He almost-smiled at me for weeks before he actually smiled. I counted. It was forty-three almost-smiles before the first real one."

"You counted?"

"I keep a list. In my notebook. Page nineteen."

"You're strange."

"I'm in love. Same thing."

She laughed. It was a small laugh. Tired. Hopeful.

"You're good for him."

"I know."

"Don't mess it up."

"I'm trying not to."

"Try harder."

At 5 PM, I closed the Café early.

Frau Schmidt would have been angry. But Frau Schmidt was at home, recovering, her shaky hand wrapped around a mug that said World's Okayest Boss. She would understand. Probably. Maybe. I'd bring her pastries tomorrow.

"Where are we going?" Andreea asked.

"To the bookstore. To see Matei."

"I told you. He won't see me."

"He'll see me. And I'll make him see you. That's what boyfriends are for."

"That's not —"

"That's exactly what boyfriends are for. Now come on. You're buying me coffee. The bookstore coffee is terrible, but it's free for employees."

"I'm not an employee."

"You're Matei's sister. That's close enough."

The bookstore was busy.

A poetry reading in the back room. Someone with a loud voice and a guitar that was slightly out of tune. The front was quieter. A few customers browsing. A woman at the counter buying a stack of children's books.

Matei was behind the counter.

He was helping a customer. An older man with a beard and a question about something in the science fiction section. Matei was explaining. Patient. Precise. The way he did everything.

Then he looked up.

He saw me. Then he saw Andreea.

His face didn't change. But his hands — his hands stopped moving.

"Yves," he said.

"Matei."

"What is she doing here?"

"She came to see you. She's been in Berlin for three days. She's been staying at a Pension in Prenzlauer Berg. She's been waiting for courage."

"Courage for what?"

"To apologize. To explain. To see her brother."

"I didn't ask for an apology."

"That's not the point."

"What's the point?"

"The point is that she's here. And she's not leaving until you talk to her. And I'm not leaving until you talk to her. And the customers are starting to stare."

They were. The woman with the children's books was watching. The man with the science fiction question was watching. Even the poet in the back room had paused mid-stanza.

"Fine," Matei said. "We'll talk. But not here."

"Where?"

"The Café. After closing. Just us."

"And me?" I asked.

"You'll be there. You're always there."

"That's not an answer."

"It's the only answer I have."

We closed the Café at 8 PM.

Andreea sat at the table with the carved heart. Matei sat across from her. I stood behind the counter, pretending to clean the espresso machine. Not listening. Definitely listening.

"I'm sorry," Andreea said.

"I know."

"I should have listened. When you said Berlin was your home. I should have trusted you."

"Yes."

"I was scared. After Sebastian left, I thought you were going to fall apart. I thought coming home would fix you. I thought I could fix you."

"I don't need fixing."

"I know that now."

"What changed?"

"You changed. You stopped answering my calls. You stopped writing. You disappeared into your life here. And I realized that I was the one who needed fixing. Not you."

Matei was quiet for a long moment. The Lampe buzzed. The Heizung clicked.

"I was angry," he said. "For a long time. Not at you. At myself. For not being enough. For not being worth staying for."

"You were enough. Sebastian was the problem. Not you."

"I know that now."

"What changed?"

"He did." Matei looked at me. "He showed up with one suitcase and a key. And he stayed. Even when it was hard. Even when I was quiet. Even when I forgot to buy groceries."

"You still forget to buy groceries," I said.

"I'm working on it."

"You're not."

"I'm working on working on it."

Andreea laughed. It was a real laugh. Wet. Hopeful.

"You're annoying," she said.

"I'm in love. Same thing."

They talked for hours.

About Romania. About their parents. About the father who drank and the mother who pretended everything was fine. About the years they raised each other. About the silence that had grown between them.

I stayed behind the counter. Made coffee. Drank coffee. Pretended not to listen.

At 11 PM, Andreea stood up.

"I should go. My Pension closes at midnight."

"Stay," Matei said.

"What?"

"Stay. With us. The Sofa is uncomfortable, but it's better than a Pension."

"The Sofa is terrible," I said. "I slept on it for two weeks. My back still hurts."

"You're not helping."

"I'm being honest. There's a Unterschied."

"Is there?"

"No. But she should still stay."

Andreea looked at me. Then at Matei.

"Are you sure?"

"I'm sure," he said.

"I don't want to intrude."

"You're not intruding. You're family. There's a Unterschied."

"Is there?"

"Yes. Family doesn't need an invitation. Family just shows up."

She hugged him. He hugged her back. It was awkward. Stiff. The way people hug when they're not used to hugging.

"I'll take the Sofa," she said.

"No, you won't. You'll take the bed. Yves and I will take the Sofa."

"The Sofa is not big enough for two people."

"We'll manage."

"You'll be uncomfortable."

"We're always uncomfortable. It's fine."

We walked home together.

The streets were dark. The Straßenlaternen cast orange light on the pavement. Andreea walked between us. Her hand brushed mine.

"Thank you," she whispered.

"For what?"

"For bringing me to him."

"I didn't bring you. You came. I just opened the door."

"That's the same thing."

"No, opening the door is passive. Coming is active. There's a Unterschied."

"You sound like him."

"I live with him. It's contagious."

She laughed. Matei almost smiled.

The stairs were siebenunddreißig steps. The Schlüssel stuck. The door opened.

The Wohnung was small. Smaller than it had ever felt. One bed. One Sofa. One plant on the windowsill.

"Matei Jr., meet Andreea," I said.

"You named the plant Matei Jr.?"

"He named it after himself. It's a whole thing."

"It's not a thing," Matei said.

"It's a thing. You talk to it."

"I water it. That's not talking."

"You told it about your day yesterday. I heard you."

"You were supposed to be asleep."

"I was pretending. I'm good at pretending."

Andreea looked between us.

"You're both insane."

"We know."

She took the bed. We took the Sofa.

It was too small. My legs hung off the end. Matei's elbow was in my ribs. The cushion was lumpy. The fabric was scratchy.

"This is terrible," I said.

"You slept on this for two weeks."

"I know. I complained every day."

"You complained every hour."

"Same thing."

He shifted. His arm went around me. His chest was warm against my back.

"Matei."

"What?"

"Are you okay?"

"I will be."

"That's not an answer."

"It's the only answer I have."

"You used that line already."

"It's a good line."

"It's an okay line."

"You liked it the first time."

"I was being polite."

"You're never polite."

"I'm always polite. I'm Nigerian."

"That's not a thing."

"It is now. I invented it."

He kissed my forehead. Soft. Brief.

"Thank you."

"For what?"

"For bringing her. For not asking permission. For being annoying."

"The last one wasn't a compliment."

"It was from me."

In the other room, Andreea was breathing. Slow. Steady. Asleep.

The plant sat on the windowsill. Alive. Thriving. Judging.

"Matei."

"What?"

"I'm glad you talked to her."

"I'm glad she came."

"What now?"

"Now we figure it out. Slowly. One day at a time."

"That's very optimistic for 1 AM."

"I'm an optimistic person."

"You're not. You're a realist who sometimes pretends to be optimistic."

"That's the same thing."

"It's not."

"It is now. I invented it. Now sleep. You have to open the Café tomorrow."

"What if Andreea steals the pastries?"

"Then you steal them back. That's what family does."

"That's not —"

"Sleep, Yves."

I closed my eyes.

The Sofa was terrible. My back would hurt tomorrow. My neck would hurt tomorrow. Everything would hurt tomorrow.

But Matei was warm. Andreea was here. The plant was alive.

And for the first time in weeks, I didn't feel like running.

I felt like staying.

Grammar Spotlight

From this chapter: "I remember those" → Ich erinnere mich daran. (sich erinnern an)

Many reflexive verbs in German are paired with specific prepositions. The preposition determines the case (usually accusative).

Common reflexive verb + preposition combinations:

Verb Preposition Case Example

sich erinnern an an (+ acc.) accusative Ich erinnere mich an den Schlüssel. (I remember the key.)

sich freuen Auf Wiedersehen Auf Wiedersehen (+ acc.) accusative Ich freue mich Auf Wiedersehen das Wochenende. (I'm looking forward to the weekend.)

sich freuen über über (+ acc.) accusative Ich freue mich über das Geschenk. (I'm happy about the gift.)

sich kümmern um um (+ acc.) accusative Ich kümmere mich um die Pflanze. (I take care of the plant.)

sich interessieren für für (+ acc.) accusative Ich interessiere mich für IT. (I'm interested in IT.)

Examples from this chapter (adapted):

English German

I remember the almost smiles. Ich erinnere mich an die fast-Lächeln.

I'm looking forward to seeing you. Ich freue mich Auf Wiedersehen dich.

Take care of him. Kümmere dich um ihn.

Why this matters: In high-density German, you will see these reflexive-preposition combinations constantly. Instead of memorizing the list, notice the pattern: sich + verb + preposition + noun. The preposition links the verb to the thing being remembered, looked forward to, or cared for.

Tip from the method: When you see sich erinnern, look for an nearby. When you see sich freuen, look for Auf Wiedersehen (future) or über (past/present). Your brain will absorb the connections.

Writing Prompt

Andreea has been waiting in a pension in Prenzlauer Berg for three days before Matei agrees to see her. Write one of those days. What does she do? What does she think about?

Or: Write the moment Matei sees Andreea for the first time in years. From Yves's perspective — he is watching both of them.

Shadowing Script

Emotional vocabulary — say these aloud, slowly:

Ich habe dich vermisst. — I missed you.

Es tut mir leid, dass ich so lange gewartet habe. — I'm sorry I waited so long.

Ich bin froh, dass du hier bist. — I'm glad you're here.

Wir haben viel zu besprechen. — We have a lot to talk about.

None of these are difficult words. But they are hard to say. That is the point. Practise saying them until they feel available — until you can reach for them when you need them.

Chapter Twenty — Die zweite Bewerbung

Before You Read

Five words for this chapter:

die zweite Bewerbung — the second application

die Cybersicherheit — cybersecurity

das Vorstellungsgespraech — job interview

vorbereiten — to prepare (separable)

selbstbewusst — self-confident

German density is now 85-95%. Trust what you have learned. You know more than you think.

Andreea stayed for four days.

She slept in the bed. We slept on the Sofa. My back hurt. My neck hurt. Everything hurt. But Matei was warm, and his sister made coffee in the mornings, and the apartment smelled like Romania for the first time in years.

"You're still here," Matei said on the fourth morning.

"I'm leaving today."

"Where are you going?"

"Back to Romania. Back to work. Back to my life."

"You could stay."

"I could. But I won't."

"Why not?"

"Because you don't need me here. You have him." She looked at me. "And he's annoying enough for two people."

"That's rude," I said.

"That's honest. There's a Unterschied."

"Everyone keeps saying that."

"Because it keeps being true."

She hugged Matei. Held on longer than usual.

"Come visit," she said.

"Maybe."

"Not maybe. Promise."

"I don't make promises."

"Then make an exception."

"I don't make exceptions either."

"You're impossible."

"You love me."

"Unfortunately."

She hugged me too. Her arms were strong. Her perfume smelled like cigarettes and something floral. I didn't pull away.

"Take care of him," she said.

"I'm trying."

"Try harder."

"I'm trying to try harder."

"That's not a thing."

"It is now. I invented it."

She laughed. Then she left. The door closed. The apartment felt bigger. Emptier. Quieter.

"Are you okay?" I asked.

"I will be."

"That's not an answer."

"It's the only answer I have."

"You need new answers."

"Then help me find them."

The interview with SecureNet Systems was in three days.

Matei had made a list. A long list. On yellow paper. With bullet points.

"You made a list," I said.

"I make lists."

"This list has sub-lists."

"Lists need sub-lists. It's hierarchical."

"You're not an IT person."

"I'm an organized person. Same thing."

The list had everything: possible questions, sample answers, vocabulary to memorize, topics to research. He had even drawn a small diagram of a server network. It was wrong. I didn't tell him.

"This is wrong," I said.

"It's symbolic. There's a Unterschied."

"Is there?"

"No. But it looks impressive."

"It looks like a stick figure having a seizure."

"That's called modern art."

We practiced every night.

He sat on the wooden chair. I sat on the plastic one. The one no one used. It was uncomfortable. That was the point.

"Tell me about yourself," he said.

"My name is Yves. I am from Nigeria. I live in Berlin. I speak German badly but I'm improving. I once asked for a glass of cow."

"Don't say that."

"It shows personality."

"It shows you don't know the difference between Milch and Kuh."

"That's the same thing."

"It's not."

"It is now. I invented it."

"You didn't invent anything. Now say it again. Without the cow."

"My name is Yves. I am from Nigeria. I live in Berlin. I speak German. I'm learning IT because I like computers and I want to stay in this country."

"Why do you want to stay?"

"Because of Matei."

"Don't say that either."

"Why not? It's true."

"Because it's not professional. They don't care about your boyfriend. They care about your skills."

"My boyfriend is a skill."

"He's not."

"He could be. I could put him on my Lebenslauf. 'Languages: English, German (basic), Matei (advanced).'"

"You're impossible."

"You love me."

"Unfortunately. Now say it again. Without the jokes."

We practiced for three hours.

I learned how to say "I have experience in customer service" (Ich habe Erfahrung im Kundenservice). I learned how to say "I am reliable and motivated" (Ich bin zuverlässig und motiviert). I learned how to say "I am willing to learn" (Ich bin bereit zu lernen) without sounding like a robot.

"You still sound like a robot," Matei said.

"I am a robot. A robot who makes coffee and cries at ducks."

"That's not a selling point."

"It's a personality. There's a Unterschied."

"Is there?"

"No. But it's all I have."

The night before the interview, I couldn't sleep.

Matei was already in bed. His breathing was slow. His arm was around my waist. But I was staring at the ceiling, thinking about servers and networks and German words I didn't know.

"You're thinking too loud," he murmured.

"I'm nervous."

"I know."

"What if I forget everything?"

"Then you remember. That's what brains do."

"What if I say something stupid?"

"Then you say something stupid. And then you say something smart. And they remember the smart thing."

"That's not how memory works."

"It's how my memory works. Now sleep."

"What if I oversleep?"

"I'll wake you."

"What if I can't find the office?"

"I'll draw you a map."

"What if they ask about my Lebenslauf and I realize I lied?"

"Did you lie?"

"I said I was 'proficient in Microsoft Office.' I'm not. I can open Word. That's it."

"That's proficiency."

"It's not."

"It is now. I invented it. Now sleep."

I didn't sleep.

But at 7 AM, Matei woke me with coffee. Black. No sugar. No milk. Perfect.

"You look terrible," he said.

"I feel terrible."

"Good. Terror means you care."

"Or it means I'm about to throw up."

"Same thing. Now drink your coffee. You have an interview to win."

The office was in Wedding.

Same neighborhood as Herr Köhler. Different building. Greyer. Smaller. The sign on the door said SecureNet Systems in a font that was definitely not Garamond. Matei would be disappointed.

I walked in. A woman at the front desk smiled. She had kind eyes. The kind that said I've seen a lot of nervous applicants and you're not the worst.

"Yves?"

"Yes."

"They're ready for you. Second door on the left."

I walked to the door. Knocked. Entered.

Three people sat at a table. Two men. One woman. They were all wearing glasses. The woman had a laptop. The older man had a beard. The younger man had a coffee stain on his shirt. I felt immediately better.

"Guten Morgen," I said.

"Guten Morgen, Herr Yves. Bitte, setzen Sie sich."

I sat. The chair was comfortable. Not plastic. Not wooden. Something with padding. It felt like hope.

The interview lasted forty-five minutes.

They asked about my background. My experience. My German. My motivation. I answered. Sometimes correctly. Sometimes not. But I kept going.

"Why do you want this Ausbildung?" the woman asked.

I thought about Matei. About the duck. About the key in my pocket. About Andreea and Sebastian and Frau Schmidt and all the people who had stayed when I wanted to run.

"Because I want to build something," I said. "A life. A future. Something that's mine. And I need the skills to do it."

The woman nodded. The older man wrote something on his notepad. The younger man smiled.

"Your German is good," the woman said.

"It's okay."

"It's better than okay. It's good. And it will get better."

"Thank you."

"We'll let you know next week."

I stood up. Shook their hands. Walked out.

The woman at the front desk smiled again.

"How was it?"

"I don't know. I said 'glass of cow' once. But I think they understood."

"You said what?"

"It's a long story. I'll write a book about it."

I walked to the bridge.

The duck was there. Paddling. Judging. Being a duck.

"I think it went okay," I told him.

The duck quacked.

"That's not helpful."

The duck quacked again.

"You're right. I should just wait. Waiting is the hard part."

The duck quacked a third time. I chose to interpret this as you're an idiot but I support you.

My phone buzzed.

Matei: How did it go?

I don't know. I said "glass of cow" again.

You said it again?

It slipped out.

How does "glass of cow" slip out?

I was nervous.

You're impossible.

You love me.

Unfortunately. Come home. I bought pastries.

The good ones?

The apricot ones. And I'm not hiding them.

That's suspicious.

I'm being supportive.

You're never supportive.

I'm always supportive. I'm Romanian.

That's not an excuse.

It's not an excuse. It's an explanation.

I walked home. The stairs were siebenunddreißig steps. The Schlüssel stuck. The door opened.

Matei was in the kitchen. Not making coffee. Making pasta. My grandmother's recipe. The sauce was bubbling. The kitchen smelled like garlic and home.

"You're making pasta," I said.

"You had an interview. That's worth pasta."

"What if I don't get the job?"

"Then you had an interview. That's still worth pasta."

"What if I never get a job?"

"Then you'll be a professional pasta eater. I'll support you."

"That's not a real job."

"It could be. You'd be good at it. You have experience."

"I have experience eating your pastries."

"That's the same thing."

He handed me a fork. I tasted the sauce. It was perfect. I hated that it was perfect.

"You're getting good at this."

"I'm getting good at a lot of things."

"Like what?"

"Like being patient. Like not murdering you when you say 'glass of cow' in interviews. Like staying."

"That's three things."

"I'm a complex person."

"You're a simple person who uses big words to seem complex."

"That's my line."

"I'm borrowing it."

"Pay me back."

"How?"

"Help me with the thank-you email. I don't know how to say 'thank you for not laughing at me' in German."

"Say 'Vielen Dank für das freundliche Vorstellungsgespräch.'"

"That's too formal."

"Formal is good. Formal gets you jobs."

"What if I want to say something funnier?"

"Then you don't get the job. And I'll be stuck with you forever."

"You're already stuck with me forever."

"I know. That's the problem."

"That's not what you said last night."

"Last night I was tired. Tonight I'm honest."

"Same thing."

He kissed me. Sauce on his lips. Garlic on his tongue.

"You're going to get the job."

"You don't know that."

"I know you. That's enough."

We ate pasta. Drank wine. The cheap kind. The one that came in a box. Matei said it was "rustic." I said it was "box wine." He said "same thing."

After dinner, we sat on the Sofa. The Lampe buzzed. The Heizung clicked. The plant sat on the windowsill. Alive. Thriving. Judging.

"Matei."

"What?"

"What if I don't get this job?"

"Then you apply to another one."

"What if I don't get any job?"

"Then you keep trying. That's what staying means."

"That's very optimistic for 9 PM."

"I'm an optimistic person."

"You're not. You're a realist who sometimes pretends to be optimistic."

"That's the same thing."

"It's not."

"It is now. I invented it. Now sleep. You have to open the Café tomorrow."

"What if I dream about the interview?"

"Then dream about getting the job. That's called manifesting. It's very trendy."

"You don't believe in manifesting."

"I believe in you. That's the same thing."

I closed my eyes.

The Sofa was still lumpy. My back still hurt. But Matei was warm, and the pasta was in my stomach, and the apartment smelled like garlic and hope.

Three days later, the email came.

Sehr geehrter Herr Yves,

Wir freuen uns, Ihnen mitteilen zu können, dass wir Sie für die Ausbildung zum Fachinformatiker ausgewählt haben.

I read it four times.

Then I called Matei.

"I got it."

"I know."

"How do you know?"

"Because you called. You only call when something happens."

"I got the Ausbildung."

"I know."

"Aren't you going to say something?"

"I bought champagne. It's in the fridge. It's been there for two weeks."

"You bought champagne before I got the answer?"

"I'm optimistic. There's a Unterschied."

"Is there?"

"No. But I was right. Now come home. We're celebrating."

"What if I had been rejected?"

"Then we would have drunk the champagne anyway. To your courage. To trying. To staying."

"You're ridiculous."

"I'm in love. Same thing."

I walked home. The stairs were siebenunddreißig steps. The Schlüssel stuck. The door opened.

Matei was standing in the kitchen. Two glasses. Champagne. The good kind. The expensive kind. The kind he had bought with his book money.

"To staying," he said, handing me a glass.

"To staying," I said.

We drank.

It was cold. Bubbly. Perfect.

I hated that it was perfect.

But I didn't hate anything else.

Grammar Spotlight

From this chapter: "You will get the job" → Du wirst den Job bekommen.

In German, the future tense is formed with the present tense of werden (to become) + the infinitive of the main verb at the end of the sentence.

Present tense of werden:

Person German English

ich werde I become/will

du wirst you become/will

er/sie/es wird he/she/it becomes/will

wir werden we become/will

ihr werdet you (plural) become/will

sie/Sie werden they/you (formal) become/will

Future tense formation: werden (conjugated) + infinitive (at the end)

English German

I will learn. Ich werde lernen.

You will succeed. Du wirst Erfolg haben.

He will stay. Er wird bleiben.

Examples from this chapter (adapted):

English German

You will get the job. Du wirst den Job bekommen.

We will celebrate. Wir werden feiern.

It will be perfect. Es wird perfekt sein.

Why this matters: In spoken German, the present tense is often used for the future (Ich mache das morgen — I'll do that tomorrow). But in written German and formal contexts, the werden + infinitive construction appears frequently. Recognizing it will help you understand when something is going to happen.

Tip from the method: Don't overthink it. When you see werde, wirst, wird, werden, werdet, look for the infinitive at the end of the sentence. That's the action that will happen.

Or: Write entirely in German. One paragraph. Yves arrives at the Betrieb for the second interview. What he sees, what he feels, what he tells himself.

Ich bin bereit is one of the first sentences in this book. It appears in Chapter One. It means something different now.

Chapter Twenty-One — Das Vorstellungsgespräch

Before You Read

Five words for this chapter:

das Vorstellungsgespraech — job interview (review)

der Bewerber — applicant

die Fachkompetenz — specialist competence

ueberzeugen — to convince

der Handschlag — handshake

The interview. Everything from the last twenty chapters has been preparing you for this.

Three days before the acceptance email. Three days before the champagne. Three days before Matei said "I told you so" with his eyes instead of his mouth.

The morning of the interview, I woke up before my Wecker.

Not because I was ready. Because I had dreamed about servers. Angry servers. Servers that spoke German too fast and laughed when I didn't understand.

"You're sweating," Matei said. He was already awake. Already dressed. Already holding coffee.

"I'm nervous."

"You're sweating. There's a Unterschied."

"Is there?"

"No. Drink this."

He handed me the coffee. Black. No sugar. No milk. Perfect. I drank it. Burned my tongue. Didn't care.

"What if they ask me something I don't know?"

"Then you say you don't know. And then you say you'll learn. That's what interviews are for."

"What if they ask me why I want to work in IT and I say 'because I like computers' and they say 'that's not a reason'?"

"Then you say 'why not?' and stare at them until they feel uncomfortable."

"That's terrible advice."

"That's excellent advice. Confidence is 90% of interviews. The other 10% is not saying 'glass of cow.'"

"I'm never going to live that down."

"No. Now put on your shirt. The one without the stain."

"All my shirts have stains."

"The one with the smallest stain."

I wore the blue shirt. The one Frau Schmidt had said made me look "professional but approachable." I didn't know what that meant. But it was clean. Mostly.

Matei walked me to the U-Bahn.

"You don't have to come," I said.

"I know."

"You have work."

"I called in late."

"You're going to get fired."

"I'm Romanian. We don't get fired. We just become more passive-aggressive until our bosses quit."

"That's not how employment works."

"It's how my employment works. Now go. Your train is coming."

The train arrived. I stepped on. The doors closed. Matei stood on the platform, hands in his pockets, watching me leave.

"Break a leg!" he yelled through the glass.

"That's for actors!" I yelled back.

"Then break a router!"

The train pulled away. I watched him disappear.

The office was in Wedding.

I had been there before. For the first interview. The one that led to nothing. The one where the interviewer had looked at my Lebenslauf and said "interesting" in a way that meant "not interesting at all."

This time was different. New building. New people. New hope.

The receptionist smiled. "Yves?"

"Yes."

"They're ready for you. Down the hall, third door on the left."

I walked down the hall. My shoes squeaked. The floor was shiny. The kind of shiny that made you feel like you were walking on water. I tried not to look down. I looked down.

The third door on the left was open.

Inside, three people sat at a table. Two men. One woman. The woman had a laptop. The older man had a beard. The younger man had a coffee stain on his shirt. I felt immediately better.

"Guten Morgen," I said.

"Guten Morgen, Herr Yves. Bitte, setzen Sie sich."

I sat. The chair was comfortable. Not plastic. Not wooden. Something with padding that bounced when I shifted my weight. It felt like hope.

"Erzählen Sie uns etwas über sich," the woman said.

Tell us something about yourself.

I had practiced this. Fifty times. With Matei. With Frau Schmidt. With Ada, who had called from across the city to wish me luck and remind me not to say anything stupid.

"Mein Name ist Yves. Ich komme aus Nigeria. Ich lebe seit vier Monaten in Berlin. Ich habe Erfahrung im Kundenservice — ich arbeite in einem Café — und ich interessiere mich für IT und Cybersecurity."

The woman nodded. The older man wrote something on his notepad. The younger man smiled.

"Ihr Deutsch ist gut," the woman said.

"Danke. Es wird besser. Jeden Tag."

Thank you. It's getting better. Every day.

"Warum möchten Sie eine Ausbildung in der IT machen?"

Why do you want to do an IT apprenticeship?

I thought about Matei. About the key. About the duck. About all the things I wanted to build.

"Weil ich etwas bauen möchte. Ein Leben. Eine Zukunft. Etwas, das mir gehört. Und ich brauche die Fähigkeiten dafür."

Because I want to build something. A life. A future. Something that belongs to me. And I need the skills for it.

The woman nodded again. The older man stopped writing. The younger man leaned forward.

"Haben Sie schon Erfahrung mit Programmierung?" the younger man asked.

Do you have any experience with programming?

"Ein bisschen. Ich habe online Kurse gemacht. HTML. CSS. Ein bisschen Python. Nicht viel. Aber ich lerne schnell."

A little. I've done online courses. HTML. CSS. A little Python. Not much. But I learn fast.

"Warum Python?"

Why Python?

"Weil es einfach ist. Am Anfang. Und weil mein Freund gesagt hat, dass es gut für Anfänger ist."

Because it's simple. At the beginning. And because my boyfriend said it's good for beginners.

The woman raised an eyebrow. The older man looked up. The younger man smiled wider.

"Ihr Freund?"

Your boyfriend?

"Ja. Er ist... sehr unterstützend. Auch wenn er zu viel korrigiert."

Yes. He's... very supportive. Even though he corrects too much.

They laughed. The older man's laugh was a wheeze. The younger man's laugh was a giggle. The woman's laugh was a smile.

"Das ist gut," the woman said. "Unterstützung ist wichtig."

That's good. Support is important.

The interview continued.

They asked about my Lebenslauf. About my time at the Café. About why I left Nigeria. About why I chose Berlin.

I answered. Sometimes in complete sentences. Sometimes in fragments. Sometimes in German that made me cringe.

But I kept going.

"Haben Sie Fragen an uns?" the woman asked at the end.

Do you have any questions for us?

"Ja. Wie ist die Arbeitskultur hier? Sind die Kollegen freundlich? Gibt es Kaffee?"

Yes. What's the work culture like here? Are the colleagues friendly? Is there coffee?

The older man laughed again. The wheeze.

"Ja, es gibt Kaffee. Sehr viel Kaffee. Vielleicht zu viel."

Yes, there's coffee. A lot of coffee. Maybe too much.

"Das ist perfekt," I said. "Ich bin süchtig."

That's perfect. I'm addicted.

The interview ended.

I stood up. Shook their hands. The woman's hand was warm. The older man's hand was rough. The younger man's hand had a coffee stain on the thumb.

"Wir melden uns in einer Woche," the woman said.

We'll contact you in a week.

"Vielen Dank für Ihre Zeit."

Thank you for your time.

I walked out. The receptionist smiled.

"How was it?"

"I said 'I'm addicted to coffee.' I think it went okay."

"You said what?"

"It's a long story. I'll write a book about it."

I walked to the bridge.

The duck was there. Paddling. Judging. Being a duck.

"I think it went okay," I told him.

The duck quacked.

"That's not helpful."

The duck quacked again.

"You're right. I should just wait. Waiting is the hard part."

The duck quacked a third time. I chose to interpret this as you're an idiot but I support you.

My phone buzzed.

Matei: How did it go?

I don't know. I said I'm addicted to coffee.

You said that?

It slipped out.

How does "I'm addicted to coffee" slip out?

I was nervous.

You're impossible.

You love me.

Unfortunately. Come home. I bought pastries.

The good ones?

The apricot ones. And I'm not hiding them.

That's suspicious.

I'm being supportive.

You're never supportive.

I'm always supportive. I'm Romanian.

That's not an excuse.

It's not an excuse. It's an explanation.

I walked home. The stairs were siebenunddreißig steps. The Schlüssel stuck. The door opened.

Matei was in the kitchen. Not making coffee. Making pasta. My grandmother's recipe. The sauce was bubbling. The kitchen smelled like garlic and home.

"You're making pasta," I said.

"You had an interview. That's worth pasta."

"What if I don't get the job?"

"Then you had an interview. That's still worth pasta."

"You're going to make pasta every time I do something scary?"

"Yes. It's a new tradition. I invented it."

"You didn't invent pasta."

"I invented the tradition. There's a Unterschied."

He handed me a fork. I tasted the sauce. It was perfect. I hated that it was perfect.

"You're getting good at this."

"I'm getting good at a lot of things."

"Like what?"

"Like being patient. Like not murdering you when you say weird things in interviews. Like staying."

"That's three things."

"I'm a complex person."

"You're a simple person who uses big words to seem complex."

"That's my line."

"I'm borrowing it."

"Pay me back."

"How?"

"Help me wait. The next week is going to be terrible."

"I know. That's why I bought extra pastries."

"How many?"

"Enough for seven days. One for each day of waiting."

"That's very calculated."

"I'm a very calculated person. Now eat. You have a week of anxiety ahead of you. You'll need your strength."

We ate pasta. Drank wine. The cheap kind. The one that came in a box. Matei said it was "vintage." I said it was "box wine." He said "same thing."

After dinner, we sat on the Sofa. The Lampe buzzed. The Heizung clicked. The plant sat on the windowsill. Alive. Thriving. Judging.

"Matei."

"What?"

"What if I don't get this job?"

"Then you apply to another one."

"What if I don't get any job?"

"Then you keep trying. That's what staying means."

"That's very optimistic for 9 PM."

"I'm an optimistic person."

"You're not. You're a realist who sometimes pretends to be optimistic."

"That's the same thing."

"It's not."

"It is now. I invented it. Now sleep. You have to open the Café tomorrow."

"What if I dream about the interview?"

"Then dream about getting the job. That's called manifesting. It's very trendy."

"You don't believe in manifesting."

"I believe in you. That's the same thing."

I closed my eyes.

The Sofa was lumpy. My back hurt. But Matei was warm, and the pasta was in my stomach, and the apartment smelled like garlic and hope.

Three days later, the email came.

But that's another chapter.

Grammar Spotlight

From this chapter: "Haben Sie Fragen an uns?" (Do you have questions for us?) — using Sie (formal) instead of du (informal).

In German, formal vs. informal matters — especially in interviews.

When to use Sie (formal):

· With people you don't know

· In professional settings (interviews, meetings, emails)

· With authority figures (bosses, professors, police)

· With people older than you (unless you're close)

When to use du (informal):

· With friends and family

· With people your age in casual settings

· With children

· Online (mostly)

Key differences in verb conjugation:

Pronoun Verb (fragen) Example

du fragst Fragst du mich? (Are you asking me?)

Sie (formal) fragen Fragen Sie mich? (Are you asking me?)

Examples from this chapter (adapted):

English German (formal) German (informal)

Do you have questions? Haben Sie Fragen? Hast du Fragen?

What is your name? Wie heißen Sie? Wie heißt du?

Where do you work? Wo arbeiten Sie? Wo arbeitest du?

Why this matters: Using the wrong form in an interview can make you seem disrespectful or overly familiar. Always use Sie until invited to use du. In the novel, Yues uses Sie with the interviewers (correct) and du with Matei, Ada, Frau Schmidt (familiar).

Tip from the method: When in doubt, use Sie. It's better to be too formal than not formal enough. The other person will tell you if you can switch to du.

Write the handshake. The moment the Ausbilder says yes. Not what Yves says out loud. What he holds onto for the walk home.

Or: Full German paragraph — Yves texts Matei from outside the building after the interview. What does he write?

Shadowing Script

Interview closing — say this aloud clearly and warmly:

Vielen Dank fuer das Gespraech. Es hat mir sehr gut gefallen. — Thank you very much for the conversation. I enjoyed it very much.

Ich freue mich Auf Wiedersehen die Zusammenarbeit. — I look forward to working together.

Wann kann ich mit einer Rueckmeldung rechnen? — When can I expect to hear back?

Wann kann ich mit einer Rueckmeldung rechnen is professional, not impatient. It shows you are organised. Use it at the end of every interview.

Part Three is done. Yves has applied, been rejected, applied again, and been accepted. The Ausbildung is real. So is the German.

What You Have Learned

Technical vocabulary now in your active range: der Fachinformatiker, die Systemintegration, die Anwendungsentwicklung, konfigurieren, das Betriebssystem, die Firewall, das Netzwerk, analysieren, die Dokumentation.

Formal register: Bewerbung structure, email openings and closings, interview vocabulary, contract language.

Grammar: Konjunktiv II appearing in formal requests (Koennten Sie bitte...), passive voice in instructions (wird neu gestartet — is being restarted), infinitive constructions with zu.

IT Production Challenge

Write a short formal email in German — six sentences maximum — to your Ausbilder. Subject: you need clarification on an assigned task. Use the templates from Chapters 11 and 16. Use Sie throughout.

This is a real task. In your Ausbildung, you will write this email. Write it now.

Technical Vocabulary Self-Test

Translate without help:

1. Das Betriebssystem muss aktualisiert werden.

2. Ich habe das Problem in der Dokumentation beschrieben.

3. Die Firewall blockiert unbekannte Verbindungen.

4. Koennen Sie die Konfiguration ueberpruefen?

5. Ich habe das Ticket dem zustaendigen Kollegen weitergeleitet.

Translations: 1. The operating system needs to be updated. 2. I have described the problem in the documentation. 3. The firewall blocks unknown connections. 4. Can you check the configuration? 5. I forwarded the ticket to the responsible colleague.

If sentences 3-5 were manageable, your IT German is functional. If not, re-read Chapters 18 and 22's shadowing scripts.

Story Recall

From memory: What did the Ausbilder's feedback reveal about Yves's first weeks? What did Andreea and Matei's reconciliation require? What does Matei propose, and when?

You don't need to answer perfectly. Recall is the goal. The effort of trying to remember is what makes the memory stick.

Part Four is 85-95% German. You are living in the language now. Keep going.

Chapter Twenty-Two — Der erste Tag

Before You Read

Five words for this chapter:

der erste Tag — first day (review)

der Ausbildungsvertrag — training contract

die Probezeit — probationary period

einarbeiten — to train in / induct (separable)

das Team — team

Part Four. He got the job. Now he has to keep it.

The first day of the Ausbildung arrived like a Zug — fast, loud, and slightly terrifying.

I had slept maybe three hours. The rest of the night I spent staring at the ceiling, running through German IT vocabulary in my head. Der Server. Die Firewall. Das Passwort. Die Hölle von Excel-Tabellen.

"You're thinking too loud," Matei murmured.

"I'm practicing."

"It's 4 AM."

"The early bird gets the Ausbildung."

"The early bird gets stepped on by people who slept."

"That's not motivational."

"I'm not motivational. I'm tired. There's a Unterschied."

"Is there?"

"No. Now go back to sleep."

I didn't sleep. But I lay there, listening to him breathe, and tried not to think about all the ways I could embarrass myself.

At 6 AM, I gave up.

I made coffee. Black. No sugar. No milk. I made coffee for Matei too. Left it on the table. Wrote a note: Don't burn the milk. There is no milk. Don't burn the coffee.

"That's not funny," he said, walking into the kitchen. His hair was a mess. His eyes were half-closed. He was wearing the shirt that said I'm silently judging you in German.

"It's a little funny."

"It's 6 AM. Nothing is funny at 6 AM."

"That's not true. I'm funny at 6 AM."

"You're loud at 6 AM. There's a Unterschied."

"Same thing."

He drank his coffee. Made a face. The face that said this is terrible but I love you anyway.

"You're nervous," he said.

"Terrified."

"Good. Terror means you care."

"Or it means I'm going to throw up on my first day."

"Then throw up. And then keep going. That's what staying means."

"You're very philosophical for 6 AM."

"I'm a very philosophical person. Now eat something. You can't learn IT on an empty stomach."

"What should I eat?"

"Pastries. The apricot ones. I hid them in the freezer."

"You hid them?"

"Behind the frozen peas. You would have found them eventually."

"You know me so well."

"I know you too well. It's a curse."

I ate three pastries. Drank two coffees. Brushed my teeth twice. Checked my bag four times. Laptop? Yes. Notebook? Yes. Pen? Yes. Spare pen? Yes. Spare spare pen? Yes.

"You have five pens," Matei said.

"What if one runs out?"

"Pens don't run out that fast."

"What if four run out?"

"Then you have a backup for the backup for the backup for the backup."

"That's called planning."

"That's called paranoia. Same thing."

He walked me to the U-Bahn. The station was crowded. People in suits. People with coffee. People who looked like they knew what they were doing. I was none of those people.

"You're going to be fine," Matei said.

"You don't know that."

"I know you. That's enough."

"What if they ask me to do something I don't know how to do?"

"Then you ask for help. That's what the Ausbildung is for."

"What if they think I'm stupid?"

"Then they're wrong. And I will write them a strongly worded letter. In Romanian. They won't understand it. But they'll know they're being judged."

"You've used that line before."

"It's a good line."

"It's an okay line."

"You liked it the first time."

"I was being polite."

"You're never polite."

"I'm always polite. I'm Nigerian."

"That's not a thing."

"It is now. I invented it."

He kissed my forehead. Right there on the platform. In front of strangers. In front of a woman who smiled and a man who looked away and a child who said "Mama, warum küssen die sich?" and the mother said "Weiß nicht, schatz, frag später."

"Your train is coming," Matei said.

"I know."

"Go."

"I'm going."

"Go."

"I'm going."

I didn't go. The train arrived. The doors opened. People got on. People got off. I stood there.

"Yves."

"What?"

"Go."

I went.

The Betrieb was in Wedding.

The same neighborhood as the interview. Different building. Bigger. Greyer. The sign on the door said SecureNet Systems in the same font that wasn't Garamond. I walked in.

The receptionist was the same woman from the interview. She smiled.

"Guten Morgen, Yves. Nervös?"

"Sehr."

"Das ist normal. Komm, ich zeige dir den Weg."

She walked me down a hallway. Past offices. Past a kitchen that smelled like old coffee. Past a room full of servers that hummed like angry bees.

"Das ist dein Platz," she said.

This is your spot.

A desk. A computer. A chair that looked comfortable. A nameplate that said Yves — Azubi. I stared at it.

"That's my name," I said.

"Yes. You're expected to sit there."

"For how long?"

"Three years. Maybe more if you're slow."

"That's not funny."

"I'm not funny. I'm practical. There's a Unterschied."

She left. I sat down. The chair was comfortable. The computer was on. The screen was blank. The keyboard was covered in dust.

"You must be the new Azubi."

I turned. A man stood in the doorway. Late thirties. Bald. Glasses. A coffee mug that said I survived another meeting that could have been an email. His nameplate said Herr Weber — Ausbilder.

"Yes. I'm Yves."

"I know. I read your Bewerbung. You're the one who said 'I make good pasta.'"

"That's not a qualification."

"It should be. I love pasta."

He sat on the edge of my desk. His coffee mug was almost empty. He didn't seem to notice.

"First day. You're nervous."

"Very."

"Good. Nervous means you care. Scared means you're paying attention. There's a Unterschied."

"Is there?"

"No. But you'll learn. That's what the Ausbildung is for."

The first hour was paperwork.

Forms. Lots of forms. Forms in German. Forms in legal German. The kind of German that made my eyes cross and my soul leave my body.

"This is terrible," I said.

"This is bureaucracy," Herr Weber said. "Same thing."

"How do people do this?"

"They complain. Then they sign. Then they forget. That's the circle of life."

"That's not —"

"Sign here. And here. And here. And then initial here. And here. And here. And then write your name again. And then again. And then again."

"Why so many times?"

"Because Germany loves paperwork. It's our national sport."

"I thought football was the national sport."

"Football is for amateurs. Paperwork is for professionals."

I signed. And initialed. And wrote my name. And signed again. By the end, my hand hurt. My brain hurt. My soul hurt.

"Congratulations," Herr Weber said. "You're officially an Azubi."

"That's it?"

"That's it. Now the real work begins."

The real work was... slow.

Herr Weber showed me the server room. The servers were loud. They blinked. They hummed. They looked important.

"This is the heart of the company," he said.

"It looks like a washing machine."

"It's a server. Washing machines are for clothes. Servers are for data. There's a Unterschied."

"They sound the same."

"They don't. Washing machines are quieter. And they have more spin cycles."

"You know a lot about washing machines."

"I'm an IT guy. We know everything about everything. It's in the contract."

"There's a contract?"

"There's always a contract. You just signed it."

He showed me the network setup. The firewalls. The backup systems. The emergency protocols. I understood maybe 30%. The rest was noise.

"You'll learn," he said.

"What if I don't?"

"Then you'll be fired. And you'll have to find another Ausbildung. And you'll start over. And you'll learn then."

"That's not encouraging."

"I'm not encouraging. I'm honest. There's a Unterschied."

"Everyone keeps saying that."

"Because it keeps being true."

At noon, the other Azubi found me.

Her name was Mira. She was in her second year. She had purple hair and a nose ring and a tattoo of a raccoon on her forearm.

"You're the new one," she said.

"I'm the new one."

"You look lost."

"I am lost."

"Good. Being lost is the first step to being found. Or whatever. I saw that on a poster once."

"That's not helpful."

"I'm not helpful. I'm funny. There's a Unterschied."

"Is there?"

"No. But I brought coffee. The good kind. From the bakery around the corner."

She handed me a cup. I took a sip. It was good. Really good. Better than Frau Schmidt's. Better than the bookstore's. Better than anything I had tasted in weeks.

"This is amazing."

"I know. That's why I'm the favorite Azubi."

"I thought Herr Weber didn't have favorites."

"He doesn't. But I bring him coffee every morning. So I'm his favorite. It's called strategy."

"That's bribery."

"That's networking. Same thing."

We ate lunch together in the break room.

Mira asked questions. Where was I from? Nigeria. How long had I been in Berlin? Four months. Did I have a boyfriend? Yes. Was he cute? Yes. Was he annoying? Very. Did he make coffee? Yes. Was it good? No. Did I tell him that? No. Why not? Because he would cry.

"Men are dramatic," Mira said.

"Yes."

"Especially German men."

"He's Romanian."

"Even worse. Eastern Europeans are the most dramatic. It's the history."

"That's not —"

"It's science. I read it somewhere."

"You didn't."

"You don't know that. I could have."

She was chaotic. Loud. Unfiltered. I liked her immediately.

The afternoon was more training.

Herr Weber showed me how to configure a firewall. I watched. I took notes. I understood maybe 40%.

"You're taking too many notes," he said.

"I want to remember."

"You won't remember. You'll forget. And then you'll ask me again. And I'll explain again. And then you'll forget again. And then you'll ask again. That's how learning works."

"That's inefficient."

"That's human. There's a Unterschied."

"Is there?"

"No. But you'll remember the third time. Maybe the fourth."

At 5 PM, the day ended.

I packed my bag. Checked for my phone. Checked for my keys. Checked for my wallet. Checked for my sanity. It was missing.

"First day done," Mira said. "How do you feel?"

"Like I ran a marathon. In German."

"That's normal. It gets easier."

"When?"

"In about two years."

"That's not soon."

"That's soon enough. Now go home. Your boyfriend is probably waiting."

"How do you know?"

"Because you checked your phone seventeen times today. I counted."

"That's creepy."

"That's observant. Same thing."

I walked to the U-Bahn. The train was crowded. I stood in the corner. Stared out the window. Thought about servers and firewalls and the nameplate that said Yves — Azubi.

My phone buzzed.

Matei: How was it?

Terrible. I understood maybe 30%.

That's good.

How is 30% good?

It's not 0%. Tomorrow it will be 35%. That's progress.

That's not how math works.

It's how my math works. Come home. I bought pastries.

The good ones?

The apricot ones. And I didn't hide them. You deserve them.

That's suspicious.

I'm being supportive.

You're never supportive.

I'm always supportive. I'm Romanian.

That's not an excuse.

It's not an excuse. It's an explanation.

I walked home. The stairs were siebenunddreißig steps. The Schlüssel stuck. The door opened.

Matei was on the Sofa. Not reading. Waiting.

"You're home," he said.

"I'm home."

"How was it really?"

"Hard. Confusing. Exhausting. Also, there's a woman with purple hair who brings coffee and has a raccoon tattoo."

"That's specific."

"Her name is Mira. She's my new favorite person."

"I thought I was your favorite person."

"You're my favorite Romanian. There's a Unterschied."

"Is there?"

"No. But Mira brings better coffee than you."

"I'll work on it."

"You'd better."

He handed me a pastry. I ate it. Then another. Then another.

"You're eating all of them," he said.

"I earned them."

"You earned three pastries?"

"I earned a bakery. But I'll settle for three."

"You're impossible."

"You love me."

"Unfortunately."

He kissed me. Pastry crumbs and all.

"You're going to be good at this," he said.

"You don't know that."

"I know you. That's enough."

After dinner, we sat on the Sofa. The Lampe buzzed. The Heizung clicked. The plant sat on the windowsill. Alive. Thriving. Judging.

"Matei."

"What?"

"Thank you."

"For what?"

"For not letting me give up."

"You didn't give up. You started. That's harder."

"That's not true."

"It is. Starting is the hardest part. Everything else is just continuing."

"That's very philosophical for 8 PM."

"I'm a very philosophical person. Now eat another pastry. You have day two tomorrow."

"What if day two is worse?"

"Then day three will be better. That's how patterns work."

"That's not —"

"Eat the pastry, Yves."

I ate the pastry.

It was perfect.

I hated that it was perfect.

But I didn't hate anything else.
